Medinan; it has one hundred and seventy-six verses.

﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾

﴿O mankind,﴾ O children of Adam, ﴿He created you from a single soul,﴾ that is, He made your stock (farra'akum) from one origin, which is the soul of Adam, your father. [Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: He made your stock from one origin, which is the soul of Adam your father, and 'alam ʿataf (on what is it coordinated?)…" etc.] Ahmad said:

The omitted element was supposed in the first interpretation, where the address is general to the species, because without that supposition, His saying ﴿and from them He spread forth many men and women﴾ would be a repetition of ﴿He created you,﴾ since both express one meaning. It is not an explanation of the first clause, because it would then be coordinated with it. As for it being coordinated with the supposed element, that supposed element stands as a descriptive clarification, and the thing coordinated with it falls under the sense of explanation, so it is consistent. As for the second interpretation, repetition is not necessary in it, since the addressees of ﴿He created you﴾ are those to whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent. And His saying ﴿and from them He spread forth﴾ refers to those other than the addressed peoples among the nations, so there is no need for the supposition mentioned in the second interpretation. And Allah knows best.

If you ask: on what is His saying ﴿and created from it its mate﴾ coordinated? I answer: there are two possibilities. The first is that it is coordinated with an omitted element, as if it were said: "from a single soul which He originated or initiated, and from it He created its mate." The element was omitted because the meaning indicates it. The meaning is: He made you from a single soul having this description, namely that He originated it from dust, and created its mate Eve from one of its ribs, and ﴿spread forth from them both﴾ the two kinds of mankind, the males and the females. So He described it with a description that explains and details the manner of their creation from it. The second possibility is that it is coordinated with ﴿He created you﴾, and the address in ﴿O mankind﴾ is to those to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent.

The meaning is: He created you from the soul of Adam, since they are part of the species from which the stock came; ﴿and created from it its mother Eve﴾, and ﴿spread forth from them both many men and women﴾ other than you, from the nations that cannot be counted. If you ask: what the soundness of the composition and its eloquence require is that after the command to piety there should come what necessitates it or calls to it and urges it; so how was His creating them from a single soul, in the detail He mentioned, a cause of piety and a call to it? I answer: because that shows great power, and whoever has power over such a thing has power over everything, and among the things within His power is the punishment of the disobedient. Reflection on it leads one to fear the One who has power over it and to dread His punishment. Also, it shows the abundant blessing upon them, so they are obliged to fear Him by not being ungrateful for it and not neglecting what is incumbent upon them of thanking Him. Or he intended by piety a specific piety, namely that they fear Him regarding what relates to preserving the rights among them, so that they do not sever what they are obliged to keep joined. Thus it is said: ﴿fear your Lord, who joined you together,﴾ since He made you counterparts (sinwan) branching from one root. Regarding what is owed by some of you to others, so preserve it and do not neglect it. This meaning agrees with the meanings of the surah.

It has been read: "wa-khaliqun minhā zawjahā" and "wa-bathth minhumā," with the active participle form, as a predicate of an omitted subject whose supposition is: "and He is the Creator." The ta' was assimilated into the sin in ﴿tasā'alūna﴾ ("you ask one another"). It has also been read ﴿tas'alūna﴾ with the second ta' dropped, meaning that some of you ask others by Allah and by the womb (kinship). He says: "I ask you by Allah and by kinship," as a plea for compassion. Or ﴿tas'alūna﴾ means that you ask others by Allah and by kinship. It is said that ﴿tafā'alūna﴾ stands in place of ﴿taf'alūna﴾ for the sense of plurality, like your saying: "I saw the crescent and we saw it together." The reading of the one who read "tasallūna bihi," with or without hamza, supports this.

It has been read ﴿wal-arḥāma﴾ with the three vowels. The accusative has two possibilities: either it is "and fear Allah and the wombs," or it is coordinated with the place of the prepositional phrase, like your saying: "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmran." The reading of Ibn Masʿud supports this: "nas'alūna bihi wa-bi-l-arḥām" [you ask by Him and by the wombs]. The genitive is coordination of a noun on a pronoun, and this is not correct, because an attached pronoun is attached like its noun, and the prepositional phrase is like one thing. So in your saying "I passed by him and Zayd" and "this is his boy and Zayd," the attachment is very strong; when the attachment is strengthened by its repetition, it resembles coordination within a single word, so it is not permitted, and it is necessary to repeat the governing element, as in your saying: "I passed by him and by Zayd" and "this is his boy and the boy of Zayd." Do you not see that your saying "I saw you and Zayd" and "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr" is correct, because the attachment is not strong, as it is not repeated? It has been strained to justify this reading by claiming that it is on the supposition of repeating the preposition and its counterpart:

*"Fa-mā bika wal-ayyāmi min ʿajab"*

[So now you have come closer to satirize us and revile us... so go, what is it to you and the days? There is no wonder in that.]

This is by al-Aʿsha. It is also said to be by ʿAmr ibn Maʿdikarib, and it is also said to be by Khafaf ibn Nadba, and it is also said to be by ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas. It is said: "qaraba al-faras taqrīban" means he ran swiftly. He says: "Today you have drawn near, running swiftly to satirize us after your slowness in it." It is narrated as "qad bitta," meaning you have become one who satirizes us. So go on your path, for it is the mark of the base and the habit of the days, so there is no wonder in it; it is a matter of abandonment and parting. "Wal-ayyām" is coordinated with the pronoun in the genitive, and this is evidence of its permissibility without repeating the preposition, though the majority prohibit it.

The nominative has the reading that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, as if it were said: "and the wombs are likewise," meaning "and the wombs are among what is to be feared," or "and the wombs are among what is asked by." The meaning is that they used to acknowledge that they had a Creator, and they used to ask one another by the mention of Allah and by kinship, so it was said to them: "fear Allah who created you, fear the One by whom you appeal to one another, and fear the wombs, so that you do not sever them." Or: "fear Allah by whose remembrance we show compassion to one another, and by the remembrance of kinship." When He, the Mighty and Majestic, joined the wombs with His name, He announced that maintaining them has a high station with Him, as He said: ﴿that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents.﴾

From al-Hasan: "If someone asks you by Allah, give him; and if someone asks you by kinship, give him." And "the womb has a hook at the Throne" (ḥujna ʿinda al-ʿarsh). [Commentary on "ḥujna": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-ḥajan with a vowel on the h means crookedness; a hawk with crooked talons is aḥjan; and the ḥujna of a spindle, with a dammah, is the bent part at its head. Also in it: "I bent the thing and it bent," i.e., I turned it and it turned; and al-taʿqīf is bending.] Its meaning is what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The womb is suspended from the Throne; when one who maintains it comes to it, it is pleased with him and speaks to him, and when one who severs it comes, it veils itself from him." [Ishaq ibn Rahawayh reported it: Jarir informed us from Qabus from his father from him. al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related it through this route too.]

Ibn ʿUyayna was asked about the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Choose well for your seed (nutaf)." [Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and al-Daraqutni related it from the hadith of Hisham from his father from ʿAʾisha. Ibn Tahir said: no trustworthy narrator related it from Hisham. Ibn ʿAdi related it through ʿIsa ibn Maymun, one of the weak narrators, from al-Qasim from ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her. Tammam related it in his Fawāʾid, and Abu Nuʿaym in al-Ḥilya, from the narration of al-Zuhri from Anas, and in it is ʿAbd al-ʿAzim ibn Ibrahim al-Salami, who is unknown. Ibn ʿAdi related it from a hadith of ʿUmar as a mawquf (ending with a Companion), and in it is Sulayman ibn ʿAṭāʾ, who is weak. Ibn Tahir said: Ishaq ibn al-Ghaydh related it from ʿAbd al-Majid from Ibn Jurayj from ʿAṭāʾ, and once he said: from Ibn ʿAbbas, and once he said: from ʿAʾisha. This is the best of its routes, if the chain up to Ishaq is strong. Ibn Abi Hatim said on the authority of his father: this hadith is weak in all its routes.]

He said: "He says: to your children." That means placing one's child in lawful union. Have you not heard His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and fear Allah, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾? The first part of its maintenance is that he chooses for him a lawful place, so he does not sever his kinship or his lineage, for "the stone is for the adulterer" (al-ʿāhir al-ḥajar). Then he chooses soundness and avoids corruption (al-daʿra, meaning corruption) [the commentary notes it may be al-daʿra with a rāʾ instead of the wāw; in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-daʿar with a vowel on the d means corruption], and does not place him in a bad position, following his desire and his whim without guidance from Allah.

(الْيَتامى) ﴿the orphans﴾ are those whose fathers have died, so that they are left alone without them. The root *yatm* means being alone and isolated. From it comes *al-ramlah al-yatimah* (the lone sand-dune) and *al-durrah al-yatimah* (the unique pearl). It is said that *yatm* among humans comes from the father's side, and among animals from the mother's side.

If you ask: how is *yatim*, which follows the pattern *fa'il* like *marid*, made plural as *yatama*? I answer: there are two possibilities. It may be pluralized as *yutma*, like *asra* (captives), because orphanhood belongs to the category of calamities and afflictions. Then *fu'la* is pluralized as *fa'ala*, as in *asara* (captives, from *asra*). It is also permissible to pluralize it as *fa'a'il*, because *yatim* functions like nouns such as *sahib* and *faris*, so one says *yata'im*, and then *yatama* by metathesis (*qalb*). The proper meaning of this noun is that it applies to young children. [[Mahmud said: "Either *al-yatama* is intended to mean the young children... etc." Ahmad said: The first interpretation is strengthened by His words after the verses, ﴿Test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property﴾, which shows that the first verse urges preserving their wealth for them so that it may be returned when they reach maturity and sound judgment, and the second urges the actual handing over when maturity and sound judgment are attained. It is also strengthened by His words after the first verse, ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ and ﴿Do not devour their property along with your own﴾. All of this is discipline for the guardian as long as the property is in his hand and the orphan is under his care. On the other interpretation, the two verses have one meaning, namely the command to actually hand over the property, and the repetition is avoided by considering that the first clause is like the second clause, clarifying the condition for handing over, namely maturity and the perception of sound judgment. And God knows best.]] It may also be applied to adults, because the meaning of being alone away from their fathers remains. However, it has become common to call them *yatama* before they reach the status of men. When they become independent of a guardian and a caretaker, and stand on their own to take care of others and look after them, this name ceases to apply to them. The Quraysh used to say of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The orphan of Abu Talib," either by analogy or as a description of the state he was in as a young child raised in the care of his uncle, to belittle him. As for his (ﷺ) saying: "There is no orphanhood after reaching puberty" [[Abu Dawud related it from Ali, and its chain is good, because it has another route from Ali which 'Abd al-Razzaq also related from al-Thawri from Juwaybir as a statement of Ali. Al-'Uqayli preferred it. 'Abd al-Karim ibn Abi al-Makhariq followed Juwaybir in it from al-Dahhak, and 'Abd al-Karim is also abandoned. It has another route in al-Tabarani's al-Awsat in the biography of Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Sufi, from the narration of 'Alqamah ibn Qays from Ali. Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani related it through Dhayyal ibn 'Ubayd ibn Hanzalah ibn Jadhim ibn Hanifah, who said: I heard my grandfather Hanzalah say: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say such-and-such. There is also a report on the subject from Anas in al-Bazzar, which contains Murthid ibn 'Abd al-Malik, who is weak. From Jabir in 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tayalisi and Ibn Ya'la through Haram ibn 'Uthman, who is abandoned. And through Sa'id ibn al-Marzuban from Yazid al-Faqir from Jabir, and Sa'id is extremely weak.]], it is merely a teaching of the Law, not of language. That is, when he reaches puberty, the rulings for children no longer apply to him. If you ask: what is the meaning of His words ﴿and give the orphans their property﴾? I answer:

It may be that *al-yatama* refers to young children, and giving them their property means that the guardians, the executors, the rulers and the wicked judges should not covet it, and should withhold their rapacious hands from it, so that when the orphans reach maturity it is returned to them intact and not diminished. Or it may be that *al-yatama* refers to adults, called orphans by analogy or because they are recently past childhood, as a pregnant she-camel is called *ushara* after giving birth. Moreover, this contains an indication that handing over their property should not be delayed beyond the age of puberty, nor should they be put off if sound judgment is perceived in them, and that it should be given to them before the name of orphan and child ceases to apply to them. It is said:

It concerns a man from the tribe of Ghatafan who had a great deal of property belonging to his orphaned nephew. When the nephew reached maturity he demanded his property, but his uncle refused. They brought the case before the Prophet (ﷺ). [[al-Tha'labi related it from Muqatil and al-Kalbi, and its chain to them is mentioned at the beginning of the book.]] Then this was revealed. When the uncle heard it he said: "We obey God and we obey the Messenger. We seek refuge in God from the great sin." He then handed over his property to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul and obeys his Lord, thus will he enter his house," meaning his Paradise. When he died, they found that he had spent his property in the way of God. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The reward is established, the reward is established, and the burden remains." They said: "O Messenger of God, we know that the reward is established, but how does the burden remain when he spent it in the way of God?" He said: "The reward of the boy is established, and the burden remains upon his father."

﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾: do not substitute the unlawful, which is the property of orphans, with the lawful, which is your own property and the gains permitted to you and God's provision scattered on the earth, so that you consume it in its place. Or: do not substitute the bad matter, which is the misappropriation of orphans' property, with the good matter, which is preserving it and abstaining from it. [[His words "and abstaining from it" perhaps should be "abstaining from them." (ʿAyn)]] The form *tafa''ala* in the sense of *istaf'ala* is not rare: for example, *ta'jil* meaning *isti'jal* (hastening), and *ta'akhkhur* meaning *isti'khar* (delaying). Dhu al-Rummah said:

"O the nobility of the dwellers who departed from the abode, and of the successor who was replaced!"

[[By Dhu al-Rummah. *Al-sakan*, with a sukun, means the inhabitants of the abode; it is a collective noun for *sakin*, as *rakb* is for *rakib* and *sahb* for *sahib*. In calling upon their nobility there is an expression of wonder at its abundance, that is: O nobility of the owners of the abode who journeyed away from it, and O baseness of the successor who was substituted, in the form of the passive participle in both cases, meaning what the abode succeeded to and what it replaced after them of wild animals. It is also said: the reference is to those who do not keep their promises, so that *tabaddul* means *istibdal* (exchange). The successor, *al-mustakhlaf*, is understood with an implied omitted noun indicated by the context.]]

He meant: O baseness of what the abode succeeded to and replaced. It is also said that it means giving someone a bad thing and taking a good thing. According to al-Suddi, it means substituting a lean sheep for a fat one. This is not really an exchange but a substitution, unless one were to show generosity to a friend by taking from him a lean sheep in place of a fat one from the orphan's property.

﴿And do not devour their property along with your own﴾: and do not combine it with your property. Its literal sense is: do not add it to your property. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: do not add it to your property..." Ahmad said: The people of rhetoric say that when a prohibition has degrees, the path of eloquence is to forbid the lowest degree in order to point to the higher one, as in His words, ﴿So do not say to them "Uff"﴾. If you apply this principle to this verse, you will find at first sight that it contradicts it, since the highest degree of consuming the orphan's property in the prohibition is that one consumes it while being rich without need of it, and the lowest is that one consumes it while poor and in need of it. Thus the principle would require that the prohibition be directed at one who is poor and in need of the property, so that the prohibition of the rich would follow a fortiori. Then a preliminary is necessary to clarify the benefit of specifying the highest case for prohibition in this verse. We say: the most eloquent speech is that which has multiple benefits. There is no doubt that the prohibition of the lower case, although it implies the prohibition of the higher, has another noble benefit that is not derived from the prohibition of the lower: whenever the forbidden thing is more ugly, the soul recoils from it more and the motive to it is weaker. There is no doubt that it is firmly established in souls that consuming an orphan's property while being rich without need of it is the ugliest form of consumption. It is therefore specified in the prohibition as a rebuke of the one who falls into it, so that when his aversion to consuming the orphan's property in this shameful form is firmly established, that leads him to refrain from consuming it in any form. This contains training of the addressee to be averse to what is forbidden. This benefit would hardly be obtained if the prohibition were specified for consuming it while poor, because in that case natures do not help one to avoid it as they help in the first case. The specification of consumption supports this meaning, although any taking of an orphan's property is forbidden in whatever way, whether by saving it, by mixing, by spending it on sexual pleasure for example, or otherwise. But the wisdom of specifying the prohibition to consumption is that the Arabs used to be ashamed of excessive eating, and regarded a big belly as a characteristic of animals, and blamed whoever made it his habit. This is not so with other pleasures, for they sometimes boast of excessive sexual intercourse and regard it as an adornment of worldly life. Since eating was for them the most ugly of pleasures, the prohibition was specified for it, so that when the soul recoils from it by its accustomed nature, that leads it to recoil from spending an orphan's property on other pleasures or anything else, whether eating or otherwise. A similar case of specifying the prohibition to the highest case is His words, ﴿Do not devour usury, doubled and redoubled﴾, where this form is singled out because the nature is more helped to refrain from it. In contrast to this view on prohibition there is another view on command: sometimes the command specifies the lower form to point to the higher, and sometimes it specifies the higher form for the same kind of benefit of training. Do you not see His words after some verses of this surah: ﴿And when the division takes place, if the relatives, orphans and needy are present, then provide for them...﴾ How He specified the case of their presence, although the higher case relative to their absence? That is because God, exalted is He, knew the avarice of souls for wealth. Had He commanded the aid of relatives and orphans from inherited property without mentioning their presence at the division, souls would not have been moved toward this good as they are moved when they are present. By contrast, when they are present the soul softens and recoils from taking a large share while a close relative is present, deprived and not helped or assisted. So when it is commanded to give aid in that case, it becomes easy for it to obey the command, and it comes to accord with obedience to nature. Then it is trained by that to aid a relative absolutely, whether present or absent. The observance of this and similar benefits is hardly found except in the Glorious Book, and it is not discovered except by the skilled, the perceptive, the assisted by success. We ask God to make us travel in this way. So take this principle as a foundation: if the prohibition specifies the lower, it is for the benefit of pointing to the higher; if it specifies the higher, it is for the benefit of training to refrain from ugliness in general, from refraining from the uglier. Consider the same in the case of command. And God is the Granter of success.]] in spending, so that you do not mix your property with theirs out of indifference to what is not lawful for you, and equating it with the lawful.

If you ask: the prohibition was already imposed on them to consume the orphans' property alone and together with their own, so why was the prohibition on consuming it together with their own mentioned? I answer: because when they were independent of the orphans' property through the lawful wealth God had given them, and yet still coveted it, the ugliness was greater and the blame more deserved. Also, because they used to do exactly that, so God rebuked them for their deed and reported it to them, so that it would deter them more.

*Al-hub* means a great sin. From it is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Indeed, the divorce of Umm Ayyub is a *huob*." [[Abu Dawud related it in al-Marasil, and Ibrahim al-Harbi in al-Gharib, from the narration of Anas ibn Sirin, who said: It reached me that Abu Ayyub wanted to divorce Umm Ayyub, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "O Abu Ayyub, indeed the divorce of Umm Ayyub is a *huob*." Yahya al-Hammani related it in his Musnad, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat through him, who said: Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us from Wasil from Muhammad ibn Sirin from Ibn 'Abbas, and added: Ibn Sirin said: *al-hub* is sin. Al-Hakim related from the narration of 'Ali ibn 'Asim from Humayd from Anas, who said: There was a dispute between Abu Talhah and Umm Sulaym. He wanted to divorce her. This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the divorce of Umm Sulaym is a *huob*."]] So it is as if it were said: indeed it was a great and grave sin.

Al-Hasan read *huban* with a fatha on the *ha'*, which is the verbal noun of *haba*, *hawban*. It is also read *haban*. The parallel of *al-hawb* and *al-hab* is like *al-qawl* and *al-qal*, and *al-tard* and *al-tard*.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 3:

When the verse about orphans was revealed, and about what it means to consume their property, which is a great sin (ḥawb kabīr), the guardians feared that they would incur sin by failing to act justly toward the orphans' rights, and they began to scrupulously avoid their guardianship. [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "When the verse of the orphans was revealed, the guardians feared..." etc. Ahmad said: It is established that the principle and creed of the al-Qadariyya (the Qadariyya, an early school that affirmed human power over action) is that a single major sin (kabīra) necessitates the servant's eternal abiding in punishment even if he is a monotheist, as long as he does not repent from it. Therefore they say that repentance from some sins does not benefit when persisting in others, because by one major sin he has equated himself with the disbeliever in eternal abiding in punishment, and neither his monotheism nor any of his deeds benefits him. This is their corrupt creed, which al-Zamakhshari wishes to impose on the interpretation of the verse, so beware of it. As for the Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna), they say: If the servant repents from some sins, the address requiring repentance from the rest remains directed at him, as if he has performed some obligations and neglected others. Repentance thus erases what he repented of, by God's permission and His promise, and he remains liable for what he did not repent of. If the interpretation of the verse is that they were addressed to be scrupulous regarding women's rights and to repent of wronging them just as they repented of injustice toward orphans, then the matter in that case is governed by the principles of the Sunna that we have explained. And God is the Guardian of success.]] Thus the sin would be incurred by them through neglect of equity in the rights of orphans, and so they were scrupulous about their guardianship. A man among them might have under him ten wives, or eight, or six, and he would not fulfil their rights or act justly among them. So it was said to them:

﴿If you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, and you are scrupulous about them, then fear also failing to act justly among women.﴾ They therefore said: "The number of those married." For whoever is scrupulous about a sin, or repents of it, while committing its like, is neither scrupulous nor repentant, because it is only obligatory to be scrupulous about a sin and to repent of it because of its ugliness, and ugliness is present in every sin. And it was said:

They were not scrupulous about adultery, [[Its speech continues: Al-Zamakhshari said: "And it was said: They were not scrupulous about adultery, while they were scrupulous about the guardianship of orphans..." etc. Ahmad said:

This interpretation which he has put forward is worthy of precedence and is the more apparent. With it the verse is an explanation of the ruling on orphans, a warning against becoming entangled in wronging them, and a command to exercise caution. There is latitude in marrying others up to four, and the clearest witness that this is what is meant is...]] while they were scrupulous about the guardianship of orphans. So it was said: "If you fear injustice toward orphans, then fear adultery, and marry what is lawful to you of women, and do not hover around what is forbidden." And it was said:

A man would find an orphan girl who had property and beauty, or he would be her guardian, and he would marry her, out of possessiveness toward her, so that ten of them would gather with him. He would fear, because of their weakness and the absence of anyone to defend them, that he would wrong them in their rights and neglect what is due to them. So it was said to them: ﴿If you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphan women, then marry from other women what is good for you.﴾ The female orphans are called yatāmā just as the males are called yatāmā, and it is the plural of yatīma by inversion (qalb), as in the saying "ayāmā," whereas the original form is "ayā’im" and "yatā’im."

Al-Nakha'i read ﴿tuqsiṭū﴾ with a fatḥa on the tā’, so that lā is extra, as it is extra in ﴿li-allā yaʿlama﴾. He means: "And if you fear that you will act unjustly, then [marry] what is good, what is lawful to you of women," because among them are those who are forbidden, such as those mentioned in the verse of prohibition. It was also said that mā here is used with reference to the attribute, and because female rational beings are treated like non-rational beings. From this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾. ﴿Two, three, or four﴾ are indeclinable forms derived from repeated numbers. They are declined only because they combine two causes of diptotic inflection: their derivation from their original forms, and their derivation from repetition. They are indefinite nouns which may be made definite by the definite article. You say: "So-and-so marries two, three, or four." Their position is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of what is good, and the meaning is: "Marry the good women, each of you a number of this count: two each, three each, and four each." If you ask: "What permits the one who marries in a group to combine two, three, or four, so what is the point of the repetition in mathnā, thulāth, and rubāʿ?" I reply: The address is to all, so the repetition was necessary so that every marrying man who wishes to combine may attain whatever number he was permitted, just as you say to a group: "Divide this property, which is a thousand dirhams, two dirhams each, three each, and four each." If it were stated singly, it would have no meaning. If you ask: "Why does the conjunction come with waw and not with aw (or)?" I reply: Just as it came with waw in the example that I have set out for you. If you were to say: "Divide this property two dirhams each, or three each, or four each," you would be informing them that they may divide it only according to one of the kinds of this division, and they may not combine among them, making some of the share in pairs, some in threes, and some in fours. The meaning of permitting a combination of the kinds of division, indicated by the waw, has gone. Its clarification is: the waw indicates the permission for those who wish to marry the women to take them in combination, whether they choose to differ in those numbers or to agree on them, while what lies beyond that is forbidden to them.

Ibrahim read "wa-thulth wa-rubʿ" (with shortening of thalāth and rubāʿ). ﴿If you fear that you will not act justly﴾ among these numbers, just as you feared failing to act justly in what exceeds them, ﴿then one﴾: so keep to one, or choose one, and abandon plurality altogether, for the whole matter revolves around justice. Wherever you find justice, you must adhere to it. It is also read as "wāḥidatan" in the nominative, meaning: "Then the sufficient one is one," or "then sufficing is one," or "then what is enough for you is one." ﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾ equates in ease and facility the single free woman with concubines, without restriction or fixing of a number. By my life, they are less burdensome, less contentious, and lighter in expense than the wives. Whether you have many of them or few, whether you act justly in dividing your time among them or do not, whether you withdraw from them or do not withdraw (in intercourse), it does not matter to you. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read: "from what your right hands possess" (mā malakat). "That" (dhālika) refers to choosing one and to concubinage. ﴿That is nearer to your not being unjust﴾: nearer than that you not incline, from the expression "ʿāla al-mīzān ʿawlan," meaning the scale tilted, and "mīzān Fulān ʿāʾil" (his scale is tilted), and "ʿāla al-ḥākim fī ḥukmihi" (the judge was unjust in his judgment) when he acted unjustly. It is reported that a Bedouin was judged against by a judge, and he said to him: "Do you act unjustly against me?" It has also been narrated that ʿĀ'isha, may God be pleased with her, related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "ألا تعولوا" means "that you not act unjustly." [[Ibn Hibban, Ibrahim al-Harbi, al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, and others narrated it from the report of ʿUmar ibn Muḥammad ibn Zayd from Hisham from his father, from her. Ibn Abi Hatim said: The correct version is that it is a statement of a Companion (mawqūf).]] As for what is related from al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him, that he explained ﴿an lā taʿūlū﴾ as "that your dependents not increase," its reasoning is that it be taken from your saying: "ʿāla al-rajul ʿiyālahu yaʿūluhum," like their saying "māna yamūnuhum," meaning he spent on them, because whoever has many dependents is obliged to support them, and in that there is what makes it difficult for him to observe the limits of earning, the limits of scrupulousness, the earning of a lawful livelihood, and good provision. Speech of this kind from the leading scholars, the imams of knowledge, and the heads of the mujtahids, deserves to be interpreted as correct and sound, and one should not suppose that "taʿīlū" was altered to "taʿūlū." It has been narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him: "Do not think ill of a word that has come from the mouth of your brother when you can find for it a good interpretation." [[Al-Muhamili narrated it: Ziyad ibn Ayyub told us: Muhammad ibn Yazid told us, from Nafi', from Ibn ʿUmar, from Sulayman, that ʿAbda said: ʿUmar said, and he mentioned it. Its isnad is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ). Al-Juhari narrated it in his Mashyakha, and al-Asbahani in al-Targhib, in a lengthy story whose beginning is from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb set down for the people eighteen words, all of them wisdom," and he mentioned it among them. There is weakness in the isnad. Al-Bayhaqi narrated in Shuʿab al-Imān from another route from him, who said: "One of my brothers among the Companions wrote to me: Place your brother's matter upon its best meaning..." (a hadith), also a mawqūf report.]] And it is sufficient, as evidence that he was of high standing and of wide reach in the science of Arabic speech, that he would not be unaware of such a matter, that our book named after "Shāfī al-ʿIyy min Kalām al-Shāfiʿī" is a witness. But scholars have their own avenues and methods, so in explaining this word he followed the method of allusions (kināyāt). If you say: "How can the dependents of one who takes concubines be few, when concubines have the same liabilities as wives?" I reply: It is not so, because the purpose of marriage is procreation and reproduction, unlike concubinage. For this reason it is permissible to practise withdrawal (ʿazl) from concubines without their permission. Concubinage was therefore a likely cause of fewer children compared to marriage, just as marrying one woman compares to marrying four. Ṭāwūs read: "an lā tuʿīlū," from "aʿāla al-rajul" when his dependents increased. This reading supports al-Shafiʿi's interpretation, may God have mercy on him, in the meaning he intended.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 4:

ṣadaqātihinna (ṣaduqātihinna): their dowries (mahr). In the ḥadīth of Shurayḥ: Ibn ʿAbbās ruled for her in favour of the ṣadaqa (dowry). It has been read ṣaduqātihinna, with a fatḥa on the ṣād and a sukūn on the dāl, as a lightened form of ṣadaqātihinna. Ṣadaqātihinna with a ḍamma on the ṣād and a sukūn on the dāl is the plural of ṣadaqa, on the pattern of ghurfa. It has also been read ṣadaqatihinna, with a ḍamma on both the ṣād and the dāl, in the singular, which is a heavier form of ṣadaqa, as in your saying, in ẓulma (ẓulmah) → ẓulma, niḥla (niḥlah) min naḥlihi kadhā, when he gives him something and bestows it upon him out of a good disposition of his soul: niḥla and niḥlan. From this is the ḥadīth of Abū Bakr (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu): "I had indeed made you a gift (naḥḥaltuka) of the produce of twenty wasqs at al-ʿĀliya." [Reported by Mālik with a sound chain, more complete than this.]

Its being in the accusative is as a verbal noun (maṣdar) [Maḥmūd said: "niḥlah is in the accusative as a verbal noun, since it carries the sense of giving (īttāʾ)... etc." Aḥmad said: this whole section is excellent, but in the phrase where the pronoun in minhu is made masculine with reference to the dowry, and then he compares it with His saying "fa-aṣṣaddaqa wa-akun mina al-ṣāliḥīn", there is a point: what is observed there is the original form, namely the absence of the fāʾ and the jazm, and the assumption of what is the original, and giving it the ruling of what exists is no novelty. This is not the case with the singular of the implied dowry, since it is not the original form of the speech; rather the original is the plural. As for the singular, it may come in such a case by way of abbreviation, dispensing with the plural through the genitive construction. It is not an objection that they have observed what is not original in His saying: "It appeared to me that I am not one who overtakes what has passed, nor one who precedes anything when it is coming," because the entry of the bāʾ, though not original, has become firmly established in this position and its occurrence has become frequent, so that it is as if its original place were in the predicate. And God knows best. The matter in this is close.] because niḥlah and ītāʾ (giving) carry the same meaning as iʿṭāʾ (giving), so it is as if it were said: "Give the women their dowries as a gift (niḥlatan)," that is, give them their dowries out of your own good dispositions; or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the addressees, that is, "give them their dowries as givers of gifts, with pleased souls in giving," or as a state of the dowries, that is, "a gift given out of good souls." It has been said: niḥlatan from God is a gift from Him and a favour bestowed upon them by Him. It has been said: al-niḥlah means the religion (milla), and "the religion of Islam is the best of religions." And "so-and-so adopts (yantaḥilu) such-and-such": that is, he professes it as his religion. The meaning is: give them their dowries as a religious duty (diyāna), as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). It may also be a circumstantial state of the dowries, that is, a religion God has prescribed and enjoined. The address is to the husbands. It has been said: the address is to the guardians, because they used to take their daughters' dowries, and they would say, "Congratulations to you on the al-nāfija," meaning for whoever has a daughter born to him: "she will take her dowry and thereby inflate (tanfajū) your wealth," that is, magnify it. The pronoun in minhu functions as a demonstrative, as if it were said: "from some of that," just as God, exalted is He, said: "Say: shall I inform you of something better than that?" after mentioning the desires. Among the arguments heard from the mouths of the Arabs is what is reported from Ruʾba, that he was asked about his saying:

"As if on the skin is the spreading of the leprosy-white (tawlīʿ al-bahaq)"

[The explanation of this witness has passed on p. 149 of this part, so consult it if you wish.] (Its corrector's note.)

He said: "I meant, as if that." Or it refers to what has the sense of the dowries, which is the ṣadāq, for if you said, "And give the women their ṣadāq," you would not have altered the meaning. So it is like His saying: "fa-aṣṣaddaqa wa-akun mina al-ṣāliḥīn," as if it were said: "I shall give charity." Nafsan is a specification (tamyīz), and its being singular is because the purpose is to state the genus, and the singular indicates it. The meaning: if they give you some of the dowry, and their souls turn away from it pleasantly, not with reluctance, being compelled to the gift by the harshness of your characters and the badness of your dealings, then "eat it" (fa-kulūhu), that is, spend it. They said: if she gives it to him and then asks him for it back after the gift, it is known that her soul was not pleased with it. From al-Shaʿbī: a man came with his wife to Shurayḥ regarding a gift she had given him, and she was asking to have it returned. Shurayḥ said: "Return it to her." The man said: "Has God not said: 'if they are pleased (fa-in ṭibna) for you'?" He said: "If her soul had been pleased with it, she would not have taken it back." And from him: "Let her retract what she gave, and I will not let her retract, for they are deceived." It is related that a man of the family of Muʿayṭ was given by his wife a thousand dinars as a dowry which she owed him; he remained a month and then divorced her, and she sued him before ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. The man said: "She gave it to me happy, her soul being pleased with it." ʿAbd al-Malik said: "Then where is the following verse: 'so do not take from it anything'? Return it to her." From ʿUmar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) that he wrote to his judges: "Women give out of desire and out of fear; so whatever woman gives and then wishes to retract, that is hers." [Reported by Ibn Abī Shayba and ʿAbd al-Razzāq through Muḥammad ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Thaqafī, who said ʿUmar wrote something similar.] From Ibn ʿAbbās: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about this verse and said: "If she graciously gives her husband the gift, willingly and not under compulsion, no authority shall judge against you concerning it, and God will not hold you accountable for it in the Hereafter." [Reported by al-Thaʿlabī and al-Wāḥidī in al-Awsaṭ through the narration of Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās.] It is also related that some people used to feel it sinful for any of them to take back anything of what he had given to his wife, so God, exalted is He, said: if one woman's soul is pleased, without compulsion or deceit, then "eat it, wholesome and agreeable." The verse indicates the narrowness of the path in this matter and the obligation of caution, since He made the condition rest on the pleasure of the soul, saying "if they are pleased," and did not say "if they give or are generous," informing that what is observed is that her soul turns away from the given thing willingly. It has been said: "if they are pleased with you concerning a part of it," and He did not say "concerning it," urging them to reduce what is given. From al-Layth ibn Saʿd: her giving of a gift is not permissible except for a small amount. From al-Awzāʿī: her giving is not permissible until she bears a child or remains in her husband's house for a year.

It is also possible that the masculine pronoun refers to the single dowry, so that it covers part of it; whereas if it were feminine it would cover the whole dowry as a gift, since some of the dowries are one or more of them. Al-hanīʾ and al-marīʾ are two adjectives from hanuʾa al-ṭaʿām and marua, when food is smooth, without any bitterness in it. It has been said: al-hanīʾ is what the eater finds pleasant, and al-marīʾ is what has a praiseworthy outcome. It has also been said that it is what goes down smoothly along its course. And the gullet from the throat to the stomach's mouth is called al-marīʾ because food passes smoothly through it, and that is its being smooth-flowing. Both are descriptions of the verbal noun, that is, "eat a pleasant, agreeable eating," or a circumstantial state of the pronoun, that is, "eat it while it is pleasant and agreeable." It may also be pausing at fakulūhu and beginning with marīʾan as an invocation, and [treating them as] two adjectives placed in the position of two verbal nouns, as if it were said: "hanaʾan, marʾan." This is an expression of permissibility, emphasis on permission, and removal of any blame.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 5:

"As-sufaha'" (the foolish): those who squander their wealth, spending it on what is not fitting, and who have no ability to manage it, to make it grow, or to dispose of it properly. The address is to the guardians (awliya'), and He attributed the wealth to them [[Mahmud said: "The meaning is the wealth of the foolish, and He attributed it to the guardians..." Ahmad said: What supports this meaning is that when He commanded providing for the near relatives by way of kindness, He said: "and provide for them from it," because what is given to them comes from the core of the wealth. And God knows best.]] because it is of the kind by which people sustain their livelihoods, just as He said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ and ﴿from what your right hands possess of your believing slave girls﴾. The evidence that the address is to the guardians regarding the wealth of orphans is His saying: ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them﴾. ﴿God has made for you a means of support (qiyam)﴾, meaning by which you stand upright and are sustained. If you were to waste it, you would be ruined; so it is in itself your support and your sustenance. It is also read as "qiyman" (qiyam), with the same meaning, just as "awadhan" comes with the meaning of "iyadhan." 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar read "qiwaman" with a waw. The qiwam (standing support) of a thing is that by which it is sustained, as when you say: "He is the mainstay of the matter, by which it is held together."

The predecessors (al-salaf) used to say: "Wealth is the believer's weapon," and: "I would rather leave what God will not hold me accountable for than need to depend on people." It is related from Sufyan, who had merchandise that he turned over: "Were it not for it, the sons of al-'Abbas would have wiped their hands on me." [[His saying "the sons of al-'Abbas would have wiped their hands on me": in al-Sihah: "al-mandil" is well known; one says from it: "tasandaltu bi'l-mandil" and "tamandaltu."(gh)]] It is also related from another, when it was said to him that it brings you closer to the world: "If it has brought me closer to the world, it has indeed preserved me from it." They used to say: "Trade and earn, for you are in a time when, if one of you is in need, the first thing he consumes is his religion." They would sometimes see a man at a funeral and say to him: "Go to your shop."

﴿and provide for them from it﴾: make it a place for their provision, by trading in it and seeking profit, so that their maintenance comes from the profits and not from the core of the wealth, lest spending consume it. It was also said: this is a command to everyone not to hand over their wealth to any of the foolish, whether a relative or a stranger, man or woman, whom one knows would place it where it is not fitting and would ruin it. ﴿a kind word﴾: Ibn Jurayj said: a pleasant promise, that if you become sound and rightly guided, we will hand over your wealth to you. It is related from 'Ata': "If you profit, I will give you (your share); and if I gain in my raid, I will set aside a portion for you." It was also said: if he is not someone whose maintenance is obligatory upon you, say: "May God grant us and you well-being; may God bless you." Everything that the soul finds comfort in and loves for its goodness, whether by reason or by sacred law, whether in word or deed, is ma'ruf (what is known and recognized as good). And what you reject and recoil from because of its ugliness is munkar (what is denied and disapproved).

**And test the orphans** (wa-btalu al-yatama): **test their intellects** (wa-ikhtabiru 'uqulahum) **and examine their circumstances** (wa-dhawwaqu ahwalahum). [Mahmud said: "Its meaning is test their circumstances... etc." Ahmad said: Testing in this sense is the position of Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, except that according to him it does not occur except after puberty, and nothing of their property is handed over before it. Likewise is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and his other opinion is like the position of Abu Hanifa, except that there is a difference of view on its form before puberty, in two ways: one is that the property is handed over to him and he conducts contracts himself like an adult, and the other is that his duty is to bargain and to fix the price, and when the matter reaches the contract, the guardian conducts it instead of him and the boy hands over the price. As for maturity (rushd), the criterion according to Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, is that he safeguards his property and develops it, even if he is morally corrupt (fasiq) in his condition. According to al-Shafi'i, the criterion is soundness of religion and property together. Our purpose now is to show the way Malik's position is applied to this verse, and Allah is the One sought for help. As for his prohibition of handing over before puberty, although the apparent meaning of the verse is that handing over is before it, it is because he made puberty and the perception of maturity an end-point (ghayah) of the handing over, and an end-point is necessarily later than what it limits, so it is necessarily that the handing over occurs before it. For this subtle point Abu Hanifa affirmed it before puberty, and Allah knows best. So, on making the combination of puberty and perceived maturity the end-point, then it is necessary that the testing occurs before both of them, I mean the combination, even if it occurs after one of them, which is puberty, because a combination of two or more is not realized except by the existence of each of its two components. What confirms this application is that if you said: "And test the orphans after puberty, until when both matters are combined and puberty and maturity are joined, then hand over to them their property," the sentence would be sound, and puberty would be before the testing, even though the testing is limited by the two matters and occurs before their combination. A parallel to this consideration is the justification of Abu Hanifa's position in his saying that the husband's return (fay'a) is only considered within the period of the oath of abstention (ila'), not after it, and its application to the words of the Exalted: "For those who swear off their wives, a waiting of four months. Then if they return, indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," so renew with it a covenant that will make clear to you the harmony of the two considerations, and Allah knows best. As for his, may Allah be pleased with him, restricting maturity to property alone, if the one under guardianship is morally corrupt, then the way of deriving it from the verse is that it attached the perception of maturity therein to the testing by handing over property to them, to see their disposal of it. If the intended meaning were only the correction of religion, the testing would not stop at handing over property to them, since it is apparent that one who is sound in religion does not differ in his condition whether he is poor or wealthy. And if the intended meaning were correction of both religion and property together, as al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, says, then correction of religion would not be contingent upon testing by property, as has passed just now. Furthermore, maturity in religion and property together is the complete maturity, and combining them is not a condition, and the indefiniteness of "maturity" (rushd) in the verse rejects that, since the apparent meaning is: "If you perceive in them some maturity, then hasten to hand over their property to them, without waiting for the complete end-point in it," and Allah knows best.] **and their knowledge of disposal** (ma'rifatahum bi-al-tasarruf) **before puberty** (qabla al-bulugh), **until when you perceive in them maturity** (rushdan), **that is, guidance** (hidaya), **you shall hand over to them their property** (fadfa'u ilayhim amwalahum) **without delay beyond the limit of puberty**. **And the puberty of marriage** (bulugh al-nikah) is that he has a wet dream, because he is then fit for marriage according to him, and for seeking what is intended by it, which is procreation and reproduction.

**And the perceiving** (al-ina's) is seeking clarity, so it is borrowed to mean making clear. The scholars differed concerning the testing and maturity. The testing, according to Abu Hanifa and his companions, is that property is handed over to him so that he disposes of it until his condition becomes clear regarding what comes from him. And maturity is being guided to the ways of disposal. And from Ibn 'Abbas: soundness in intellect and preservation of property. According to Malik and al-Shafi'i: the testing is that one follows his conditions and his disposal in taking and giving, and examines his signs and his inclination toward religion. And maturity is soundness in religion, because immorality corrupts property. If you say: what if maturity is not perceived in him up to the limit of puberty? I say:

According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, one waits until twenty-five years of age, because the period of a male's puberty by age is, according to him, eighteen years, so when seven years are added to it, and this is a period considered in the change of a person's conditions, due to his, peace be upon him, saying: "Command them to pray at seven" [Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Khuzayma and al-Hakim, from the narration of 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Rabi' ibn Sabra al-Juhani, from his father, from his grandfather, raised: "Command your children to pray when they are seven years old." Abu Dawud and al-Hakim narrated it via Sawwar ibn Dawud, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, and al-'Uqayli criticized it in al-Du'afa' because of Sawwar. al-Bazzar narrated it from the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Atiyya, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from him, and al-'Uqayli criticized it because of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and said: The earlier one is the narration of the one who narrated it from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman as mursal (with a missing companion). Ibn Hibban mentioned it in al-Du'afa' from 'Abd al-Mun'im ibn Na'im al-Riyahi, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra. al-Daraqutni narrated it in al-Awsat from the hadith of Anas, and in it is Dawud ibn al-Mujbir, who is abandoned (matruk).] he hands over to him his property, whether maturity was perceived in him or not. And according to his companions: he never hands it over except upon perceiving maturity.

If you say: what is the meaning of the indefiniteness of "maturity"? I say: its meaning is a kind of maturity, namely maturity in disposal and trade, or a portion of maturity and an indication of its signs, so that it is not awaited until complete maturity. If you say: how is this sentence structured? [Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "What is the arrangement of the sentence that occurs after 'until' up to His saying 'then hand over to them their property'... etc." Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He intends by this estimation to apply Abu Hanifa's position regarding the priority of testing over puberty according to the requirement of the verse, and we have already set out the way of applying Malik's position to it in the clearest and nearest manner. The summary is that the requirement of considering the combination as such, and the requirement of Abu Hanifa's position, is considering the two components separately, and the apparent meaning is considering the combination, since the conjunction with "fa" (then) requires it, and Allah knows best.] I say: What follows "hatta" (until) up to "fadfa'u ilayhim amwalahum" is made an end-point of the testing, and it is the "hatta" after which sentences occur, like the one in the saying:

"So the slain did not cease to pour out their blood / in the Tigris, until the water of the Tigris became reddish." [By Jarir. He says: so the slain did not cease to pour out, that is, to cast and emit their blood on the bank of the Tigris. "Hatta" here is inceptive, after which sentences occur, and it does not lack the meaning of an end-point. "Ashkal" is the predicate of the subject, which is the whitish mixed with redness. And "azhar" was placed in the position of the pronoun for the sake of terror and magnification. That is: until the water of that great river is mixed with redness.]

And the sentence after it is a conditional sentence, because "idha" (when) includes the meaning of a condition, and the condition-verb is "balaghu al-nikah" (they reach marriageable age), and His saying "fa-in ansartum minhum rushdan fadfa'u ilayhim amwalahum" (then if you perceive in them maturity, hand over to them their property) is a sentence of condition and consequence, occurring as an answer to the first condition, which is "idha balaghu al-nikah." So it is as if it were said: "And test the orphans until the time of their puberty; then their entitlement to hand over their property to them is on condition of perceiving maturity in them."

And Ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-in ahsitum" (if you sense), meaning "ahsastum" (you sensed). He said:

"They sensed him, so they were fierce toward him..." [Then they spent the night traveling, and he spent the night guiding, / a seer in the darkness, a strong guide. / Until they halted, and he separated from them / near, such that nothing is heard from his touch. / Except that the she-camels, the noble ones, / sensed him, so they were fierce toward him. / By Abu Zubayd al-Ta'i. "Al-idlaj" is traveling at the beginning of the night; "al-tadlij" is traveling at its end; "al-sara" is night travel. "Basir" is a description of an omitted noun; "bi-al-duja" is connected to it. "Al-basir" is one who perceives with insight or who sees, so the "ba" means "fi" (in). "Al-duja" is darkness. "Al-hadi" is meant as the one guided. "Al-'amus" is strong and powerful. "Arasu" means they alighted. "Al-hatt" is plucking, rubbing, cutting, and swiftness. "Fa-nhatta" means he withdrew from them swiftly, or hastened near them: "ma yamassu" meaning no sound of his touch to the ground in walking is heard. "Al-'itaq" are noble or aged she-camels. "Ahsan" originally was "ahsasan," the fatha of the sin was moved to the ha and then deleted. It is also narrated as "hasin." In one dialect: "hasin," with a kasra on the sin, and its origin is "hassan," the second sin was changed into a weak letter. The addition of the "ba" after the verb "hass" (to sense) is frequent, even if it is transitive by itself. "Al-shus" is the plural of ashus or shawsa'; it is one who looks with the corner of his eye, describing travelers and a lion seeking prey from among them, and they often omit the described noun, like "al-asad" (the lion) here, because the attribute specifies it, or for the claim of its specificity.]

And it is read: "rushdan" with two fathas, and "rushdan" with two dammas. **Extravagantly and hastily** (israfan wa-bidaran), meaning wasteful and hasty, [fearing] their growing up, or because of your extravagance and haste toward their growing up, wasting it in spending, and saying: "We spend as we desire before the orphans grow up and snatch it from our hands." Then He divided the matter between the guardian being wealthy and being poor. The wealthy one abstains from eating it [the phrase "min akliha" (from eating it) is perhaps "'an" (from), (Ayn)] and does not covet, and is content with what Allah has provided of wealth, out of compassion for the orphan and preservation of his property. And the poor one eats a fixed sustenance, carefully estimating it, by way of wage, or borrowing, with the difference of opinion on that. And the wording "eat in a reasonable way" and "abstention" indicates that the guardian has a right because he takes charge of it. And from the Prophet, peace be upon him: that a man said to him: "I have an orphan in my custody; may I eat from his property?" He said: "In a reasonable way, without making property a means of accumulation, and without protecting your property with his property." He said: "May I beat him?" He said: "Whatever you would beat your own son with." [Al-Tha'labi narrated it through Mu'awiya ibn Hisham: al-Thawri narrated to us from Ibn Abi Najih, from al-Hasan al-'Urani, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, and said: 'In my custody is an orphan,'" in the wording of the author, the same. 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated it in al-Musannaf, and Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Birr wa-al-Sila, and al-Tabari from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from Ibn Dinar, from al-Hasan al-'Urani, "that a man said: O Messenger of Allah," and mentioned it as mursal. It is in Ibn Abi Shayba in al-Buyu' from Isma'il, from Ayyub ibn 'Amr likewise. Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Maja and others narrated from the narration of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: "A man came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and said: 'I do not find anything, and I have no property. I have an orphan who has property.' He said: 'Eat from your orphan's property without extravagance, without making property a means of accumulation, and without protecting your property with his property.'" Ibn Hibban narrated from the narration of Salih ibn Rustum, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Jabir who said: a man said to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him: "With what may I beat my orphan?" He said: "Whatever you would beat your own son with, without protecting your property with his property, and without making accumulation of property from his property." Ibn 'Adi narrated it in al-Kamil in the biography of Salih ibn Rustum, who is Abu 'Amir al-Kharraz, and he was weakened by Ibn Ma'in, who said: "I did not find for him a dubious hadith." Abu Nu'aym narrated it in al-Hilya in the biography of 'Amr ibn Dinar, and said: "Al-Kharraz alone narrated it, and he is one of the trustworthy Basrans."] And from Ibn 'Abbas: that the guardian of an orphan said to him: "May I drink from the milk of his camels?" He said: "If you seek its strays, and smear its trough, and apply tar to its mange, and give it to drink on the day of its watering, then drink without harming its offspring, and without excessive milking." [Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq from the narration of Yahya ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, who said: "A man came to Ibn 'Abbas," and mentioned it, except that he said, instead of "seek its strays": "seeks its lost (naditha)." Al-Tabari narrated it through him, and al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi from another route, from al-Qasim. al-Baghawi narrated it through Malik from Yahya ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim, and it is in the Muwatta'.] And from him: he strikes with his hand along with their hands, so he eats in a reasonable way, and does not wear a turban or anything above it. And from Ibrahim: he does not wear linen or fine garments, but only what fills hunger and covers nakedness. And from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: he becomes thin like a beast (yataqarram taqarrum al-bahima), and makes himself like a hired worker in what is unavoidable. And from al-Sha'bi: he eats from his property an amount by which he is helped in it. And from him: like carrion, he takes it when necessary and repays it. And from Mujahid: he borrows, and when he becomes wealthy he pays back. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: if he wishes, he drinks the surplus milk, rides the back, wears clothing that covers him, and takes sustenance, and does not exceed it; if he becomes wealthy he repays it, and if he becomes poor, he is in permissibility. And from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have placed myself from Allah's property in the position of the guardian of the orphan: if I become wealthy I abstain, and if I become poor I eat in a reasonable way, and when I become wealthy I repay." [Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Tabari narrated it from the narration of Isra'il and Sufyan, both from Abu Ishaq, from Haritha ibn Mudarrib, who said: 'Umar said. Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated it from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', who said: 'Umar said to me,' and mentioned it.] "Istu'if" (be abstinent) is more emphatic than "'uffa" (abstain). [Mahmud said: "'Istu'if' is more emphatic than 'uffa,' as if he seeks an increase of abstinence from himself." Ahmad said: In this there is an indication that it is of the form istaf'ala with the meaning of seeking; but it is not so, for the seeking form istaf'ala is transitive, and this is intransitive. The apparent view is that it is of a kind in which "fa'ala" and "istaf'ala" have the same meaning, and Allah knows best.] As if he seeks an increase of abstinence. **So call witnesses against them** (fa-ash-hidu 'alayhim), that they received them and took possession of them, and your liability is discharged from them. That is more distant from disputes and mutual denials, and more conducive to trust and clearing of accountability. Do you not see that if one does not call witnesses and then someone claims against him, he is believed with an oath according to Abu Hanifa and his companions? And according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, he is not believed except with evidence. So in calling witnesses there is safeguarding against the imposition of an oath that leads to accusation, or against the obligation of liability if he does not establish evidence. **And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner** (wa-kafa bi-Allahi hasiban), that is, sufficient as a witness against you for the handing over and receiving, or as one who calls to account. So be truthful to one another, and beware of lying to one another.

Al-aqrabun (the nearest relatives) are those who inherit from among the kin, to the exclusion of others, "of what little or much it may be," a substitution (badal) for "what was left," with the governing verb repeated.

Nasiban mafrudan (an allotted share) is in the accusative of specification (nasb 'ala al-ikhtisas), meaning: "I mean an allotted share, a determined, obligatory portion which they must necessarily take possession of and which no one may monopolize." It may also be in the accusative of the emphatic verbal noun, like His words ﴿an obligation from God﴾; as if it were said: "a divided share that is prescribed."

It is related that Aws ibn al-Samit al-Ansari left behind his wife Umm Kahha and three daughters, and that his paternal cousins Suwayd and 'Arfaja (or Qatada and 'Arfaja) took his inheritance from them. The people of the Jahiliyya did not give inheritance to women and children, and they would say: "None inherits except one who thrusts with spears, defends the territory, and seizes the spoils." So Umm Kahha came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the Mosque of al-Fudaykh and complained to him. He said: "Return until I see what God will bring about," and then the revelation came. He sent to the two of them: "Do not divide anything of Aws's property, for God has made a share for them, and He has not clarified it until it is clarified." Then the verse ﴿God enjoins you﴾ was revealed, and Umm Kahha was given an eighth, the daughters two-thirds, and the remainder went to the two cousins.

[Al-Tha'labi then al-Baghawi transmitted this without a chain. Al-Wahidi in al-Asbab said: the exegetes said: "Aws ibn Thabit al-Ansari died and left a wife called Umm Kahha, and he had three daughters by her. Two men, paternal cousins and executors of the deceased, called 'Afija and Suwayd, stood up, took his wealth, and gave his wife and daughters nothing. In the Jahiliyya they did not give inheritance to women or to small children, even if male; they gave it only to grown men. They would say: 'None is given except one who fights on horseback and seizes spoils.' Umm Kahha came and mentioned it, to the end, the same." It is evident that by "the exegetes" he meant al-Kalbi, Muqatil and their likes. al-Tabari related this story through Ibn Jurayj from 'Ikrima in a different context, its wording being: "It was revealed concerning Umm Kahha, Tha'laba and Aws ibn Suwayd, who were of the Ansar; one of them was her husband and the other the paternal uncle of her son. She said: 'O Messenger of God, my husband died and left me and his daughter, and we were not given inheritance.' The paternal uncle of her son said: 'Her son does not ride a horse, carry a burden, or strike an enemy.' So God revealed ﴿For men is a share﴾, the verse." He also related through al-Suddi, concerning God's words ﴿God enjoins you concerning your children﴾: the people of the Jahiliyya did not give inheritance to girls or weak male slaves, and they gave inheritance only to one who could fight. 'Abd al-Rahman, father of Hassan the poet, died and left a wife called Umm Kahha and five sisters. The heirs came and seized his property, and Umm Kahha complained to the Prophet (ﷺ), and God revealed ﴿If they are women above two, they have two-thirds of what he left﴾, then He said concerning Umm Kahha ﴿and for them is a quarter of what you leave, if you have no child﴾, the verse.]

As for ﴿and when the division takes place﴾, that is, the division of the estate, ﴿those of kinship﴾ who do not inherit are present, ﴿then provide for them from it﴾. The pronoun refers to what the parents and the nearest relatives left. This is a command of recommendation (nadb). Al-Hasan said: "The believers used to do this: when the heirs gathered, these people were present, and they gave them some of the worn-out goods (ruththat al-mata')," (in al-Sihah, ruththa means the discarded items of household furniture, of worn-out sorts; plural ruth, like qirba and qurab). So God urged them to do this as a moral training, without it being an obligation. They said: "If it were an obligation, a limit and measure would have been set for it, as with other rights." It is related that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr (may God be pleased with him) divided his father's inheritance while 'A'isha (may God be pleased with her) was alive, leaving no one in the house without giving them something, and he recited this verse.

It is said: it is obligatory. It is also said: it is abrogated by the verses of inheritance, like the bequest. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Some people say it was abrogated, but by God, it was not abrogated; rather, it is among the things people neglect." The customary words are that they speak to them gently, saying: "Take it, may God bless you," apologize to them, consider what they give them as little and not as much, and not reproach them. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: "We found people dividing among the kin, the needy and the orphans from the 'ayn," meaning silver and gold. When silver and gold were divided and the division moved to lands, slaves and the like, they would say to them a kind word, such as: "May God bless you."
