Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 9:

"Law" (if) together with what is in its scope is a relative clause (silah) for "those who". What is meant by them are the guardians (al-awsiya'), who are commanded to fear Allah [[Mahmud said: "What is meant is the guardians, who are commanded to fear Allah... etc." Ahmad said: He was compelled to posit the supposition (taqdir) "tarakû" (they leave) by his saying "they were about to leave", because its response is his saying "they would fear for them" (khafû 'alayhim), and fearing for them can only occur before they leave them, and that is in the abode of this world. This shows that the meaning of "leaving" is "being about to leave" by necessity; otherwise the response would precede the condition, which is invalid. Its parallel is "when they have reached their term, then retain them with kindness or release them with kindness" (fa-balaghna ajalahunna fa-amsikuhunna bi-ma'ruf aw sarrihuhunna bi-ma'ruf), meaning: they were about to reach the term. The figurative use of expressing being about to leave by leaving has a wonderful secret: it is the threat with a state in which no hope remains for life nor for defending weak offspring. This state, although it belongs to this world, is, because of its nearness to the Hereafter and its adjacency to parting, counted within its scope, and is expressed by the same term used for the state that exists after parting, namely leaving. And Allah knows best.]] so that they should fear for those in their charge of the orphans and be compassionate toward them: their fear for their own offspring if they left them weak, and their compassion for them, and that they should imagine that in themselves and picture it so that they do not dare to act contrary to compassion and mercy. It is also permissible that the meaning be: and let them fear for the orphans from being lost. It has been said: they are those who sit with the sick person and say: "Your offspring will not avail you anything against Allah; so advance your property," and he then exhausts it through bequests. So they were commanded to fear their Lord, or to fear for the children of the sick person and be compassionate toward them, as they would be compassionate toward their own children if they had them. It is also permissible that it be connected to what precedes it, and that it be a command to the heirs to show compassion toward the weak relatives, orphans and needy who attend the division, and to picture that if they were their own children, left behind them destitute and needy, would they fear for them deprivation and disappointment? If you say: what is the meaning of "if they leave" with its response being a relative clause for "those who"? I say: its meaning is:

And let those fear whose description and state is that if they were about to leave behind them offspring who are weak, and that is at their dying, they feared for them loss after them, due to the departure of their guardian and earner, as the poet said:

"Indeed my love for life has increased for me... my daughters, for they are among the weak.
I dread that they will see misery after me, and that they will drink turbid water after clear."

[[The explanation of these verses was mentioned on page 404 of this part, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

It was recited: du'afa', da'ifa, da'ifa, like sukara and sukara. The right speech from the guardians is that they should not harm the orphans, and should address them as they address their own children, with good manners and warmth, calling them "my son" and "my boy." And from those sitting with the sick person: when he intends to make a bequest, they should say to him: "Do not be extravagant in your bequest, lest you harm your children," like the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Sa'd: "That you leave your heirs wealthy is better than that you leave them poor, begging of people." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas in a story.]] The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, preferred that the bequest not reach a third, and that a fifth is better than a quarter, and a quarter is better than a third. And as for those dividing their inheritance: they should speak gently and make their speech beautiful to those present.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 4, verse 10:

ظُلْماً ظالمين [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is 'wrongfully' (ظالمين), or 'in the manner of injustice' ... etc." Ahmad said: Similar to it is (قَدْ بَدَتِ الْبَغْضاءُ مِنْ أَفْواهِهِمْ) ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾ — meaning they spread it wide (شدقوا بها) and uttered it with the full capacity of their mouths. Or the mention of the bellies may be intended to depict the act of eating for the listener, so that the heinousness of this crime becomes firmly established in his mind through increased depiction. And to emphasize the censure of the one who wrongs an orphan in his property, eating is singled out because it is the most abominable state in which the property of an orphan is consumed. And God knows best.]] Or in the manner of injustice on the part of the evil guardians and their judges. ﴿In their bellies﴾ means filling their bellies. It is said: "So-and-so ate in his belly," and "in some of his belly." He said:

كُلُوا فِى بَعْضِ بَطْنِكُمُوا تَعِفُّوا [[Eat in some of your bellies, and you will be chaste. / Indeed your time is a time of hunger.]] — that is, eat in some of your bellies. The singular "belly" is used to avoid ambiguity, i.e., do not fill them; if you obey me, you will abstain from food. The imperfect of عف is يعف (with kasra on the ع in the present), from the pattern ضرب يضرب. Then he said: "Indeed your time" — that is, I commanded you to do this because your time is barren.

والخميص: the one whose belly is lean. So the barren time is likened to a hungry man by way of metaphor (الكناية), and describing it with leanness is an imaginative embellishment (تخييل) of that.

The meaning of ﴿they eat fire﴾ is that which leads to the Fire, so it is in reality as if it were fire. It is narrated that the one who eats the property of an orphan will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with smoke coming out of his grave [[The phrase "from his grave" (من قبره) is also narrated as "from his rear" (من دبره). This is supported by what is in al-Khazin from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that stones of fire are placed in their mouths and it comes out from their lower parts. Examine it. (ʿ)]] and from his mouth, nose, ears and eyes [[al-Tabari narrated it through al-Suddi, who said: "God will raise the one who eats the property of an orphan unjustly on the Day of Resurrection, and the flame of fire will come out of his mouth and nose," to the end. In the Sahih of Ibn Hibban, through the narration of Zannad Abu al-Mundhir from Nafi' ibn al-Harith from Abu Barzah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): God will raise up on the Day of Resurrection people from their graves, their mouths blazing with fire. It was said: "Who are they, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Have you not seen that God says (﴿Indeed those who eat the property of orphans unjustly﴾) the verse." In its chain is Zannad mentioned above; Ibn Ma'in declared him a liar, and his shaykh Nafi' ibn al-Harith is also weak. Ibn 'Adi also cited him among the weak narrators in the biography of Zannad and criticized him for it.]] — so people will know that he used to eat the property of an orphan in the world. It is read ﴿wa-sayaslawna﴾ with a damma on the yā' and with the lām lightened or doubled; ﴿saʿīran﴾ means a fire among the fires, of indefinite description.

He (Allah) instructs you concerning your children, that is, concerning their inheritance, in what is just and beneficial. This is a general statement whose detail follows: ﴿For the male, the equivalent of the share of two females.﴾

If you ask: why was it not said, "For the two females, the equivalent of the share of the male," or "For the female, half the share of the male"?

I say: The male's share is mentioned first because of his superiority, just as his share was doubled for that reason. Moreover, the statement ﴿For the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ aims to show the male's superiority, whereas your phrase "For the two females, the equivalent of the share of the male" aims to show the female's deficiency. What is intended to show his superiority is more indicative of it than what is intended to show the deficiency of another relative to him. Also, they used to give inheritance to males only, not to females.

[[Mahmud [al-Zamakhshari] continued: "And because they used to give inheritance to males only, not to females..." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: According to this reasoning, the ruling on the son when he is alone would not be mentioned in the verse, because when it mentions him, it means only the case of his being together with females, according to al-Zamakhshari's interpretation. This may be disputed: the first-mentioned is the male's inheritance in general, both when together with females and when alone. The reason his ruling is derived in the case of togetherness is what al-Zamakhshari established. As for deriving his ruling in the case of being alone, it is because Allah, exalted is He, made for him the equivalent of the share of two females. If a female is with him, that is the case; if she is alone without him, He has given her, when alone, half. This requires that the male, when alone, has twice her share when she is alone, and that is the full amount. And Allah knows best.]]

And this (the rule of giving the male a double share) was the cause of the revelation of the verse. It was said: It suffices the males that their share is doubled over the females' share; so let them not overstep concerning the females' shares until the females are deprived, despite their kinship which is like theirs.

If you ask: the share of the two females is two-thirds, so it is as if it were said that the male gets two-thirds?

I say: It refers to the case of togetherness, not of being alone; that is, when the male and the two females are together, he has two shares, just as they have two shares. As for the case of being alone, the son takes all the wealth and the two daughters take two-thirds. The evidence that the purpose is the ruling of togetherness is that He followed it with the ruling of being alone, which is His saying: ﴿But if they (the females) are more than two, for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾. The meaning is: for the male among them, that is, among your children, so the returning pronoun was omitted because it is understood, like the saying of the Arabs: "Ghee is two ratls for a dirham" [the pronoun is omitted].

﴿But if they are females﴾: that is, if the daughters or the girls are females purely, with no male among them.

﴿More than two﴾ may be a second predicate of *kana* (was), or it may be an attribute of *nisa'* (females), meaning females exceeding two.

﴿And if she is one﴾: and if the daughter or the girl is alone, singular, with no other with her, ﴿then for her is half﴾.

It is read *wahidatun* (one) in the nominative, with *kana* as a complete verb. The reading in the accusative is more fitting with His saying: ﴿But if they are females﴾.

Zayd ibn Thabit read *al-nisf* (the half) with a *damma*.

The pronoun in *taraka* (he left) refers to the deceased, because since the verse concerns inheritance, it is known that the one who leaves is the deceased.

If you ask: His saying ﴿For the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ is a statement designed to explain the male's share of the children, not the share of the two females. How then is it correct for it to be followed by ﴿But if they are females﴾, which explains the share of the females?

I say: Although it was designed to explain the male's share, when its understanding and the share of the two females along with their brother became clear from it, it was as if it were designed for both matters together. That is why it is correct to say ﴿But if they are females﴾.

If you ask: Is it correct that the two pronouns in *kunna* (they were) and *kanat* (she was) are ambiguous, and that *nisa'* (females) and *wahidah* (one) are their explanation, with *kana* being a complete verb?

I say: No, I do not consider that.

If you ask: Why was it said ﴿But if they are females﴾, and why was it not said, "But if she is a woman"?

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask: why was it said ﴿But if they are females﴾ and not ﴿But if she is a woman﴾..." Ahmad said: He means that the ruling for two daughters when together with a son is mentioned in His saying ﴿For the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾; the ruling for daughters when alone is mentioned in His saying ﴿But if they are females﴾; and the ruling for a single daughter when alone is mentioned in His saying ﴿And if she is one, then for her is half﴾. What remains is that the son's ruling when alone is derived from His saying ﴿For the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ when you combine it with His saying ﴿And if she is one, then for her is half﴾, according to the explanation I have previously stated.]]

I say: Because the purpose there is that the females be purely female, with no male among them, so as to distinguish between what was mentioned of their being together with males in His saying ﴿For the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ and their being alone. Here the intention is to distinguish between a daughter being with others and her being alone, with no companion.

If you ask: The ruling for two daughters when together with a son has been mentioned, and the ruling for daughters and a single daughter when alone. But the ruling for two daughters when alone has not been mentioned. What is their ruling, and why was it not mentioned?

I say: Their ruling is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) refused to treat the two as a group, because of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿But if they are females more than two﴾, so he gave the two the ruling of one. This is plain and clear. As for the rest of the Companions, they gave the two the ruling of a group. The reasoning behind their view is that His saying ﴿For the male, the equivalent of the share of two females﴾ indicates that the ruling for two females is the ruling for a male. Just as a male may receive two-thirds along with one female, so two females may receive two-thirds. So when He mentioned what indicates the ruling for two females, He said ﴿But if they are females more than two, for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾, meaning: if they are a group of female adults, however many they are, then for them is what is due to two females, which is two-thirds, and they do not exceed it because of their number. This makes it known that the ruling for a group is the ruling for two, without difference.

It is also said: The two (daughters) are closer in kinship to the deceased than two sisters, so they assigned to them what Allah assigned to two sisters, and they did not think it right to reduce their portion below that of someone further in kinship than them.

It is also said: When a daughter is due one-third along with her brother, she is more deserving of one-third when she is with a sister like her; and her sister, along with her, would have what would also be due to her if she were alone with her brother. So two-thirds became due to both of them.

﴿And for his parents﴾: the pronoun refers to the deceased.

﴿For each one of them﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿for his parents﴾ by repetition of the governing word.

The benefit of this substitute is that if it were said, "And for his parents is a sixth," its apparent meaning would be that they share in it. And if it were said, "And for his parents are two sixths," it would give the impression that the two sixths are divided between them equally or unequally.

If you ask: Why was it not said, "And for each one of his parents, a sixth"? What is the benefit in mentioning the parents first and then substituting for them?

I say: Because in the substitution and detail after the general statement there is emphasis and reinforcement, like what you see in combining the explained term with its explanation.

"A sixth" is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is "for his parents." The substitute is placed between them for clarification.

Al-Hasan and Na'im ibn Maysara read *al-sudus* (the sixth) with a light pronunciation, and likewise *al-thuluth* (the third), *al-rub'* (the quarter), and *al-thumun* (the eighth).

The word *walad* (child) applies to male and female, and the father's ruling differs in this respect. If the child is male, the father is restricted to a sixth. If the child is female, the father becomes a residuary (*'asaba*) in addition to receiving a sixth.

If you ask: The ruling for the parents in inheritance has been explained when there is a child, and then their ruling when there is no child. Why was it not said, "If he has no child, then his mother has one-third"? And what is the benefit of His saying ﴿And his parents inherit from him﴾?

I say: Its meaning is: If he has no child and only his parents inherit from him, then his mother has one-third of what he left, as He said ﴿For each one of them, a sixth of what he left﴾. This is because if his parents inherit along with one of the spouses, the mother has one-third of what remains after the spouse's share is taken out, not one-third of what he left, except according to Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning is that when the two parents are alone, they share the inheritance: for the male, the equivalent of the share of two females.

If you ask: What is the reason that the mother has one-third of what remains rather than one-third of the wealth?

I say: There are two aspects. The first is that the spouse only receives what is allotted to him by the right of the marriage contract, not by kinship, so he resembles a bequest in the division of what is left after him. The second is that the father is stronger in inheritance than the mother, as is shown by the fact that when the two are alone, he receives more than her, and he is both a fixed-share holder and a residuary, combining both. So if one-third were fully assigned to her, it would lead to reducing his share below hers. Do you not see that if a woman leaves a husband and two parents, the husband gets a half, the mother gets a third, and the rest goes to the father, the mother then takes two shares and the father one share, so the ruling becomes that the female receives the equivalent of the share of two males?

﴿But if he has siblings, then for his mother is a sixth.﴾ The siblings block the mother from the one-third, even though they do not inherit along with the father. So she has a sixth, and the father has five-sixths. Two siblings and more are equal in blocking, except according to Ibn 'Abbas. From him it is reported that they take the sixth from which they blocked the mother.

If you ask: How can the word "siblings" (*ikhwah*) include two brothers, when the plural is different from the dual?

I say: The word "siblings" conveys the meaning of plurality in an absolute sense without a specific number, whereas the dual, like the triple and the quadruple, conveys a specific number. This is the place where the absolute plural is indicated, so it is indicated by "siblings."

It is also read *fa-li-ummihi* (for his mother) with a kasra on the hamza, following the kasra of the preceding word. Do you not see that it is not pronounced with a kasra in His saying ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾?

﴿After a bequest﴾ is connected to everything preceding it, namely the division of all the inheritance, not only to what immediately follows it. As if it were said: the division of these shares is after a bequest that is made.

It is read *yuwsi bi-ha* with light and heavy pronunciation, and *yuwsa bi-ha* with the passive voice and light pronunciation.

If you ask: What is the meaning of *aw* (or)?

I say: Its meaning is permission: that if one or both of them exist, it is to be executed before the division of the inheritance, like your saying, "Sit with al-Hasan or with Ibn Sirin."

If you ask: Why was the bequest put before the debt?

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask: why was the bequest put before the debt?..." Ahmad said: Bequests are of two kinds: one to an unspecified party, which is not demanded except by the ruler if he finds it; and one to a specified party, who has the right to demand it. They differ in strength between the creditor's demand for his debt and the legatee's demand for his bequest, because the creditor demands a right fixed in the obligation that preceded him as a favour over his debtor, whereas the legatee only seeks a charity that the deceased bestowed upon him, not one due by prior entitlement. So the strength the creditor has makes it unnecessary to mention him first, and the weakness of the legatee is supported by mentioning him first, to help him obtain the benefit of the bequest. The objection may also be answered in another way, which I shall state: the order of the verse does not contradict the order established by the law, so the question does not arise. The first thing to begin with is paying the debt, then the bequest, then the division among the heirs. Notice how the payment of inheritance shares comes last, after the bequest, which comes after the debt, which agrees with our saying...]]

The division of inheritance after the bequest and the debt is the form of the actual situation in the Shari'ah. And if the mention had been dropped, and the speech had been: "Bring out the inheritance, the bequest and the debt," then the aforementioned question could not arise. And Allah knows best.]] And is the debt given precedence over it in the Shari'ah? I say: since the bequest (wasiyya) resembles inheritance in being taken without compensation, its payment is burdensome to the heirs, who find it great and whose souls are not content with it, so its discharge is prone to neglect. Unlike the debt, their souls are at peace with paying it. Therefore the bequest was placed before the debt, to urge its obligation and to hasten its discharge along with the debt. For this reason the word "or" (aw) was used, to equate the two in obligation. Then this was emphasized and encouraged by the words "your fathers and your sons," meaning: you do not know which of your fathers and sons who die is more beneficial to you, the one who bequeathed or the one who did not bequeath. The meaning is that whoever bequeaths part of his wealth, thereby exposing you to the reward of the Hereafter by carrying out his bequest, is closer to you in benefit and more present in usefulness than one who leaves no bequest. Thus he spared you the goods of this world and made the reward of the Hereafter closer and more present than the goods of this world, going by the reality of the matter. For the goods of this world, though immediate and near in appearance, are perishable, so in reality they are the most distant and remote. The reward of the Hereafter, though deferred, is lasting, so in reality it is the nearest and most proximate. It was said: if a son is higher in rank than his father in Paradise, he asks that his father be raised to him, and he is raised. Likewise, if a father is higher in rank than his son, he asks that his son be raised to him.

So you do not know in this world which of them is closer to you in benefit. It was also said: Allah prescribed the obligations as He deemed wise. Had He left that to you, you would not know which of them is more beneficial to you, and you would have distributed the wealth without wisdom. It was also said: the father is obligated to maintain the son if the son is in need, and likewise the son if the son is in need. Each of them benefits the other through maintenance, and it is not known which of them is closer in benefit. None of these sayings fits the meaning or corresponds to it, because this sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). A parenthetical clause should confirm what it interrupts and be suitable to it, and the correct view is what preceded.

"Obligation" (fariydah) is in the accusative as an emphatic infinitive (masdar), meaning: Allah obligated that obligation as an obligation. Indeed Allah is All-Knowing (alim) of the interests of His creatures, All-Wise (hakim) in everything He has prescribed and apportioned of inheritances and other matters.

[[His statement "upon him" ('alayhi): perhaps it is "to him" (lahu), so reflect. End of quote, its editor.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 12:

﴿If there are children for them, whether yours or of others,﴾ The woman has been made half of the man's share by the right of marriage, just as she has been made so by the right of kinship. The one and the many are equal in the quarter and the eighth. ﴿And if a man﴾ — meaning the deceased — ﴿leaves an inheritance (yurathu)﴾.

"Yurathu" means: it is inherited from him, and it is an attribute of "rajul" (a man). "Kalalah" is the predicate of "kana" (was), meaning: and if there is a man from whom an inheritance is left as kalalah. Or "yurathu" may be the predicate of "kana," and "kalalah" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "yurathu." It is also read as "yurathu" and "yuwarrathu" (with light and heavy emphasis), in the active voice, and "kalalah" is then a circumstantial accusative or an object.

If you ask: what is the kalalah? I say: the term applies to three things: to one who leaves neither a child nor a parent; to one who is neither a child nor a parent among the deceased; and to kinship from a direction other than child and parent. From this is the saying: "The glory was not inherited from kalalah," just as you say: "I did not keep silent out of ignorance," and "he did not refrain out of cowardice." Originally, "kalalah" is a verbal noun in the sense of "kalal," which is the going away of strength through weariness. Al-A'sha said:

*So I swore I would not pity her for weariness*
*(And when she travels by night, you see for her two watchers, Jady and Farqad, that never set)*
*Nor for lameness, until I meet Muhammad.*

[The poet describes his she-camel, which he rode when he came as a delegation to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the polytheists prevented him, and he died in al-Yamamah. "Adlajat" means traveled by night. "Jadiyyan" and "Farqadan" are substitutes for what precedes them. This is a metaphor for the length of her night, or rather her boredom from travel. "Fa-ālaytu" means I swore. "Lā arthī" means I do not feel pity for her, out of tiredness and weariness. "Al-wajy" is the injury of the hoof or the like from travel. It is narrated instead as "fa-mā laka ʿindī mushtakā min kalālatin wa lā min ḥafā," where "mushtakā" means complaint and "ḥafā" means wajy. He says: when my she-camel travels by night, its night lengthens, and I swear I will not pity her for fatigue or injury, until I meet Muhammad (ﷺ) with her. He attributed the action to her, to indicate that she knows him, and she is the one traveling to him.]

It was therefore borrowed for kinship from a direction other than child and parent, because in relation to their kinship it is like a weak instrument. When it is made an attribute of the deceased or the heir, it means "one with kalalah," just as you say: "So-and-so is from my kin," meaning from my close relatives. It is permissible for it to be an attribute like "hajjāja" and "faqqāqa" for a fool.

[The phrase "hajjāja and faqqāqa for a fool": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: a man "hajjāja" means a fool. Also in it: a man "faqqāqa" means a foolish babbler. Also in it: "al-hadhr" (with vowel on the ḥa) means delirium, and "rajul hadhr" (with a kasra on the dhāl) means a babbler. (ʿ).]

If you ask: if you make it a noun for kinship in the verse, what do you make it governed by? I say: it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning he is inherited for the sake of kalalah, or he leaves an inheritance to others for its sake. If you ask: if you make "yurathu" in the passive voice from "awrath," what is its meaning? I say: then the man is the heir, not the one from whom inheritance is taken. If you ask: to whom does the pronoun in His saying "for each one of them (wāḥidin minhumā)" refer then? I say: to the man and his brother or sister, and on the first reading, to both of them. If you ask: if the pronoun refers to both of them, it conveys equality in taking the sixth without preference of the male over the female; does this benefit remain in this aspect? I say: yes, because when you say the sixth is for him, or for one of the brother or sister by choice, you have equated male and female.

It is reported from Abu Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he was asked about kalalah and said:

*I will say about it with my opinion. If it is correct, it is from Allah, and if it is wrong, it is from me and from Satan, and Allah is free of it.*

Kalalah: what is other than child and parent. [Reported by Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Ṭabarī, and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr. From the narration of al-Shaʿbī he said: Abu Bakr said. In the narration of Saʿīd and al-Ṭabarī there is also a statement of ʿUmar.] It is reported from ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk that kalalah is the deceased. It is reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that it is the heir. They agreed that the intended meaning is the maternal siblings. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "And he has a brother or sister from the mother." And the reading of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ: "And he has a brother or sister from a mother." It was said: the argument that kalalah here specifically means maternal siblings comes from what is mentioned at the end of the surah, that the two sisters take two-thirds and the brothers take the whole estate. So it is known here, since one is given the sixth and two are given the third, and they are not increased beyond the third, that by them is meant the maternal siblings. Otherwise, kalalah is general for all those other than child and parent, from all other siblings: consanguine and full siblings and half-siblings (ʿallāt) and others.

[The phrase "all other siblings: consanguine and full siblings and half-siblings": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "ikhwa akhyāf" are siblings when their mother is one and fathers differ; "al-aʿyān" are siblings who share one father and one mother; "banū al-ʿallāt" are children of one man from different mothers. Summarized from various places. (ʿ).]

*ghayra muḍārr* is a circumstantial clause: that is, he bequeaths it while not harming his heirs. This is when he bequeaths more than a third, or bequeaths a third or less while intending to harm his heirs and to anger them, not for the sake of Allah the Exalted. From Qatadah: Allah disliked harm during life and at death and forbade it. From al-Ḥasan: harm in religion is to bequeath a debt that is not owed, and its meaning is acknowledgment.

*waṣiyyatan min Allāh* is an emphatic verbal noun, meaning He enjoins you with this as an injunction, as in His saying: "an obligation from Allah." It is permissible that it be in the accusative governed by "ghayra muḍārr," meaning no harm is done to an injunction from Allah, which is the third or less, by increasing it beyond the third, or an injunction from Allah concerning the children, and that he should not leave them in need through extravagance in bequest. This aspect is supported by the reading of al-Ḥasan: "ghayra muḍārrin waṣiyyatan min Allāh," with the construct form.

﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾ of whoever wrongs or acts justly in his bequest, ﴿Forbearing﴾ toward the wrongdoer, not hastening to punish him. This is a warning.

If you ask: in "yūṣā" there is a pronoun for the man if you make him the one from whom inheritance is taken; how do you treat it if you make him the heir? I say: as you treated it in His saying, "For them is two-thirds of what he left," because it is known that the one who leaves and the one who bequeaths is the deceased.

If you ask: where is the circumstantial referent for the one who reads "yūṣā bihā" in the passive voice? I say: "yūṣā" is supplied and made accusative from its agent, because when it is said "yūṣā bihā" it is known that there is a bequeather, as He said: "He is glorified therein in the mornings and evenings," in the passive voice, so it is known that there is one who glorifies. So "yusabbiḥ" is supplied, and just as "rijāl" is the agent of what "yusabbiḥ" indicates, "ghayra muḍārr" is a circumstantial clause for what "yūṣā bihā" indicates.

"That" refers to the rulings mentioned in the sections on orphans, bequests and inheritance. He called them "limits" (ḥudūd), because the sacred laws are like the fixed boundaries set for the responsible persons (mukallafīn): it is not permissible for them to exceed them or to step over them to what is not rightfully theirs. ﴿He will admit him﴾ is read with the ya' and with the nun, and likewise ﴿He will admit him to a fire﴾. It is also said: ﴿yudkhilhu﴾. ﴿Abiding therein﴾ (khālidīn) is taken in agreement with the wording of "man" (whoever), and its meaning. ﴿Abiding﴾ (khālidīn) and ﴿abiding﴾ (khālidan) are in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl). If you say: may these two be adjectives of "gardens" and "a fire"? I say: No, because they follow something other than those to whom they belong, so a pronoun is necessary, which is your saying: "abiding therein they are" (khālidīna hum fīhā), and "abiding therein he is" (khālidan huwa fīhā).

He called them "limits" (ḥudūd), because the sacred laws are like the fixed boundaries set for the responsible persons (mukallafīn): it is not permissible for them to exceed them or to step over them to what is not rightfully theirs. ﴿He will admit him﴾ is read with the ya' and with the nun, and likewise ﴿He will admit him to a fire﴾. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 15–16:

"Who commit an indecent act" (يَأْتِينَ الْفاحِشَةَ) — yurhiquhunna (يرهقنها). It is said: atā al-fāḥishah (أتى الفاحشة), jā'ahā (جاءها), ghashiyahā (غشيها) and rahiqahā (رهقها) all have the same meaning. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "who come with the indecency" (يأتين بالفاحشة). Al-fāḥishah (the indecency, i.e., fornication) is zina, because it exceeds many other abominations in its ugliness.

"Then confine them to their houses" (فَأَمْسِكُوهُنَّ فِي الْبُيُوتِ). It has been said that its meaning is: keep them confined in your houses for life (فخلدوهن محبوسات في بيوتكم). This was their punishment at the beginning of Islam, and then it was abrogated (nusikha) by the words of the Most High: "The fornicatress and the fornicator..." (الزَّانِيَةُ وَالزَّانِي) — the verse. It is also permissible that it is not abrogated, by leaving out mention of the prescribed punishment (al-ḥadd) because it is known from the Book and the Sunnah, and [the verse] enjoins keeping them in their houses after they have been restricted, as a protection for them from what befell them because of going out of the houses and exposing themselves to men.

"Or God makes for them a way" (أَوْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ لَهُنَّ سَبِيلًا) — this is marriage (al-nikāḥ), by which they become independent of illicit intercourse (al-sifāḥ). It has also been said: the way (al-sabīl) is the prescribed punishment (al-ḥadd), because that had not yet been legislated at that time.

If you say: what is the meaning of "death takes them" (يتوفاهن الموت), since al-tawaffī and al-mawt have one meaning, as if it were said: "until death causes them to die"? I say: it is permissible that it means "until the angels of death take them" (يتوفاهن ملائكة الموت), like His words: "those whom the angels take" (الَّذِينَ تَتَوَفَّاهُمُ الْمَلائِكَةُ), "those whom the angels take" (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ تَوَفَّاهُمُ الْمَلائِكَةُ), "say: the angel of death will take you" (قُلْ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ). Or it means "until death takes them and their souls are fully taken" (يأخذهن الموت ويستوفى أرواحهن).

"And the two of you who commit it" (وَالَّذانِ يَأْتِيانِها مِنْكُمْ) — he means the male fornicator and the female fornicatress. "Then harm them" (فَآذُوهُما): rebuke them, blame them, and say to them: "Have you no shame? Do you not fear God?" (أما استحييتما، أما خفتما اللَّه). "If they repent (فَإِنْ تابا) and make amends (وَأَصْلَحا) and change their condition (وغيرا الحال), then turn away from them (فَأَعْرِضُوا عَنْهُما)": stop the rebuke and blame, for repentance prevents the deserving of blame and punishment.

It may be that this is addressed to the witnesses who came upon their secret, and that "harm" means blaming them, rebuking them, and threatening them with referral to the imam and the prescribed punishment (al-ḥadd). If they repent before being referred to the imam, then turn away from them and do not bother them.

It has been said: the first verse was revealed concerning female homosexuals (al-siḥāqāt), and this one concerning male homosexuals (al-lūwāṭiyyīn).

It is also read: "wa-l-lazāni" with a shadda on the nun (واللذانّ بتشديد النون), and "wa-l-lazāni" with a hamza and a shadda on the nun (واللذانّ: بالهمزة وتشديد النون).

This was their punishment at the beginning of Islam, and then it was abrogated (nusikha) by the words of the Most High: "The fornicatress and the fornicator..." (الزَّانِيَةُ وَالزَّانِي) — the verse. It is also permissible that it is not abrogated, by leaving out mention of the prescribed punishment (al-ḥadd) because it is known from the Book and the Sunnah, and [the verse] enjoins keeping them in their houses after they have been restricted, as a protection for them from what befell them because of going out of the houses and exposing themselves to men.

"Or God makes for them a way" (أَوْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ لَهُنَّ سَبِيلًا) — this is marriage (al-nikāḥ), by which they become independent of illicit intercourse (al-sifāḥ). It has also been said: the way (al-sabīl) is the prescribed punishment (al-ḥadd), because that had not yet been legislated at that time.

If you say: what is the meaning of "death takes them" (يتوفاهن الموت), since al-tawaffī and al-mawt have one meaning, as if it were said: "until death causes them to die"? I say: it is permissible that it means "until the angels of death take them" (يتوفاهن ملائكة الموت), like His words: "those whom the angels take" (الَّذِينَ تَتَوَفَّاهُمُ الْمَلائِكَةُ), "those whom the angels take" (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ تَوَفَّاهُمُ الْمَلائِكَةُ), "say: the angel of death will take you" (قُلْ يَتَوَفَّاكُمْ مَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ). Or it means "until death takes them and their souls are fully taken" (يأخذهن الموت ويستوفى أرواحهن).

"And the two of you who commit it" (وَالَّذانِ يَأْتِيانِها مِنْكُمْ) — he means the male fornicator and the female fornicatress. "Then harm them" (فَآذُوهُما): rebuke them, blame them, and say to them: "Have you no shame? Do you not fear God?" (أما استحييتما، أما خفتما اللَّه). "If they repent (فَإِنْ تابا) and make amends (وَأَصْلَحا) and change their condition (وغيرا الحال), then turn away from them (فَأَعْرِضُوا عَنْهُما)": stop the rebuke and blame, for repentance prevents the deserving of blame and punishment.

It may be that this is addressed to the witnesses who came upon their secret, and that "harm" means blaming them, rebuking them, and threatening them with referral to the imam and the prescribed punishment (al-ḥadd). If they repent before being referred to the imam, then turn away from them and do not bother them.

It has been said: the first verse was revealed concerning female homosexuals (al-siḥāqāt), and this one concerning male homosexuals (al-lūwāṭiyyīn).

It is also read: "wa-l-lazāni" with a shadda on the nun (واللذانّ بتشديد النون), and "wa-l-lazāni" with a hamza and a shadda on the nun (واللذانّ: بالهمزة وتشديد النون).

Repentance (tawba): one whom God forgives is one whom God has accepted in repentance and pardoned. That is, acceptance and forgiveness are binding upon God, exalted is He. [[Mahmud said: "That is, acceptance and forgiveness are binding upon God... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: It has been mentioned in several places that the use of such phrasing, as in the statement "it is binding upon God to do such-and-such," is something we seek refuge in God from. Exalted is the Lord of lords above obligation and compulsion. The principle of Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni community) is that whatever favour God bestows, He bestows it not out of any prior entitlement. They say that the acts which the Qadariyya (the school that affirms human power over one's acts) imagine the servant to deserve from God are all creations of God. It is He who created obedience for His servant and rewarded him for it, and He who created repentance for him and accepted it from him. He is the Benefactor first and last, inwardly and outwardly. This is unlike the Qadariyya, who claim that the servant created repentance for himself by his own power and strength, so that he may merit forgiveness from his Lord by the requirement of divine wisdom, which, in their view, necessitates recompense for deeds as a rational obligation. That is why they use this expression with the tongue of audacity. How monstrous is al-Zamakhshari's reinforcement of this corrupt belief with his words: "It is binding upon God to accept repentance, just as it is binding upon the servant to perform some acts of obedience." He has equated the Creator with the created and compared the Lord with the servant. This is an expression from which the tongue of the sensible restrains itself, whose skin shivers at hearing it, and at which the pen stumbles as it writes it down. Yet it is one of God's kindnesses that He did not make one who repeats unbelief a disbeliever, nor one who repeats an innovation an innovator, for the necessity of rejecting it and warning against it. Al-Zamakhshari went to this extreme in this expression only out of eagerness to seize an opportunity to argue for its soundness through the word "upon" (ʿala), which suggests obligation. He made it a pretext to permit this expression, but God did not grant him any ease in it. We, the people of the Sunna, say that God has promised acceptance of repentance that fulfils the conditions of validity, and the fulfilment of this promise is necessary by the certainty of the report. Whenever forms of obligation occur, they are to be understood as the obligation of fulfilling a promise. The meaning of our saying "the truth of the report is necessary" is like the meaning of our saying "the existence of God is necessary," for no one can impose any obligation upon God. May God grant us proper manners toward His majesty and protect us from deviation of speech and misguidance.]] These are the ones (who are forgiven). In ignorance (bi-jahala) is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: they commit evil while ignorant and foolish, because the commission of ugly acts is prompted by folly and desire, not by wisdom and reason. It is related from Mujahid: "Whoever disobeys God is ignorant until he withdraws from his ignorance." Soon (min qarib) means within a near time. The near time is what precedes the presence of death. Do you not see His saying, ﴿until when death comes to one of them﴾? This makes clear that the time of the approach of death is the time when repentance is no longer accepted, so what lies before that falls under the ruling of "near." It is related from Ibn Abbas: "Before the authority of death descends upon him." It is related from al-Dahhak: "Every repentance before death is near." It is related from al-Nakha'i: "As long as the soul has not been seized by the throat."

Abu Ayyub narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "God accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not begun the death rattle." [[I have not found it in the hadith of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari as this wording suggests. Al-Tabari only cited it through the chain of Qatada, from al-Ala' ibn Ziyad, from Abu Ayyub Bashir ibn Ka'b, and mentioned it. Bashir is a well-known Successor, and his name is written with a b and a sh, diminutive form. Qatada has another chain for it, which al-Tabari also cited through the same chain. He said: from Qatada, from Ubada ibn al-Samit. By this route Ishaq ibn Rahawayh also cited it, and it is a broken chain (munqati') between Qatada and Ubada. On this topic there is also a report from Ibn Umar, cited by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani, in whose chain is Abd al-Rahman ibn Thabit ibn Thawban, about whom there is disagreement. There is also one from Abu Hurayra, cited by al-Bazzar, in which is Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik al-Nawfali, who is weak. But it has another route, cited by Ibn Mardawayh from a Companion who was among those cited by Ahmad and al-Hakim through the narration of Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami. He said: Four of the Companions gathered, and he mentioned the hadith, and the fourth said: "I heard him (ﷺ) say to me: 'God accepts the repentance of the servant before he begins the death rattle.'"]] It is related from Ata': "Nor before his death by the span of a she-camel's milking." It is related from al-Hasan that when Iblis was sent down to the earth he said: "By Your might, I will not leave the son of Adam as long as his spirit is in his body." God said: "By My might, I will not close the door of repentance upon him as long as he has not begun the death rattle." [[Al-Tha'labi cited it through the narration of Amr ibn Ubayd from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said... and mentioned it. I say: It has a witness from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, cited by Ahmad, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani.]]

If you say: What is the meaning of "from" (min) in His saying, ﴿soon﴾? I say: Its meaning is partitive, that is, they repent within some part of a near time. It is as though he called the period between the committing of the sin and the approach of death a near time. So whatever part of this time he repents in, he repents soon; otherwise he repents late.

If you say: What is the benefit of His saying, ﴿then those, God will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, after His saying, ﴿Repentance is only upon God for those﴾? I say: His saying, ﴿Repentance is only upon God﴾, is an announcement that it is binding upon Him, just as some acts of obedience are binding upon the servant. His saying, ﴿Those, I will turn to them﴾, is a promise that He will fulfil what is binding upon Him, and an announcement that forgiveness will certainly occur, just as the servant promises the fulfilment of what is obligatory.

﴿Nor those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ is conjoined to "those who do evil deeds." He equated those who postponed their repentance until the approach of death with those who died in disbelief, in that neither has repentance, because the approach of death is the first of the states of the Hereafter. Just as the one who dies in disbelief has certainly missed repentance, so the one who postpones to the approach of death has, because each of them has passed beyond the time of obligation and choice. ﴿For those, We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ corresponds in the threat to His saying, ﴿then those, God will turn to them﴾ in the promise, so that it becomes clear that both matters will certainly occur.

If you say: Who is meant by "those who do evil deeds"? Are they the sinners among the people of the qibla (the Muslim community), or the disbelievers? I say: There are two possibilities. One is that disbelievers are meant, on the apparent basis of His saying, ﴿and they are disbelievers﴾. The other is that sinners are meant, because the discourse concerns the two adulterers, and turning away from them is if they repent and reform. His saying, ﴿and they are disbelievers﴾ would then be stated as a form of severe warning, like His saying, ﴿And whoever disbelieves, God is independent of the worlds﴾, and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Let him die, if he wishes, as a Jew or a Christian," [[This was mentioned in the discussion of the verse of the pilgrimage in Al-i-Imran.]] and "Whoever abandons prayer deliberately has disbelieved." [[This was mentioned in al-Baqara.]] This is because whoever believes and dies without having resolved in himself to repent is close in state to the disbeliever, for only a hardened heart would dare to do that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 19:

The people used to persecute women with various kinds of trials and wrong them in various ways, so they were forbidden from that. A man, when a relative of his, a father, brother or close kinsman [[The phrase "akh hamim" in the Sihah is "hamimuk," meaning your relative whose affairs concern you. (ʿA)]] died, would throw his garment over a widow and say, "I have a greater right to her than anyone." [[Mahmud said: "When a man's relative died, he would throw his garment over his wife and say, 'I have a greater right to her than anyone...' etc." Ahmad said: God specifically mentioned those who had given a qintar of wealth in the prohibition, as a way of drawing attention from the greater to the lesser. For if this is forbidden despite the great amount he has given his wife in wealth, then to reclaim something small and insignificant from her in this way is forbidden, and one who has given only a little is forbidden from reclaiming it all the more. The meaning of His words "and you have given" (wa-ataytum), God knows best, is "and you had given," since the intention to exchange (al-istibdal) in the apparent sense occurs after the giving of the wealth and the establishment of the marriage.]] Then it was said: ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾, that is, to take them by way of inheritance as inheritances are seized while they are unwilling to be so; or they are being compelled. And it was said: a man would keep his wife until she died, so it was said:

﴿It is not lawful for you to keep them in your custody until you inherit from them while they are unwilling for you to keep them.﴾

When a man married a woman whom he did not need, he would detain her, treating her badly and oppressing her, so that she would ransom herself from him with her property and seek khul' (divorce in exchange for compensation). So it was said: ﴿Do not constrain them in order to take away part of what you have given them.﴾ *Al-ʿadl* (constraint) means detaining and restricting. From it comes the expression "the woman was constrained (ʿadalat) with her child," when her womb became tight around it, so that part of the child came out while part of it remained. ﴿Unless they commit a clear indecency﴾, which is rebellion (nushuz), bad character, and harming the husband and his family with abuse and foul speech. That is, unless the bad treatment comes from them, in which case you are excused for seeking khul'. This is supported by the recitation (qiraʾa) of Ubayy: "unless they commit indecency against you." It is reported from al-Hasan that "indecency" means fornication; if she does this, it becomes lawful for her husband to ask her for khul'. It was also said that when a woman committed indecency, they would take back what they had given her and expel her. It is reported from Abu Qilaba and Muhammad ibn Sirin: khul' is not lawful until a man is found upon her belly.

It is reported from Qatada: it is not lawful for him to detain her out of harm until she ransoms herself from him, meaning even if she has committed adultery. It was also said that this ruling was abrogated (naskh) by the prescribed punishments (hudud). They used to treat women badly in their dealings, so it was said to them: ﴿Live with them honourably﴾, which means justice in the matter of sleeping arrangements and maintenance, and kindness in speech. ﴿If you dislike them﴾, then do not separate from them merely because of the aversion of your souls, for the soul may dislike what is in fact better for religion, more beneficial and closer to good, and may love what is its opposite. Rather, one should look at the causes of what is right.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 20–21:

And when a man's eye was lifted (ṭamaḥat) [[His words "idhā ṭamaḥat ʿaynuh" mean: when his eye rose toward admiring a woman, to enjoy her in place of his wife. Reported by al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿA).]] toward taking a rare woman (istiṭrāf) , he would slander (bahata) the one under him and accuse her (ramāhā) [[His words "wa-ramāhā" mean: he accused her of what was not in her, as will be taken from what follows. (ʿA).]] of an indecency, until he compelled her to ransom herself from him with what he had given her, so that he could turn it toward marrying someone else. So it was said: ﴿And if you desire to exchange a wife in place of another wife...﴾ [4:20]. Al-qinṭār: great wealth, from qanṭartu al-shay’ idhā rafaʿtahu (I lifted the thing up). From it comes al-qanṭara (the bridge), because it is a lofty construction. He said:

*Like the bridge of the Roman, whose owner swore*
*that it would be surrounded until it is built with brick.*

[[From Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd in his Mu'allaqa, comparing his she-camel to the bridge of the Roman man, or the Roman river, which is more fitting to the definite article (lām al-ʿahd) and to mentioning the apparent noun after it. "Aqsama" is a circumstantial clause, meaning: he swore that it would not be surrounded with qirmid, that is gypsum, until it is built and raised with baked brick, or that the workmen would surround it until it is raised with gypsum. "Tuktanafan" is an imperfect verb in the passive voice, emphasized with the nūn.]]

And from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he stood up to deliver a sermon and said: "O people, do not exaggerate in the bridal gifts of women [[His words "lā tughālū bi-ṣadaq al-nisāʾ" : ṣadāq is the plural of ṣadāq, like suḥub the plural of saḥāb. (ʿA).]], for if it were an honour in this world or piety before Allah, the most deserving of you would be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He did not give any of his wives a bridal gift exceeding twelve ūqiyyas." Then a woman stood up to him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, why do you prevent us from a right that Allah has granted us, while Allah says: ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾ [4:20]?" ʿUmar said: "Every person knows more than ʿUmar." Then he said to his companions: "You hear me say such a statement, and you do not object to it, until a woman answers me who is not among the most knowledgeable of women." [[Narrated by the authors of the Sunan, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, Aḥmad, al-Dārimī, Ibn Abī Shayba and al-Ṭabarānī, all through Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn from Abū al-ʿAjfāʾ, who said: ʿUmar addressed us and mentioned it, without what is at its end. Al-Ḥākim narrated it from other routes from ʿUmar in the same way.

Al-Dāraquṭnī in al-ʿIlal mentioned many variations of this hadith. ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated it from the first route and added: a woman stood up and said to him, "That is not for you, O ʿUmar, and Allah says ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾, the verse." He said: "A woman argued with ʿUmar and defeated him." Abū Nuʿaym narrated it in al-Ḥilya in the biography of Shurayḥ from the route of Ashʿath ibn Sawwār from al-Shaʿbī from Shurayḥ, who said: ʿUmar said ... and mentioned it with the wording of the Sunan, and he considered it strange from this route. Isḥāq narrated it from the narration of ʿAṭā’ al-Khurasānī from ʿUmar, and it is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), and he added in it: "Then ʿUmar proposed to Umm Kulthūm, the daughter of ʿAlī, and he gave her a dowry of forty thousand." Abū Yaʿlā narrated from the route of Ibn Isḥāq: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to me from Mujālid from al-Shaʿbī from Masrūq, who said: ʿUmar mounted the pulpit and said, "O people, what is this excess in the bridal gifts of women? The bridal gifts between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions were four hundred dirhams or less. If excess in that were piety before Allah or honour, you would not have preceded them to it." Then he descended, and a woman of Quraysh confronted him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, you forbade people from increasing the bridal gifts of women beyond four hundred." He said: "Yes." She said: "Did you not hear Allah say ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾ ... the verse?" ʿUmar said: "O Allah, forgive me; everyone understands more than ʿUmar." Then he returned, mounted the pulpit, and said: "Whoever wishes to give from his wealth what he likes, let him do so."]]. And bahtān: that you confront a man with an ugly matter, slandering him with it while he is innocent of it, because he is then struck dumb (yabhat), that is, bewildered. Bahtānan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: stupefied and sinful; or it is an object of purpose even though it is not the motive, like your saying: he sat down out of cowardice at the battle. The solemn covenant (mīthāq ghalīẓ) is the right of companionship and intimacy, as if it were said: and they have taken from you a solemn covenant, that is, by the mutual union of some of you with others. Its description as "solemn" is due to its strength and greatness; they said: companionship for twenty days creates kinship, so how much more is what occurs between spouses of union and blending? It was also said: it is the statement of the guardian at the contract: "I have married you on what is in the Book of Allah, by keeping with kindness or releasing with goodness." And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Be good to the women [[This is composed of two hadiths. The first was narrated by al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Māja from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn al-Aḥwaṣ, who said: I witnessed the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he mentioned a hadith, in which: "Be good to women, for they are prisoners with you." (Benefit): ʿawān is the plural of ʿāniya, which means a captive.]] , for they are captives in your hands [[His words "fa-innahunna ʿawān fī aydīkum" : in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-ʿānī is the captive; a people are ʿunā and women are ʿawān. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 20–21:

And when a man's eye was lifted (ṭamaḥat) [[His words "idhā ṭamaḥat ʿaynuh" mean: when his eye rose toward admiring a woman, to enjoy her in place of his wife. Reported by al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿA).]] toward taking a rare woman (istiṭrāf) , he would slander (bahata) the one under him and accuse her (ramāhā) [[His words "wa-ramāhā" mean: he accused her of what was not in her, as will be taken from what follows. (ʿA).]] of an indecency, until he compelled her to ransom herself from him with what he had given her, so that he could turn it toward marrying someone else. So it was said: ﴿And if you desire to exchange a wife in place of another wife...﴾ [4:20]. Al-qinṭār: great wealth, from qanṭartu al-shay’ idhā rafaʿtahu (I lifted the thing up). From it comes al-qanṭara (the bridge), because it is a lofty construction. He said:

*Like the bridge of the Roman, whose owner swore*
*that it would be surrounded until it is built with brick.*

[[From Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd in his Mu'allaqa, comparing his she-camel to the bridge of the Roman man, or the Roman river, which is more fitting to the definite article (lām al-ʿahd) and to mentioning the apparent noun after it. "Aqsama" is a circumstantial clause, meaning: he swore that it would not be surrounded with qirmid, that is gypsum, until it is built and raised with baked brick, or that the workmen would surround it until it is raised with gypsum. "Tuktanafan" is an imperfect verb in the passive voice, emphasized with the nūn.]]

And from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he stood up to deliver a sermon and said: "O people, do not exaggerate in the bridal gifts of women [[His words "lā tughālū bi-ṣadaq al-nisāʾ" : ṣadāq is the plural of ṣadāq, like suḥub the plural of saḥāb. (ʿA).]], for if it were an honour in this world or piety before Allah, the most deserving of you would be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He did not give any of his wives a bridal gift exceeding twelve ūqiyyas." Then a woman stood up to him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, why do you prevent us from a right that Allah has granted us, while Allah says: ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾ [4:20]?" ʿUmar said: "Every person knows more than ʿUmar." Then he said to his companions: "You hear me say such a statement, and you do not object to it, until a woman answers me who is not among the most knowledgeable of women." [[Narrated by the authors of the Sunan, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, Aḥmad, al-Dārimī, Ibn Abī Shayba and al-Ṭabarānī, all through Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn from Abū al-ʿAjfāʾ, who said: ʿUmar addressed us and mentioned it, without what is at its end. Al-Ḥākim narrated it from other routes from ʿUmar in the same way.

Al-Dāraquṭnī in al-ʿIlal mentioned many variations of this hadith. ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated it from the first route and added: a woman stood up and said to him, "That is not for you, O ʿUmar, and Allah says ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾, the verse." He said: "A woman argued with ʿUmar and defeated him."
