Isḥāq narrated it from the narration of ʿAṭā’ al-Khurasānī from ʿUmar, and it is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), and he added in it: "Then ʿUmar proposed to Umm Kulthūm, the daughter of ʿAlī, and he gave her a dowry of forty thousand." Abū Yaʿlā narrated from the route of Ibn Isḥāq: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to me from Mujālid from al-Shaʿbī from Masrūq, who said: ʿUmar mounted the pulpit and said, "O people, what is this excess in the bridal gifts of women? The bridal gifts between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions were four hundred dirhams or less. If excess in that were piety before Allah or honour, you would not have preceded them to it." Then he descended, and a woman of Quraysh confronted him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, you forbade people from increasing the bridal gifts of women beyond four hundred." He said: "Yes." She said: "Did you not hear Allah say ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾ ... the verse?" ʿUmar said: "O Allah, forgive me; everyone understands more than ʿUmar." Then he returned, mounted the pulpit, and said: "Whoever wishes to give from his wealth what he likes, let him do so."]]. And bahtān: that you confront a man with an ugly matter, slandering him with it while he is innocent of it, because he is then struck dumb (yabhat), that is, bewildered. Bahtānan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: stupefied and sinful; or it is an object of purpose even though it is not the motive, like your saying: he sat down out of cowardice at the battle. The solemn covenant (mīthāq ghalīẓ) is the right of companionship and intimacy, as if it were said: and they have taken from you a solemn covenant, that is, by the mutual union of some of you with others. Its description as "solemn" is due to its strength and greatness; they said: companionship for twenty days creates kinship, so how much more is what occurs between spouses of union and blending? It was also said: it is the statement of the guardian at the contract: "I have married you on what is in the Book of Allah, by keeping with kindness or releasing with goodness." And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Be good to the women [[This is composed of two hadiths. The first was narrated by al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Māja from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn al-Aḥwaṣ, who said: I witnessed the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he mentioned a hadith, in which: "Be good to women, for they are prisoners with you." And in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, from the hadith of Abū Ḥāzim from Abū Hurayra, in the course of a hadith: "Be good to women, for they were created from a rib..." 

The second was narrated by Muslim in the lengthy hadith of Jābir about the description of Hajj, in which he said: "Fear Allah concerning women, for you have taken them under the trust of Allah and have made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah." Abū Yaʿlā, al-Bazzār and al-Ṭabarī narrated from the route of Mūsā ibn ʿUbayda al-Rabadhī, one of the weak narrators, from Ṣadaqa ibn Yasār from Ibn ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet: "O people, women are prisoners in your hands; you have taken them under the trust of Allah and made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah." (Benefit): ʿawān is the plural of ʿāniya, which means a captive.]] , for they are captives in your hands [[His words "fa-innahunna ʿawān fī aydīkum" : in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, al-ʿānī is the captive; a people are ʿunā and women are ʿawān. (ʿA).]]. You have taken them by the trust of Allah, and you have made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah."

Those who used to marry their stepmothers, and some of them would despise (the one who does so). Their saying "they used to marry their stepmothers" appears in *al-Sihah*: *al-Rabb* is the husband of one's mother, *al-Rabbah* is the wife of one's father, and *rabib* (stepson) is a man's son by his wife from another husband. *Nikah al-maqt* (the marriage of abhorrence) was the practice in the pre-Islamic period of marrying one's father's wife.

Commentary of Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari): "They used to marry their stepmothers, and some of them would despise (the one who does so)..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "In my view there is another secret in this exception, which is that this prohibited act, because of its heinousness and ugliness to most people, to the extent that it was abhorred even before the revelation of the Law, is worthy of having the prohibition obeyed, so that it is avoided. It is as though one has already obeyed the prohibition against it, until it becomes a report of its not occurring. It is as though it were said: the marriage of sons to the wives of their fathers does not occur, and nothing is taken from it except what has already passed. As for the future after the prohibition, nothing of it occurs at all. A similar reasoning applies to the words of God Most High: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: You shall worship none but Allah﴾. He made it a declarative statement and raised the verb, although the intended meaning is a prohibition against worshipping other than Allah. But since this prohibited thing is worthy of being avoided and it is as though it has been avoided, the prohibition was expressed in the form of a report and the verb was raised. This same estimation has already been made, but a similar one has not been applied in this verse, and God knows best."

"And it was an abomination (*maqtan*)," so it is said: "It is an indecency in the religion of God, extremely ugly, an abhorrent ugliness in manliness (*muruwwah*), and nothing can be added to what combines the two ugliness." It is read *la tahillu lakum* with a *ta'* (feminine form), taking *tarithu* to mean inheritance. *Karhan* is read with a fatha and with a damma, from *al-karahah* (dislike) and *al-ikrah* (compulsion). It is also read ﴿bi-fahishatin mubayyinatin﴾ from *abanat* in the sense of *tabayyanat* or *bayyanat*, just as ﴿mubayyinatin﴾ is read with a kasra and with a fatha on the *ya'*. ﴿Yaj'al Allah﴾ is read with a *raf'* (damma), as it is in the place of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). ﴿Wa-ataytum ihdahunna﴾ is read with the hamza of *ihdahunna* connected, just as ﴿fa-la ithma 'alayhi﴾ is read.

If you ask: what is the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of ﴿ta'dulunahunna﴾? I say: it is in the accusative, conjoined to ﴿an tarithu﴾, and the *la* is for emphasizing the negation. That is, "It is not lawful for you to inherit women, nor to prevent them (from remarrying)."

If you ask: what is the difference between transitivizing *dhahaba* with the *ba'* and with the hamza? I say: when it is transitivized with the *ba'*, its meaning is taking and accompanying, as in His words: ﴿falamma dhahabu bihi﴾. As for *idhhab*, it is like removal.

If you ask: what is this exception in ﴿illa an ya'tina﴾? I say: it is an exception from the most general of general circumstances or objects of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). It is as though it were said: "Do not prevent them at any time except the time when they commit an indecency." Or: "Do not prevent them for any reason except that they commit an indecency."

If you ask: in what respect is His words ﴿fa-'asa an takrahu﴾ valid as the answer (*jaza'*) to the condition? I say: in that the meaning is: "If you dislike them, then be patient with them despite your dislike, for perhaps God will place in what you dislike much good that is not in what you love."

If you ask: how is what your fathers married excepted from the prohibition, when it has already passed? I say: just as "except that their swords" is excepted from "and there is no fault in them" (the poet's saying), meaning: if it is possible for you to marry what has already passed, then marry it, but nothing else is lawful for you.

That is not possible. The purpose is to emphasize its prohibition and to close the path to its permissibility, just as things impossible are attached to eternity, like their saying: "until the crow turns white" and ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾.

The meaning of ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ is the prohibition of marrying them. [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is the prohibition of marrying them…" Ahmad said: This is a ramification of the view that a homonym (mushtarak) carries all its meanings together, so attaching the preposition to both was sound. And God knows best.]] This is based on His saying ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾. Also, the prohibition of marrying them is what is understood from their being forbidden, just as the prohibition of drinking is understood from the prohibition of wine, and the prohibition of eating is understood from the prohibition of the flesh of swine.

It was recited ﴿And the daughters of the sister﴾ with the hamza lightened. God has placed nursing (al-rada'a) in the position of lineage (nasab), so that the nursing mother is called "mother" of the nursling, and the women who nursed together are called "sisters." Likewise, the husband of the nursing mother is her "father," and her parents are his "grandparents." Her sister is his "paternal aunt." Every child born to her husband, whether before or after the nursing, from a woman other than the nursing mother, are his "brothers and sisters" from the father. The mother of the nursing mother is the nursling's "grandmother," and her sister is his "maternal aunt." Every child born to her from this husband are "brothers and sisters" from the father and mother, and whoever is born to her from another husband are "brothers and sisters" from the mother only.

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing." [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of 'A'isha and Ibn 'Abbas.]] They said: The prohibition by nursing is like the prohibition by lineage, except in two matters. The first: it is not permitted for a man to marry his son's sister by lineage, but it is permitted for him to marry his son's sister by nursing. This is because the impediment in lineage is his having intercourse with her mother, and this meaning does not exist in nursing. The second: it is not permitted to marry his brother's mother by lineage, but it is permitted by nursing, because the impediment in lineage is the father's intercourse with her, and this meaning does not exist in nursing.

﴿of your women﴾ is connected to ﴿your stepdaughters﴾ (rabā'ib). Its meaning is that the stepdaughter of a woman with whom one has consummated the marriage is forbidden to the man, but is lawful to him if he has not consummated the marriage with her mother.

If you say: Can it be connected to ﴿and the mothers of your women﴾? I say: It must be either that it is connected to them and to the stepdaughters, so that the prohibition of both is not restricted, or that it is connected to them without the stepdaughters, so that the prohibition of them is not restricted while the prohibition of the stepdaughters is restricted. The first is not permissible, because the meaning of "min" (from) with one of the two connections differs from its meaning with the other. Do you not see that when you say "and the mothers of your women from your women with whom you have consummated" you make "min" a specification of the women, distinguishing those consummated with from those not consummated with? But when you say "and your stepdaughters from your women with whom you have consummated," you make "min" indicate the starting point of the action, as you say: "The daughters of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from Khadija." It is not correct that one word in a single address should carry two different meanings. The second is not permissible either, because what follows the word is the one that requires it to be connected to it, unless some matter arises that cannot be avoided. Unless you say: I connect it to the women and the stepdaughters, and make "min" indicate continuity, as in His saying: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾, and as in the saying: "I am not of you and you are not of me," and "I am not of the enemy, nor is the enemy of me." The mothers of the women are continuous with the women, because they are their mothers, just as the stepdaughters are continuous with their mothers, because they are their daughters. [[End of his words. He said: "The second is not permissible because what follows it is what requires it to be connected to it, unless some matter arises that cannot be avoided, except that you say: I connect it to the women and the stepdaughters, and make 'min' indicate continuity, as in His saying: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾, and I am not of you and you are not of me… and the mothers of the women are continuous with the women because they…" Ahmad said: He means that this grammatical analysis (i'rab) has a valid form, and in this case "min" is used in one of its meanings, which is continuity, so its connection to both is sound. This view has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas. Also a recitation has been transmitted from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn al-Zubayr: ﴿and the mothers of your women, those with whom you have consummated﴾. Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "By God, it was revealed only in this way." End of al-Zamakhshari's quotation.]] The well-known view of the majority is that the prohibition of the mother is unrestricted, and the prohibition of the stepdaughter is restricted by the consummation with the mother, as is the apparent meaning of the verse.

There is a wisdom and secret behind this distinction. The man who marries a woman's daughter is not free, after the contract and before consummation, from conversation, address and close interaction between himself and her mother. So there is a need for the prohibition to take effect immediately, to cut off his desire for the mother, so that he treats her as one of the unmarriageable kin (dhawāt al-maḥārim). This is not so for one who contracts marriage with the mother, since he is far from addressing her daughter before consummation with the mother. So there is no need to hasten the spread of the prohibition.

As for when consummation with the mother has taken place, the likelihood of close association with the stepdaughter arises, and then the need calls for the prohibition to spread between them. And God knows best.

Here 'Umar and 'Imran ibn Husayn (may God be pleased with them both) said that the mother is forbidden by the contract itself. From Masruq: "It is unrestricted, so let loose what God has let loose." From Ibn 'Abbas: "Leave unrestricted what God has left unrestricted," except what was transmitted from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn al-Zubayr, that they recited: ﴿and the mothers of your women, those with whom you have consummated﴾, and Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "By God, it was revealed only in this way." From Jabir there are two reports. From Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Zayd: if the woman dies while married to him and he takes her inheritance, he dislikes marrying her mother. If he divorces her before consummation, then he may do as he wishes. The death takes the place of consummation in this matter, just as it takes its place in the matter of the dower (mahr).

The child of a woman from a husband other than the man is called "rabīb" (stepson) and "rabība" (stepdaughter), because he raises them (yurabbīhimā), as one usually raises one's own child. Then the term was extended to them, so they were called by it even if he did not raise them.

If you say: What is the benefit of His saying ﴿in your guardianship﴾? [[End of his words. He said: "If you say, what is the benefit of His saying 'in your guardianship'…" Ahmad said: This is from what I have already mentioned, the restriction of the highest form of what is forbidden to the forbidden. The prohibition of marrying the stepdaughter whose mother has been consummated with is general in all cases, whether she is in the husband's guardianship or separated from him in distant lands. But his marrying her while she is in his guardianship is the most abhorrent case, and the natural disposition recoils from it most. So it was singled out in the prohibition, so that human nature would be helped to submit to the rulings of the religion. Then this would be a training and a gradual step toward regarding the forbidden as abhorrent in all its forms. And God knows best.]] I say: Its benefit is the causal explanation of the prohibition, that they are unlawful to you because they are under your care, or because they are about to be under your care, and in the situation of being raised in your guardianship once you have consummated with their mothers. Your consummation takes the place of marriage, and close association and affection are established, and God has placed between you affection and mercy. The situation is fit for you to treat their children as your own children, as though, in contracting marriage to their daughters, you were contracting marriage to your own daughters.

From 'Ali (may God be pleased with him): he made this a condition of the prohibition, and Dawud (al-Zahiri) took this view.

If you say: What is the meaning of ﴿with whom you have consummated﴾? I say: It is a metaphor (kināya) for intercourse, like the expressions "he built upon her" and "he drew the veil upon her," meaning that you brought them behind the curtain. The "bi" (with) is for transitivity. Touching and the like take the place of consummation according to Abu Hanifa.

From 'Umar (may God be pleased with him): he was alone with a slave girl and stripped her, then his son asked her to be given to him as a gift, and he said: "She is not lawful to you." From Masruq: he ordered that his slave girl be sold after his death, and said: "As for me, I did not have from her except what would make her forbidden to my son by touching and looking." From al-Hasan, concerning a man who owns a female slave and caresses her out of desire, or kisses her, or uncovers her: she is not lawful to his son in any way. From 'Ata' and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman: if he looks at a woman's private part, he may not marry her mother or her daughter. From al-Awza'i: if he has consummated with the mother, by undressing her, touching her with his hand, closing the door and letting down the curtain, then the daughter is not lawful to him. From Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus and 'Amr ibn Dinar: the prohibition does not take effect except by intercourse alone.

﴿Of your loins﴾ excludes those whom you have adopted. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyya, the daughter of his paternal aunt Umayma bint 'Abd al-Muttalib, after Zayd ibn Haritha divorced her. [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Anas, with a different wording.]] The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿So that there will be no discomfort for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons﴾.

﴿And that you combine﴾ is in the accusative position (fī mawḍi' al-rafʿ) as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the prohibited things, meaning: and it is forbidden to you to combine two sisters. The intended meaning is the prohibition of marriage, because the prohibition in the verse is the prohibition of marriage. As for combining them in ownership by the right hand (milk al-yamīn), 'Uthman and 'Ali (may God be pleased with them both) said: "One verse made them lawful and another verse made them forbidden." [[As for the hadith of 'Uthman, it is in the Muwatta' from al-Zuhri, from Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb: "'Uthman was asked about two sisters whom one owns, and he said: I will not command you nor forbid you; one verse made them lawful and another made them forbidden." Al-Shafi'i reported it from Malik, and Ibn Abi Shayba through the route of Malik, and al-Daraqutni through the route of Ma'mar from al-Zuhri, and this is closer to the wording of the author. As for the hadith of 'Ali, al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Shayba and Abu Ya'la narrated it from the report of Abu Salih al-Hanafi who said: 'Ali said to the people: Ask me. Ibn al-Kawwa said: Inform us, O Commander of the Faithful, about two owned sisters. He said: One verse made them lawful and another made them forbidden, and I do not make them lawful, nor forbid them, nor do I do it, nor does anyone of my family.]] They mean this verse and His saying ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾. The prohibition was given precedence, while 'Uthman (took the view of) permissibility. [[As for 'Uthman, I did not find an explicit statement of permissibility from him, but rather he abstained. As for 'Ali, in the Muwatta' narration: then the questioner went out and met a man of the Companions, al-Zuhri said: I think he said 'Ali, and asked him, and he said to him: "But I forbid you, and if I had the power over doing it, I would make it a deterrent punishment."]]

﴿Except what has already passed﴾ [[Ahmad said: The placement of this exception is like the placement of its counterpart mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿and do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾ in the manner I explained, namely that this prohibition, being worthy of being obeyed, is treated as though it were a report of its being obeyed, as if it were said: none of these forbidden things occurs except what has already passed, and nothing else. Or in the manner explained by al-Zamakhshari earlier, namely that what is meant is "except what has already passed," since it is not forbidden, so do it if it is possible, as a conditional on the impossible used as a means of prohibition. However, al-Zamakhshari did not follow this course here, because His saying ﴿Indeed God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ indicates that what is meant by "except what has already passed" is that it is forgiven, by the exception in the first verse, because it is followed by His saying ﴿Indeed it was an abomination and hatred and an evil way﴾. So each verse is given the interpretation that fits its context. And God, glory be to Him, knows best.]] But what has passed is forgiven, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Indeed God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 4, Verse 24:**

The reading of ﴿وَالْمُحْصَنَاتُ﴾ is with a fatha on the ṣād (*al-qirā'a bi-fatḥ al-ṣād*). It is also narrated from Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif that he read it with a kasra on the ṣād. They are the women who have husbands, because they have guarded their chastity (*ahṣanna furūjahunna*) through marriage, so they are *muḥṣanāt* and *muḥṣanāt*. ﴿إِلَّا مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ﴾ means: what your right hands possess, referring to those captives who were taken while they had husbands in the land of disbelief. They are lawful for the warriors of the Muslims even though they are *muḥṣanāt*. A similar meaning is found in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*"And a woman with a husband, whom our spears have married off, is lawful for whoever consummates with her, so long as she was not divorced."*

[[Al-Farazdaq recited this verse in the assembly of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was asked about taking a captive woman who had a husband as a concubine. He said: "I used to think you were a better poet, but now you are both a better poet and a better jurist." The meaning is: many a woman with a husband has had the spears cause her marriage, so the attribution of marrying her to the spears is a figurative attribution (*majāz 'aqlī*). *Ḥalāl* is the predicate of *dhāt ḥalīl* (a woman with a husband). *Al-binā' bihā* is a metaphor for consummation, because a husband customarily builds a dwelling for her upon entering. *Lam tuṭallaq* ("who has not been divorced") is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*) from the pronoun in *bihā*.]]

﴿كِتَابَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun: that is, Allah has prescribed this for you as a written decree (*kitāban*), and has imposed it as an obligation (*farḍan*). It refers to the prohibition of what He has prohibited.

If you ask: what does ﴿وَأُحِلَّ لَكُمْ﴾ coordinate with? The answer: it coordinates with the implied verb that governs ﴿كِتَابَ اللَّهِ﴾. The meaning is: Allah has prescribed for you the prohibition of those, and has made lawful for you what lies beyond that. This is supported by the reading of al-Yamānī: *kataba Allāhu 'alaykum wa-uḥilla lakum*. It is also narrated from al-Yamānī: *kitāba Allāhi 'alaykum*, in the plural and nominative, meaning: these are the obligations of Allah upon you. Whoever reads *wa-uḥilla lakum* in the passive form has coordinated it with *ḥurrimat*.

﴿أَنْ تَبْتَغُوا﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lah*), meaning: He has clarified for you what is lawful and what is prohibited, with the intent that you seek [women] with your wealth (*bi-amwālikum*), which Allah has made a means of support for you, while you are chaste (*muḥṣinīna*) and not committing fornication (*ghayra musāfiḥīna*). This is so that you do not waste your wealth and impoverish yourselves in what is not lawful for you, and thus lose both your worldly life and your religion. There is no corruption greater than that which combines both losses.

*Al-iḥṣān* means chastity and the guarding of the self from falling into what is forbidden. *Al-amwāl* means the dower (*mahr*) and what is spent on marriage. If you ask: where is the object of *tabtaghū*? The answer: it may be understood as "the women," but the better view is that it is not to be supposed; it is as if it were said: that you spend your wealth. It may also be that *an tabtaghū* is a substitute (*badal*) for *warā'a dhālikum*.

*Al-musāfiḥ* is the fornicator, from *al-safḥ*, which is pouring out semen. The immoral man would say to the immoral woman: "Pour yourself out for me" (*sāfiḥīnī*), and "Give me your fluid" (*māḏīnī*), from *al-madhy* (pre-seminal fluid).

﴿فَمَا اسْتَمْتَعْتُمْ بِهِ مِنْهُنَّ﴾: whatever you have enjoyed from them among those married women, whether by intercourse, by a valid privacy (*khalwa ṣaḥīḥa*), or by a valid contract with them, ﴿فَآتُوهُنَّ أُجُورَهُنَّ﴾ give them their wages for it. The returning pronoun to *mā* is omitted because it causes no confusion, as in His saying: ﴿فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ مِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ﴾, with the pronoun dropped from it. It is also permissible that *mā* refers to the women, and *min* is partitive or explanatory. The pronoun then refers to it by its wording in *bihi*, and by its meaning in ﴿فَآتُوهُنَّ﴾. *Ujūrahunna* means their dowers (*mahurahunna*), because the dower is a reward for the use of the womb (*al-buḍ'*).

﴿فَرِيضَةً﴾ is a circumstantial accusative from *al-ujūr*, meaning "obligated," or it has been placed in the position of *ītā'* (giving), because giving is obligatory, or it is an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: He has made that an obligation as an obligation.

﴿فِيمَا تَرَاضَيْتُمْ بِهِ مِنْ بَعْدِ الْفَرِيضَةِ﴾: there is no fault in what you mutually agree upon after the obligation, such as one reducing something of the dower, or the wife giving up all of it, or the husband increasing it for her beyond its amount. It is said that it means what the two agree upon of continuing the marriage or separation.

It is also said that this verse was revealed concerning the *mut'ah* (temporary marriage) which was for three days, [[The phrase "which was for three days" means that this period was permitted and then abrogated (*nusikhat*, from *naskh*, abrogation). (Ibn 'Aṭiyya? — marked (ʿ) in the source.)]] when Allah opened Makkah to His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and then it was abrogated. A man would marry a woman for a set time, a night or two nights or a week, for a garment or something else, and would satisfy his desire from her and then release her. It was called *mut'ah* because of his enjoyment of her, or because of his giving her enjoyment by what he gives her.

From Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I will not be brought a man who marries a woman for a fixed term except that I will stone them both with stones." [[Narrated by Muslim and Ibn Ḥibbān through the route of Jābir from him, within a longer hadith.]]

From the Prophet (ﷺ) that he permitted it, then in the morning he said: "O people, I had commanded you to enjoy these women. Indeed, Allah has prohibited it until the Day of Resurrection." [[Narrated by Muslim from the report of al-Rabī' ibn Maysara from his father. (Benefit): His saying "then in the morning" does not mean that he said this on the morning after the night in which he had permitted it the day before; rather, he meant that he said it in the morning.]]

It is also said: it was permitted twice and prohibited twice.

From Ibn 'Abbās: "It is muḥkam," meaning it was not abrogated, and he used to recite: *famā istamtaʿtum bihi minhunna ilā ajalin musammā* ("whatever you have enjoyed from them for a specified term"). It is narrated that he retracted this at his death and said: "O Allah, I repent to You from my saying about mut'ah, and my saying about *al-ṣarf*." [[As for his retraction regarding mut'ah, al-Tirmidhī narrated it from him through a weak chain. As for his statement "O Allah, I repent to You from my saying about mut'ah," I have not found it. As for "I repent to You from my saying about *al-ṣarf*," the meaning of it is narrated from him through several routes. Among them is what Abū Ya'lā narrated through the route of 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Nu'aym, who said: Abū Sa'īd came to Ibn 'Abbās and mentioned his debate with him about *al-ṣarf*, and in it: "Then I heard him say afterwards, 'O Allah, I repent to You from what I used to issue fatwā about to the people regarding *al-ṣarf*.'" Al-Nasā'ī has in *al-Kunā* another route from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he heard him say: "I seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him from my saying about *al-ṣarf*." Ibn 'Adī has, through the narration of Dāwūd ibn 'Alī from his father from his grandfather, that he abandoned his saying about *al-ṣarf* when he heard Abū Sa'īd narrate the prohibition of it. Ibn Mājah has, through the narration of Abū al-Jawzā', "I heard Ibn 'Abbās command *al-ṣarf*, then it reached me that he had retracted. Then I met him in Makkah and he said: 'Yes, it was only my own opinion.'" Al-Ḥākim has a similar report through the same route. Al-Ṭabarānī has, through the narration of Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Zunā, a lengthy report, and in it: "And I seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him." Al-Bukhārī in *al-Tārīkh* has, through the narration of Ibn Sīrīn, who said: "I bear witness, concerning twelve of the companions of Ibn Mas'ūd, that they witnessed Ibn 'Abbās repent from his saying about *al-ṣarf*," among them 'Ubayda al-Salmānī. 'Abd al-Razzāq said: al-Thawrī informed us from Abū Hishām al-Wāsiṭī from Ziyād, who said: "I was with Ibn 'Abbās in al-Ṭā'if, and he retracted regarding *al-ṣarf* seventy days before he died."]]

**al-Ṭawl** means favour and superiority. One says, "So-and-so has a *ṭawl* over so-and-so," meaning an excess and a superiority. One also says, "He has *ṭāl* over him" (*ṭawlan*), and such a man is *ṭā'il* (possessing superiority). The poet said:

*"He has increased my love for myself, that I am hateful to every man who is not superior (ghayr ṭā'il),*
*When he sees me he averts his gaze from between him and me, like the act of one who knows and yet feigns ignorance."*

These lines are by al-Ṭirimmāḥ ibn Ḥakīm. He means: my hatred of the one who does not show kindness has increased my love for myself, because when I hate him for his stinginess, I know that I am the opposite of him, and that my own soul is generous, so I love it. When he sees me, he lowers his gaze from me, as if he cuts off his line of sight between him and me, as the one who knows a thing does when he pretends not to notice it, out of dislike of seeing me or out of shame before me.

From this comes their saying, "He did not benefit from it with any *ṭā'il*," that is, with anything of worth that has excess and standing. From the same root comes *al-ṭawl* in reference to the body, because it is an addition to it, just as shortness (*qaṣr*) is a deficiency and lack in it.

The meaning: *"And whoever among you cannot afford (lam yastaṭi') an increase in wealth and abundance (ṭawlan) by which he can reach marriage with a free woman, let him marry a slave girl."* Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Whoever possesses three hundred dirhams, the Pilgrimage (ḥajj) becomes obligatory for him, and marriage with slave girls becomes forbidden to him."

This is the apparent meaning, and it is the position of al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him. As for Abū Ḥanīfa, may Allah have mercy on him, he says: the wealthy and the poor are equal in the permissibility of marrying a slave girl. He interprets the verse to mean that whoever does not possess a free woman's bed (*firāsh*), and since *nikāḥ* means intercourse, he may marry a slave girl. In a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, he said: "Among what Allah has granted this community in latitude is marriage with a slave girl, a Jewish woman, and a Christian woman, even if one is well-off."

Likewise His saying, *"from your believing slave girls" (min fatayātikumu l-mu'mināt)*: the apparent meaning is that marriage with a slave girl who is a People of the Book is not permissible. This is the position of the people of the Ḥijāz. The people of Iraq, however, say it is permissible. Marrying a believing slave girl is more excellent, so they interpret the phrase as indicating excellence and not obligation. They also cited, as evidence that faith is not a condition, that the description "believing" is attached to the free women as well, although we know that it is not a condition for them by consensus, but it is more excellent.

If you ask: why is marriage with a slave girl lower in rank than marriage with a free woman? I say: because it involves the child following the mother in slavery, because the master's right is established over her and over her service, and because she is humiliated, debased, going out and coming in, and all of that is a deficiency that returns to the one who marries her, and a disgrace. Honour is one of the attributes of the believers.

His saying *"from your slave girls"* means from the slave girls of the Muslims, not from the slave girls of others, who are those who differ in religion.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying, *"And Allah knows best your faith" (wa-llāhu aʿlamu bi-īmānikum)*? I say: its meaning is that Allah knows the difference between you and your slaves in faith, its superiority and its deficiency, in them and in you. It may be that the faith of a slave girl is weightier than the faith of a free woman, and that a woman is more excellent in faith than a man. It is incumbent on the believers not to consider anything except the excellence of faith, and not the excellence of lineage and ancestry. This is a means of making the marriage with slave girls agreeable and removing the aversion to it.

*"You are one from another" (baʿḍukum min baʿḍ)*: that is, you and your slaves are connected and related, because you share in faith. A free man has no superiority over a slave except through a superiority in faith.

*"With the permission of their people" (bi-idhni ahlihinna)*: this is a condition of the permission of their masters for their marriage. [Ibn al-Munayyir's note:] Ibn al-Munayyir said: there is no condition in the verse that the master's permission is needed for one who undertakes the marriage contract for his slave girl. The one who conducts the contract and handles it is left unmentioned in the verse. It is therefore taken to mean his permission to his agent to contract on his slave girl. It does not follow that the slave girl herself must conduct it, and there is no proof in the verse for that. And Allah knows best.

This verse is cited by those who hold, like Abū Ḥanīfa, that they may conduct the contract themselves, because it made the permission of the masters the condition, not their contract.

*"And give them their bridal payments (ujūrahunna) in accordance with what is reasonable"*: pay them their dowries (mahr) without procrastination, harm, or the need to demand them and to press for them. If you ask: the masters are the owners of their dowries, not the women, and what is obligatory is to pay them to the masters, not to the women, so why was it said *"give them"*? I say: because they and what is in their hands are the property of the masters, so paying them is paying the masters. Or the original phrase is "give their masters," and the object has been omitted.

*"Chaste (al-muḥṣanāt)"*: modest, virtuous.

*"Secret lovers" (akhdān)*: friends in secret. As if it were said: not openly committing fornication, nor secretly doing so.

*"And when they are chaste (uḥṣinna)"* by marriage. It is also read *uḥṣina* (passive). *"Half of the punishment for the free women (al-muḥṣanāt)"*: that is, the free women, *"of the punishment"*, meaning of the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), like His saying, *"and let a group of the believers witness their punishment"* and *"it averts from her the punishment."* There is no stoning (rajm) for them, because stoning cannot be halved.

*"That"* refers to marriage with slave girls, *"for him who fears (khashiya) distress (al-ʿanat)"*: for one who fears the sin to which the overpowering of desire leads. The root meaning of *ʿanat* is the breaking of a bone after it has been set, so it is used figuratively for any hardship and harm. No harm is greater than falling into sins. It has also been said that what is meant is the prescribed punishment, because when one desires her he fears that he will have intercourse with her and be punished, so he marries her.

*"And that you be patient" (wa-an tasbirū)*: in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), meaning: your patience in refraining from marriage with slave girls, while being chaste, *"is better for you"*.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Free women are the righteousness of the house, and slave girls are the ruin of the house." [The commentator's note:] Al-Thaʿlabī narrated it through the report of Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Yūnus al-Yamāmī: Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf al-ʿIjlī narrated to us; Yūnus ibn Mirdās, servant of Anas, narrated to us, who said: "I was with Anas and Abū Hurayrah, and Anas said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, 'Whoever loves to meet Allah pure and purified, let him marry free women.' Abū Hurayrah said: I heard him say, 'Free women are the righteousness of the house, and slave girls are the ruin of the house,' or he said, 'the destruction of the house.'" I say: in its chain is Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, who is abandoned (matrūk), and Abū Ḥātim called him a liar; and Yūnus, I do not know him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on Surah 4, verses 26–28:

﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ Its original form is يريد الله أن يبين لكم, and the *lam* was added to emphasise the intention of making clear, just as it was added in لا أبالك (*la abālak*, "may you have no father"), to emphasise the attribution of the father. The meaning is: God wills to make clear to you what is hidden from you of your welfare and of the most excellent of your deeds, and to guide you to the paths of those before you, the prophets and the righteous, and to the ways they followed in their religion, so that you may follow them. ﴿وَيَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ and He will turn to you in forgiveness, and guide you to acts of obedience which, if you perform them, will be expiations for your misdeeds, so He will forgive you and expiate for you.

﴿وَاللَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ means: God wills that you do the things that make you deserving of His forgiveness.

﴿وَيُرِيدُ الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ الشَّهَوَاتِ أَنْ تَمِيلُوا مَيْلًا عَظِيمًا﴾ The wicked ones who follow their desires want you to deviate with a great deviation, which is turning away from the right course and from truth. No deviation is greater than this, through helping them and agreeing with them in following desires. It is said: they are the Jews. It is said: they are the Magians, who used to permit marriage to sisters on the father's side, to the daughters of a brother and the daughters of a sister. When God forbade these, they said: "You permit marriage to the daughter of the maternal aunt and the paternal aunt, yet the maternal aunt and the paternal aunt are forbidden to you, so marry the daughters of the brother and the sister." Then this was revealed. God says: they want you to become fornicators like them.

﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُخَفِّفَ عَنْكُمْ﴾ This refers to the permission to marry a slave woman and other concessions.

﴿وَخُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ ضَعِيفًا﴾ Man is created weak, unable to be patient with desires or with the hardships of acts of obedience.

It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: "Satan has never despaired of the children of Adam except that he came to them through women. Eighty years have passed over me, one of my eyes has gone, and I see with the other. Indeed, what I fear most for myself is the temptation of women."

It is read as أن يميلوا (*an yamīlū*) with the *yā'*, and the pronoun refers to "those who follow their desires".

Ibn 'Abbas read ﴿وَخُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ﴾ with the verb in the active form (*al-bināʾ lil-fāʿil*) and with الإنسان in the accusative (*naṣb*), as the object.

It is also related from him, may God be pleased with him: "Eight verses in Surah al-Nisa' are better for this Ummah than all that the sun rises upon and sets over":

[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab*, in the forty-seventh chapter, through the narration of Salih al-Mizzi from Qatadah, who said, Ibn 'Abbas said: "Eight verses in Surah al-Nisa' are better for this Ummah than all that the sun rises upon: the first of them is (﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾), and so on." It is also in al-Tabari by this route. Salih is weak, and Qatadah's report from Ibn 'Abbas is discontinuous (*munqaṭiʿ*).]]

﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾, ﴿وَاللَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, ﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُخَفِّفَ عَنْكُمْ﴾, ﴿إِنْ تَجْتَنِبُوا كَبَائِرَ مَا تُنْهَوْنَ عَنْهُ﴾, ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَغْفِرُ أَنْ يُشْرَكَ بِهِ﴾, ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَظْلِمُ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ﴾, and ﴿مَنْ يَعْمَلْ سُوءًا أَوْ يَظْلِمْ نَفْسَهُ﴾,

﴿مَا يَفْعَلُ اللَّهُ بِعَذَابِكُمْ﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on Surah 4, verses 26–28:

﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ Its original form is يريد الله أن يبين لكم, and the *lam* was added to emphasise the intention of making clear, just as it was added in لا أبالك (*la abālak*, "may you have no father"), to emphasise the attribution of the father. The meaning is: God wills to make clear to you what is hidden from you of your welfare and of the most excellent of your deeds, and to guide you to the paths of those before you, the prophets and the righteous, and to the ways they followed in their religion, so that you may follow them. ﴿وَيَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ and He will turn to you in forgiveness, and guide you to acts of obedience which, if you perform them, will be expiations for your misdeeds, so He will forgive you and expiate for you.

﴿وَاللَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ means: God wills that you do the things that make you deserving of His forgiveness.

﴿وَيُرِيدُ الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ الشَّهَوَاتِ أَنْ تَمِيلُوا مَيْلًا عَظِيمًا﴾ The wicked ones who follow their desires want you to deviate with a great deviation, which is turning away from the right course and from truth. No deviation is greater than this, through helping them and agreeing with them in following desires. It is said: they are the Jews. It is said: they are the Magians, who used to permit marriage to sisters on the father's side, to the daughters of a brother and the daughters of a sister. When God forbade these, they said: "You permit marriage to the daughter of the maternal aunt and the paternal aunt, yet the maternal aunt and the paternal aunt are forbidden to you, so marry the daughters of the brother and the sister." Then this was revealed. God says: they want you to become fornicators like them.

﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُخَفِّفَ عَنْكُمْ﴾ This refers to the permission to marry a slave woman and other concessions.

﴿وَخُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ ضَعِيفًا﴾ Man is created weak, unable to be patient with desires or with the hardships of acts of obedience.

It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: "Satan has never despaired of the children of Adam except that he came to them through women. Eighty years have passed over me, one of my eyes has gone, and I see with the other. Indeed, what I fear most for myself is the temptation of women."

It is read as أن يميلوا (*an yamīlū*) with the *yā'*, and the pronoun refers to "those who follow their desires".

Ibn 'Abbas read ﴿وَخُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ﴾ with the verb in the active form (*al-bināʾ lil-fāʿil*) and with الإنسان in the accusative (*naṣb*), as the object.

It is also related from him, may God be pleased with him: "Eight verses in Surah al-Nisa' are better for this Ummah than all that the sun rises upon and sets over":

[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab*, in the forty-seventh chapter, through the narration of Salih al-Mizzi from Qatadah, who said, Ibn 'Abbas said: "Eight verses in Surah al-Nisa' are better for this Ummah than all that the sun rises upon: the first of them is (﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾), and so on." It is also in al-Tabari by this route. Salih is weak, and Qatadah's report from Ibn 'Abbas is discontinuous (*munqaṭiʿ*).]]

﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾, ﴿وَاللَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, ﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُخَفِّفَ عَنْكُمْ﴾, ﴿إِنْ تَجْتَنِبُوا كَبَائِرَ مَا تُنْهَوْنَ عَنْهُ﴾, ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَغْفِرُ أَنْ يُشْرَكَ بِهِ﴾, ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَظْلِمُ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ﴾, and ﴿مَنْ يَعْمَلْ سُوءًا أَوْ يَظْلِمْ نَفْسَهُ﴾,

﴿مَا يَفْعَلُ اللَّهُ بِعَذَابِكُمْ﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 29–30:

bil-batil (unjustly): by what the Shari'ah has not permitted, such as theft, embezzlement, usurpation, gambling, and contracts of usury. ﴿Illa an takuna tijaratan﴾ (except that it be a trade): i.e., except that a trade take place. It is also read as tijaratun (a trade), meaning: except that the trade be a trade. ﴿'An taradin minkum﴾ (by mutual consent from among you): the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), its meaning being: "but intend that it be a trade by mutual consent from among you."

Or: "but that it be a trade by mutual consent which is not forbidden." The phrase ﴿'an taradin﴾ is an attribute of tijaratun, i.e., a trade proceeding from mutual consent. Trade was singled out for mention because most of the causes of provision are connected with it.

Mutual consent (taradi) is the agreement of the two contracting parties to what they have concluded at the time of the sale, at the moment of offer and acceptance; this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, it is their separation from the session of the contract while still in mutual consent.

﴿Wa la taqtulu anfusakum﴾ (and do not kill yourselves): those among you who are of your own kind, the believers. It is reported from al-Hasan: "Do not kill your brethren," or: "A man should not kill himself, as some ignorant people do." It is reported from Amr ibn al-As that he interpreted it in the case of tayammum for fear of cold, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not censure him. [[Abu Dawud related it from the narration of Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr, from Ibn al-As, who said: "I had a wet dream on a cold night during the expedition of Dhat al-Salasil, and I feared that if I performed ghusl I would perish, so I performed tayammum and then led my companions in the dawn prayer. They mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'O Amr, you led your companions in prayer while you were junub?' I informed him of what had prevented me from bathing, and I said: 'I heard Allah say: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed and said nothing."

Al-Bukhari suspended it, saying: "It is related from Amr ibn al-As." This hadith has been differed upon regarding Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Imran ibn Anas, from Abd al-Rahman. Yahya ibn Ayyub related it thus, but Amr ibn al-Harith differed in both isnad and matn. As for the isnad, he added Abu Qays, the freedman of Amr, between Abd al-Rahman and Amr. As for the matn, he said, in place of tayammum: "he performed wudu' and washed his folds (maghabin)." Ibn Lahi'ah agreed with Yahya ibn Ayyub on it, according to Ishaq ibn Rahawayh; Ahmad related it with the first isnad, Ibn Hibban with the second, and al-Hakim and al-Daraqutni related it with both isnads.]]

And he (Ali, may Allah be pleased with him) read ﴿wa la taqtullu﴾ with the doubled letter. ﴿Inna Allaha kana bikum raheema﴾ (indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you): He forbade you only what would harm you, out of His mercy toward you. It has also been said: the meaning is that He commanded the Children of Israel to kill themselves, as a repentance for them and an expiation of their sins; and "He was merciful to you, O community of Muhammad," in that He did not impose upon you those harsh obligations.

﴿Dhalika﴾ (that): refers to killing. I.e., whoever commits the killing of souls ﴿'udwanan wa zulman﴾ (in transgression and wrongdoing), not by mistake and not by retaliation. It is read ﴿'udwanin﴾ with kasrah. ﴿Nuslihi﴾ is read with the lam lightened and with it doubled. ﴿Nuslihi﴾ with fath on the nun, from salaha yaslihi (to roast/burn), whence comes shatun musallah (a roasted sheep). ﴿Yuslihi﴾ with ya', the pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted, or to that, because it is the cause of being roasted in fire, i.e., a specific fire of severe torment. ﴿Wa kana dhalika 'ala Allahi yasira﴾ (and that is ever easy for Allah): because wisdom calls for it, and nothing turns Him away from it, such as injustice or the like.
