Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 31:

﴿Kabā'ira mā tunhawna 'anhu﴾ (the major sins that you are forbidden from). It is also read: kabīra mā tunhawna 'anhu (kabīra in the singular), meaning: whatever is great of the sins which Allah and the Messenger have forbidden you. ﴿Nukaffir 'ankum sayyi'ātikum﴾ (We will remove from you your bad deeds), in proportion to what you deserve of punishment at every time for your minor sins, and We will make them as if they had never been, in order to increase the reward due for your avoidance of the major sins and your patience in refraining from them, over the punishment for the bad deeds. The major sin (kabīra) and the minor sin (ṣaghīra) are described as great and small only by their being attributed either to obedience or to disobedience, or to the reward of their doer [[The phrase "or to the reward of their doer": i.e., its recompense. It is possible that the original wording was "the reward of the one who abstains from them", and the copyist altered it, so let it be checked. (ʿ)]]. Takfīr (expiation) is the removal of the punishment that is due by a greater reward, or by repentance.

Iḥbāṭ (nullification) is its opposite, and it is the removal of the reward that is due by a greater punishment, or by regret over an act of obedience. It is narrated from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: The major sins are seven: polytheism (shirk), killing, slander (qadhf), fornication (zinā), consuming the property of an orphan, fleeing from the battlefield, and becoming a bedouin again after migration (taʿarrub baʿda al-hijra) [[Al-Ṭabarī narrated it through Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq from Muḥammad ibn Sahl ibn Khuthayma from his father, who said: "I was in this mosque, the mosque of Kufa, and ʿAlī was giving a sermon," and he mentioned it. His saying "Ibn ʿUmar added the violation of the Sacred House (istiḥlāl al-bayt al-ḥarām)" was narrated by Abū Dāwūd through the same route as a marfūʿ report, and al-Thaʿlabī narrated it as mawqūf.]]. Ibn ʿUmar added: sorcery (siḥr), and violating the sanctity of the Sacred House (istiḥlāl al-bayt al-ḥarām). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man said to him: "Are the major sins seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seven hundred, for there is no minor sin with persistence, and no major sin with seeking forgiveness" [[ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: Maʿmar narrated to us from Ibn Ṭāwūs from his father, who said: It was said to Ibn ʿAbbās, "The major sins are seven." He said: "They are nearer to seventy." Al-Ṭabarī narrated from the report of Qays ibn Saʿd from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās that a man asked him about the major sins, "Are they seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seven hundred, for there is no minor sin..." to the end.]]. And it is reported as "nearer to seventy." It is also read: yukaffir (with the ya'), in the third person.

And (mudkhalan) is read with a damma and with a fatha on the mīm, and in both readings it means either a place or a verbal noun.

Do not envy one another. (The verse says:) "And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others." This forbids envy and forbids wishing for what Allah has favoured some people with over others, in rank and wealth, because that distribution is an apportionment from Allah, issuing from wisdom, providence, and knowledge of the circumstances of His servants and of what befits the one to whom it is apportioned, whether expansion or restriction of provision. (As Allah says:) "And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely transgress upon the earth." So every person must be content with what has been apportioned to him, knowing that what has been apportioned to him is his benefit, and that had it been otherwise it would be a corruption for him. Nor should he envy his brother for his share.

"For men there is a share of what they have earned." The apportionment made to each of men and women is according to what Allah knows of their condition, which necessitates expansion or restriction, and it is their acquisition (kasb).

"And ask Allah of His bounty." That is, do not wish for the shares of others of the bounty, but ask Allah from His treasures, which never run out.

It is said: The men said, "Allah has favoured us over the women in this world: we have two shares and they have one share, so we hope that we will have two rewards in the Hereafter for our deeds, and they will have one reward." Then Umm Salamah and some women with her said, "Would that Allah had prescribed jihad upon us as He prescribed it upon the men, so that we would have a reward like theirs." Then this verse was revealed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 33:

"For each" (likull) is an explanation: that is, for each thing of what the parents and the close relatives leave of wealth, We have made heirs (mawali) who inherit it and take possession of it. Or: for each people We have made heirs, a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave, on the basis that "We have made heirs" (ja'alna mawali) is a qualifier of "for each" (kull), and the pronoun referring back to "kull" is omitted, and the statement is a subject and predicate, as you would say: "for each of those whom God created as a human being, from God's provision," meaning a portion of God's provision. Or: "and for each person We have made heirs (mawali) of what he leaves," meaning inheritors of what he leaves, on the basis that "min" (of) is connected to "mawali," since they carry the sense of inheritors (warrath), and in "taraka" (he leaves) there is a pronoun referring to "kull." Then the mawali are explained by His words: "the parents and the close relatives," as if it were said: "Who are they?" and it was answered: "the parents and the close relatives."

"And those with whom your oaths have made a pact" (alladhina 'aqadat aymanukum) is a subject (mubtada') that carries the sense of a conditional. Its predicate is therefore introduced with the fa', which is His words: "then give them their share" (fa-atuhum nasibahum). It is permissible for it to be in the accusative, as in your saying: "Zayd, so strike him." It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with "the parents" (al-walidan), with the pronoun in "fa-atuhum" referring to the mawali. The intended meaning of "those with whom your oaths have made a pact" is the mawali of alliance (muwalat). A man would make a pact with another man, saying: "My blood is your blood, and my ruin is your ruin (damī damuka, wa-hadmī hadmuka), and my vengeance is your vengeance, and my war is your war, and my peace is your peace; you inherit from me and I inherit from you; you seek retribution on my behalf and I seek it on yours; you pay blood-money on my behalf and I pay it on yours." Then the ally would receive a sixth of the ally's inheritance, and this was abrogated.

[[The words "my blood is your blood and my ruin is your ruin" are explained in the Sihah: "al-hadm" (with a vowel on the first letter) is what collapses from the sides of a well and falls into it. It is said: "their blood is between them hadm," meaning wasted (hadr). Hadm is also pronounced with a sukun, when they do not pay blood-money.]]

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he gave a sermon on the day of the Conquest and said: "Whatever alliance existed in the Jahiliyyah, hold fast to it, for Islam has not increased it except in strength, and do not create a new alliance in Islam." [[This is composed of two hadiths recorded by al-Tabari: from the hadith of Qays ibn 'Asim, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whatever alliance existed in the Jahiliyyah, hold fast to it." And from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said in his sermon on the day of the Conquest: "Fulfil the alliance, for Islam does not increase it except in strength. And do not create an alliance in Islam." And on this subject there is a report from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, traced back to the Prophet: "There is no alliance in Islam." Both of them (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it.]]

According to Abu Hanifa: if a man embraces Islam at the hand of another man, and they make a contract that they will pay blood-money for each other and inherit from each other, it is valid in his view, and he inherits by the right of alliance (muwalat), contrary to al-Shafi'i. It was also said: the pact (mu'aqada) is adoption (tabanni). The meaning of "your oaths have made a pact" is: your hands have made a pact with them and wiped over them (masahtumuhum). It is also read as "'aqadat" with shadda and without shadda, with the meaning that your oaths have bound their covenants.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 34:

﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ (qawwamuna 'ala al-nisa'), meaning they stand over them as those who command and forbid, as rulers stand over their subjects. They were called qawwamun (those who stand in charge) for this reason. The pronoun in ﴿some of them﴾ (ba'dahum) refers to men and women together. The meaning is that they have authority over them only because Allah has preferred some of them, namely the men, over others, namely the women.

In this is evidence that authority (wilaya, guardianship or governance) is deserved through merit, not through domination, overpowering, or coercion. They have mentioned the merits of men: intellect, firm judgment, resolve, strength, writing (generally), horsemanship, archery; that among them are prophets and scholars; and that to them belong the greater and lesser leadership (imama), jihad, the call to prayer (adhan), the sermon (khutba), i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque), the takbirat al-tashriq according to Abu Hanifa, testimony in the hudud (fixed punishments) and retaliation (qisas), the extra share of inheritance, residual inheritance by agnatic kinship (ta'sib) in inheritance, bearing blood-money (hamala), the qasama (oath procedure in homicide), guardianship in marriage, divorce and reconciliation (raj'a), the number of wives, that lineage is traced to them, and that they are the people of beards and turbans. ﴿And what they spend﴾ (wa-bima anfaqu), meaning because of what they have spent of their wealth on them in dowries and maintenance.

It is narrated that Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', who was one of the nuqaba' (chieftains) of the Ansar, was disobeyed by his wife Habiba bint Zayd ibn Abi Zuhayr, so he struck her. Her father then took her to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said:

"I gave my noble daughter in marriage to him, and he struck her."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let her take retaliation from him." Then ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We wanted one thing and Allah wanted another, and what Allah wanted is better."

[This is how al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi transmitted it from Muqatil. Abu Dawud in al-Marasil, Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Tabari transmitted from al-Hasan that a man slapped his wife's face, and she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and complained to him. He said: "Retaliation." Then ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ was revealed. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ali with a chain, or something similar, but he did not say "retaliation," and he added "I wanted one thing and Allah wanted something else."]

Retaliation was thus lifted. There is disagreement about this. It was said: there is no retaliation between a man and his wife for anything short of death, even if he wounds her, but blood-money is due. It was also said: there is no retaliation except for wounds and killing. As for a slap and the like, there is none.

﴿Obedient women, guarding the unseen﴾ (qanitatun hafizatun lil-ghayb). Al-ghayb (the unseen) is the opposite of the witnessed. That is, they guard what is required of them in the absence of their husbands, from their private parts, homes and property.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of women is the one who, when you look at her, pleases you; when you command her, she obeys you; and when you are absent from her, she guards you in her property and her self." And he recited the verse.

[Abu Dawud, al-Hakim and al-Tirmidhi transmitted it through Mujahid from Ibn Abbas: "When ﴿those who hoard gold and silver﴾ was revealed..." – the hadith, in which: "Shall I not tell you of the best treasure? A righteous wife: when he looks at her, she pleases him; when he commands her, she obeys him; and when he is absent from her, she guards him." Al-Nasa'i transmitted through Sa'id al-Maqbari from Abu Hurayra who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the best women, and he said: 'The one who obeys when commanded and pleases when looked at, and guards him in herself and his property.'" Its chain is good. Al-Bazzar, al-Hakim, al-Tabari and others transmitted it through various routes from Sa'id. On this topic there is also a report from Abu Umama in Ibn Majah, whose chain is weak; a report from Abdullah ibn Salam in al-Tabarani; and one from Thawban and others.]

It was said that "for the unseen" means for their secrets. ﴿With what Allah has guarded﴾ (bima hafiza Allah), meaning with what Allah has guarded them, when He enjoined them upon husbands in His Book and commanded His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), saying: "Be good to women." [Agreed upon from the hadith of Abu Hazim from Abu Hurayra. It has been mentioned earlier through another route.] Or: with what Allah has guarded and protected them, and granted them success in guarding the unseen. Or: with what Allah guarded them when He promised them a great reward for guarding the unseen and threatened them with severe punishment for betrayal. Here "ma" is a verbal noun (masdariyya).

It was also read as bima hafiza Allah with a fatha (accusative) on hafiza, taking "ma" as a relative pronoun (mawsula), meaning: guarding the unseen by means of that which guards Allah's right and Allah's trust, which is chastity, self-restraint, and sincere care and counsel for the men.

Ibn Mas'ud read: "So the righteous women are obedient, guarding the unseen with what Allah has guarded; so make them righteous toward them."

Nushuz and nushus: her disobedience to her husband, and she does not feel at ease with him. Its root meaning is agitation.

﴿In the beds﴾ (fi al-madaji'), meaning in the sleeping places. That is, do not let them under the grave (lahd), or it is a metaphor for intercourse. It was said: it means that he turns his back to her in bed. It was also said: "in the beds" means in their homes where they spend the night, that is, do not stay the night with them away. It was also read as fi al-madja' and fi al-mudtaji'. This is so that their condition may be known and their matter in disobedience may be verified. He first commanded admonition of them, then abandonment in the beds, then striking them if admonition and abandonment do not work on them.

It was said: the meaning is "compel them" to intercourse. [Mahmud [al-Zamakhshari] said: "And it was said that its meaning is compel them ..." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: Perhaps this interpreter is supported by His words ﴿if they obey you﴾, for it indicates that compulsion toward some matter came first, and the context of "the beds" points to intercourse. Al-Zamakhshari's wording against this interpreter is excessive.] And "wadribuhunna" (strike them) from "hajara al-ba'ir," when he tied the camel with a rope (hijar).

This is from the interpretation of the weak-minded. They said: the striking must be non-severe, one that does not wound her, does not break a bone, and avoids the face. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hang your whip where your family can see it." [Al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad transmitted it from Ibn Abbas, in whose chain is Ibn Abi Layla the judge, who is weak. On this topic there is also a report from Ibn Amr, transmitted by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya in the biography of al-Hasan ibn Salih from his narration from Abdullah ibn Dinar from him, with the wording "Hang the whip where the people of the house can see it." And from Jabir, raised to the Prophet: "May Allah have mercy on a man who hangs a whip in his house with which to discipline his family." Its chain includes Abbad ibn Kathir, who is weak.]

It is reported from Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "I was the fourth of four women with al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam. When he became angry with one of us, he would strike her with the stick of a clothes-rack (mashjab) until he broke it upon her." [Al-Tha'labi transmitted it from Abu Usama from Hisham ibn Urwa from his father from her, in these words. Abd al-Razzaq said: Mu'mar informed us from Hisham from his father who said: "al-Zubayr was harsh with women and would break the sticks of clothes-racks upon them." Ibn Abi Shayba said: Hafs ibn Ghiyath related to us from Hisham with the same.]

Poetry is also reported from al-Zubayr, among which:

"And were it not for her sons around her, I would have beaten her..."

So "fa-la tabghu 'alayhinna sabila" (do not seek a way against them): remove from them harm, reproach and false accusation. Repent toward them, and treat what was done by them as if it had not been, after their return to obedience, submission and abandonment of disobedience. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Most High and Great﴾ (inna Allaha kana 'aliyyan kabiran): so beware of Him, and know that His power over you is greater than your power over those under your hands.

It is narrated that Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari raised his whip to strike a slave of his, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him and called out to him: "Abu Mas'ud! Allah is more capable of power over you than you are over him." So he threw down the whip and freed the slave. [Muslim transmitted it from his hadith similarly, and at its end he said: "Indeed, if you had not done so, the Fire would have seized you."]

Or: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Most High and Great﴾, and you disobey Him despite His exalted rank and the majesty of His dominion, then you repent and He accepts your repentance. So you are more deserving of pardon toward those who come back to you when they return.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 35:

﴿Shiqaq bayni-himā﴾ (a breach between the two of them). Its original form is *shiqāqan baynahumā*, and the *shiqāq* is attributed to the adverbial noun of place by way of extension (*ittisā'*), as in His saying: ﴿Rather, it is the scheming of the night and the day﴾, whose original form is: rather, scheming in the night and the day. Or it is because the *bayn* (the between) is made into one who breaks the bond, and the night and the day into those who scheme, following their saying: "Your day is fasting." The pronoun refers to the spouses. Although they were not mentioned, their mention is understood from what indicates them, namely the men and the women.

﴿A judge from his family﴾: a man who is trustworthy and content, suitable to judge with justice and to reconcile between them. The sending of the two arbiters from their families is because relatives know the inner states better and are more eager for reconciliation. The souls of the spouses are at ease with them, and what is in their hearts of love, hatred, desire for companionship or separation, the causes and requirements of these, and what they conceal from strangers and do not want anyone to see, is revealed to them.

If you say: Do the two arbiters have the authority to bring the couple together or to separate them, if they see that? I say: This has been disputed. It was said: They have no such authority except with the permission of the spouses. It was also said: That authority belongs to them, and they were not appointed as arbiters except that the matter be left to them to decide according to what their judgment requires.

It is related from Ubaydah al-Salmani: "I witnessed Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) when a woman and her husband came to him, and with each of them was a group (*fi'ām*) of people. He appointed an arbiter from these and an arbiter from those." (Note: "*fi'ām min al-nās*" in al-Sihah: *al-fi'ām* is a group of people, having no singular from its own form.) [This was related by al-Shafi'i through Ibn Sirin from him, and by Abd al-Razzaq, al-Daraqutni, al-Tabari and others by his chain.] Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) then said to the two arbiters: "Do you know what is incumbent upon you? If you see that you should separate them, then separate them; and if you see that you should bring them together, then bring them together." The husband said: "As for separation, no." Ali said: "You lie! By Allah, you will not leave until you accept the Book of Allah for you and against you." The woman said: "I accept the Book of Allah for me and against me."

It is related from al-Hasan: "They bring them together and do not separate them." It is related from al-Sha'bi: "Whatever the two arbiters decide is valid."

The *alif* in ﴿if they both intend reconciliation﴾ refers to the two arbiters. In ﴿Allah will bring about harmony between them﴾, the pronoun refers to the spouses; that is, if the two arbiters intend to set right the state of affairs between them, and their intention is sound and their hearts are sincere for the sake of Allah, then their mediation is blessed, and Allah causes, through the goodness of their hearts and the goodness of their efforts, harmony and affection between the spouses, and places in their souls love and mercy.

It was also said: the two pronouns refer to the arbiters; that is, if they both intend to set right the state of affairs and to advise the spouses, Allah brings harmony between them, so they agree upon one word, support one another in seeking concord, until the aim is achieved and the purpose is fulfilled.

It was also said: the two pronouns refer to the spouses; that is, if they both wish to set right what is between them and seek good, and for the breach to be removed from them, Allah casts affection between them, and replaces their breach with harmony and their enmity with love.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Acquainted﴾: He knows how to bring together those who differ and to unite those who are separated. ﴿Had you spent all that is in the earth, you could not have brought their hearts together, but Allah brought them together﴾.

And to parents, good treatment; and to kinsfolk, and to orphans, and the needy, and to the neighbour who is near of kin, and the neighbour who is a stranger, and the companion by your side, and the wayfarer, and what your right hands possess.

Wait, I must translate exactly the given text, not the verse. Here is the translation of the passage:

And (be good) to parents, showing kindness; and to the kinsman (dhi al-qurba), and to everyone between whom and you there is kinship, such as a brother or an uncle or others. And to the neighbour who is near of kin (al-jar dhi al-qurba), the one whose neighbourhood is close; and to the distant neighbour (al-jar al-junub), the one whose neighbourhood is remote. It has been said: "al-jar" (the neighbour) is the near relative by lineage, and "al-jar al-junub" is the stranger (al-ajnabi). And he recited the verse of Bal'a' ibn Qays:

*"Never let a neighbour of ours, near of kin or a stranger neighbour, find us distasteful."*

[[Balghan ibn Qays; it is also narrated as Bal'a'. "al-rahim" means kinship. "al-junub" is an adjective in the sense of "stranger," used for masculine and feminine, singular and plural alike. He means: the near neighbour and the distant neighbour will never dislike us, because of the goodness of our companionship.]]

It was also read: "wa-al-jar dha al-qurba," in the accusative, as a specification (ikhtisas). Just as it was read, "Guard over the prayers and the middle prayer" (ḥāfiẓū ʿalā al-ṣalawāti wa-al-ṣalāti al-wusṭā), as an alert to the great weight of his right, since he is entitled to it through the right of neighbourhood and kinship. And al-ṣāḥib bi-al-janb: he who accompanies you by being at your side, whether as a companion on a journey, or an adjacent neighbour, or a partner in learning a science or a craft, or one sitting beside you in a gathering, a mosque, or elsewhere — from the least degree of companionship that joins you and him. So you must observe that right, not forget it, and make it a means to goodness. It has been said: al-ṣāḥib bi-al-janb is the wife. And ibn al-sabil is the traveller cut off from his means. It has been said: the guest. And al-mukhtāl is the arrogant, ignorant boaster who disdains to honour his relatives, companions and servants, so he does not show them kindness and does not turn to them.

[[His saying "fa-la yataḥaffā bihim" — in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: taḥaffaytu bihi, meaning I went to great lengths in honouring and being gentle with him. (ʿ)]]

It was also read: "wa-al-jar al-junub," with a fatḥa on the jīm and sukūn on the nūn.

The phrase ﴿Those who are miserly﴾ is either a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution) for ﴿whoever is arrogant and boastful﴾, or it is in the accusative of censure. It may also be in the nominative as a continuation of that, or it may be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, as if it were said: "Those who are miserly, who act and who make [others act] that way, deserve every reproach." ﴿Miserliness﴾ was read as bi-l-bukhl, with a damma and with a fatha on the ba' (the variant readings, qira'at, of this word are also given), and with two fathas, and with two dammas. The meaning is that they are miserly with what is in their own hands and with what is in the hands of others, so they order them to be stingy with it, out of hatred for generosity wherever it is found.

Among the proverbs of the Arabs: "More miserly than one who withholds the gift of another." Someone said:

"And a man whose hands are withheld from a person
from the gain of another's hand is indeed a miser."

[[I will cut the reins of the tents with a speech
short, but the labour of thought in it is long.

And a man whose hands are withheld from a person
from the gain of another's hand is indeed a miser.

These are by Abu Tammam, and it was also attributed to al-Buhturi. The ar-arsan (singular rasan) are ropes. The qibab that have ropes are the woven tents, the plural of qubba, which is a tent.

A howdah (hawdaj) that is muqabbab has a dome on top of it. The intended meaning is that he causes a people who are miserly to depart, so there is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli, the attribution of an act to its cause) where cutting is attributed to its cause, and a metonymy (kinaya) where departure is expressed by cutting the ropes of the tents. It may also be that the intended meaning is that he silences a people who claim glory, destroys their nobility and greatness, and reveals their lowliness and baseness. This state is compared to the state of cutting the ropes of tall, firmly stretched tents, so that they sink after rising and collapse after standing, as an allegorical image (isti'ara tamthiliyya), and this is closer to the context. It may also be that he likened the boasts to tents, with the common factor of greatness and general nobility and height, by way of explicit comparison (tasrih). Attributing ropes to them is a supporting element (tarshih). That is: I will nullify the claim of one who claims glory without being of its people, with a short speech, but the labour of thought in it is long. In it there is antithesis (tibaq) between "short" and "long." He expressed that speech with his words "and a man whose hands were withheld," and he attributed the miserliness to the hand because it is the instrument of giving, so withholding from it is like the withholding of the gain of a blessing by the hand. It may also be that the hand is literal, and he attributed the gain to it because it is its instrument. ﴿A miser﴾ means one who is extremely miserly, so the tanwin (nunation) is for magnification.]]

We have seen among those afflicted with the disease of miserliness someone who, when he hears that someone has been generous to another, is shaken, lets his buttocks go, is agitated, and his eyes spin in his head, as if his baggage had been looted and his storeroom broken into, out of distress at that and grief at its existence. [[The words "shakhsa bihi wa hall hibwatahu" in al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): it is said of a man when a matter reaches him that disturbs him: shakhsa bihi. (ʿ)]]

It was also said: they were the Jews, who used to come to men of the Ansar and give them advice, saying: "Do not spend your wealth, for we fear poverty for you, and you do not know what will happen." Allah censured them for concealing the blessing of Allah and what He had given them of the abundance of wealth and of their need of people. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When Allah bestows a blessing on a servant, He loves to see the effect of His blessing on His servant." [[Related by Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim through Abu Ishaq from Abu al-Ahwas from his father: that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him in a bad state and said: "Do you not have wealth?" He said: "From every kind of wealth Allah has given me." He said: "Then let it be seen upon you. Indeed, when Allah bestows a blessing on a servant, He loves to see it upon him." And al-Tirmidhi, through Hammam from Qatada from Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather, raised to the Prophet: "Indeed Allah loves to see the trace of His blessing on His servant." And al-Tabarani has a similar report from the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn. And Ahmad and Ishaq, through Ibn Wahb from Abu Hurayra, raised: "Allah has bestowed no blessing on a servant except that He loves to see its trace upon him." And Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, through 'Atiyya from Abu Sa'id, raised: "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, and He loves to see the effect of His blessing on His servant, and He dislikes misery and affecting misery." And Ibn 'Adi from Jabir, raised: "Indeed Allah loves to see the trace of His blessing on His servant." In its chain is 'Isma ibn Muhammad al-Ansari, who is weak in narration (munkar al-hadith). And al-Tabarani in Musnad al-Shamiyyin from Anas, raised: "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, and loves to see the trace of His blessing on His servant." It is through the narration of Uthman ibn 'Ata al-Khurasani from his father from him. He also narrated it in al-Awsat through the narration of Musa ibn 'Isa al-Qurashi from 'Ata al-Khurasani from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar, similarly.]] A governor of al-Rashid built a palace opposite his palace, and someone informed him about it. The man said: "O Commander of the Faithful, the generous man is pleased to see the trace of his blessing, so I wished to please you by looking at the traces of your blessing." He was pleased with his words.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning the Jews who concealed the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

"to be seen by people" and "for boasting," and so that it may be said: "How generous they are, how bountiful they are!"—not seeking the Face of Allah. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah who spent their wealth in hostility to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Evil is the companion﴾ — for he led them to stinginess, ostentation, and every evil. It is permissible that it be a threat to them, that Satan will be their companion in the Fire. ﴿And what would it have cost them?﴾ — what harm or burden would there be upon them in believing and spending in the way of Allah? The intended meaning is blame and rebuke. Otherwise, every benefit and success lies in that. This is like saying to one who takes revenge: "What harm would it do you if you pardoned?" And to one who is undutiful to his parents:

"What would it have cost you had you been dutiful?" — though it is known that there is no harm or loss in pardoning and in dutifulness. Rather, it is blame, rebuke, and a reproach for ignorance of the place of benefit. ﴿And Allah was ever Knowing of them﴾ — a warning.

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah who spent their wealth in hostility to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Evil is the companion﴾ — for he led them to stinginess, ostentation, and every evil. "What would it have cost you had you been dutiful?" — though it is known that there is no harm or loss in pardoning and in dutifulness. Rather, it is blame, rebuke, and a reproach for ignorance of the place of benefit. ﴿And Allah was ever Knowing of them﴾ — a warning.

The dhharra (ذرّة, the smallest ant): the tiny ant. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "mithqal namla" (the weight of an ant). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he put his hand into the dust, lifted it, then blew on it and said: each one of these is a dharra. It was also said: every particle of the dust motes in a window-opening is a dharra. And in this is evidence that if anything, even the least and smallest, were subtracted from the reward, or added to the punishment, it would be injustice; and that He does not do so because it is impossible within wisdom, not because it is impossible within power. ﴿And if it is a good deed﴾, and if the weight of a dharra is a good deed. He made the pronoun feminine [[Mahmud said: "He made the pronoun feminine, though it refers to the mithqal ... etc." Ahmad said: He had already made a similar statement regarding His words: (And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it). I have explained there that returning the pronoun to the pit is permissible, indeed preferable. Likewise its return here to the dharra. This does not preclude that the genitive noun is not the subject of the predicate, because the return of a pronoun does not necessitate predicating it in the first statement.

It is permissible to say: kanat dabbatuka (your beast was), and all of that is easier than the noun in the genitive construction taking the feminine gender from the noun it is annexed to. Abu 'Ali explicitly stated in al-Ta'liqat that this is anomalous.]] because it is annexed to a feminine noun. It is also read with the nominative, as kana being complete (kāna al-tāmma). ﴿He doubles it﴾: He multiplies its reward, because it deserves reward from Him at every time of the future, which has no end. It is reported from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi that he said to Abu Hurayra: "It has reached me that you say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah the Exalted gives His believing servant, for one good deed, a thousand thousand good deeds.'" Abu Hurayra said: "No, rather I heard him say: 'Allah gives him two thousand thousand good deeds.'" [[Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bazzar, al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Shayba through the narration of 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jad'an from Abu 'Uthman. Its wording: "It has reached me that Abu Hurayra narrates from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Allah multiplies the good deed for His believing servant a thousand thousand times." So I went and met Abu Hurayra and said: "It has reached me from you that you say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Allah gives for one good deed a thousand thousand good deeds." Abu Hurayra said: "Rather, I heard him say: Allah gives him two thousand thousand good deeds." Then he recited (Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of a dharra) up to His words (a great reward). Who knows whether the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "a great reward," was raised by Ibn Abi Shayba? Al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it being narrated from Abu Hurayra except with this chain." Thus he said. It was also narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Zuhd through the route of Ziyad al-Jassas from Abu 'Uthman in similar terms. 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Aban, from Abu al-'Aliya, who said: "I came to Abu Hurayra and he mentioned it," as a statement (mawquf) of Abu Hurayra. And Aban is abandoned (matruk).]] Then he recited this verse. What is meant is abundance, not a fixed limit. ﴿And gives from Himself a great reward﴾: He gives its possessor from His own presence, by way of bounty, a great gift. He called it "reward" (ajr) because it follows the reward and does not exist except by its existence. It is read: yudha'ifha, with tashdid and takhfif, from aḍ'afa and ḍa'afa. And Ibn Hurmuz read: nudā'ifhā with the letter nun.

﴿So how will these disbelievers, Jews and others, fare, when We bring from every nation a witness﴾, who will testify against them for what they did, and he is their prophet, like His words: (And I was a witness over them while I was among them). (And We bring you as a witness over these deniers.) It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited Surat al-Nisa to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he reached His words: (And We bring you as a witness over these), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wept and said: "Enough." [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) through the narration of 'Ubayda al-Salmani from him, and in its end he said: "Enough for you now." Then he turned to him and his eyes were shedding tears.]]

﴿They wish the earth were levelled over them﴾: that they would be buried so that the earth would be levelled over them as the dead are. It was also said: they wish they had not been raised, and that they were, along with the earth, equal. It was also said: the beasts turn into dust, so they wish for their state. ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah a statement﴾: they will not be able to conceal it, because their limbs will testify against them. It was also said the waw is for the state, meaning: they wish to be buried under the earth while they do not conceal from Allah any statement. They will not lie in their saying: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists," because when they say that and deny their polytheism, Allah sets a seal upon their mouths at that moment, and their hands and feet speak out in refutation of them and testify against them with polytheism. So, due to the severity of the matter for them, they wish that the earth were levelled over them. It is read: tusawwa, with the ta' dropped from tatasawwa, as one says: sawwaytuhu, fatasawwa, like lawwaytuhu, fatalawa. And tusawwa with the ta' assimilated into the sin, as in His words: yasma'un. Its past form is asawa, like azka.

﴿They wish the earth were levelled over them﴾: that they would be buried so that the earth would be levelled over them as the dead are. It was also said: they wish they had not been raised, and that they were, along with the earth, equal. It was also said: the beasts turn into dust, so they wish for their state. ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah a statement﴾: they will not be able to conceal it, because their limbs will testify against them. It was also said the waw is for the state, meaning: they wish to be buried under the earth while they do not conceal from Allah any statement. They will not lie in their saying: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists," because when they say that and deny their polytheism, Allah sets a seal upon their mouths at that moment, and their hands and feet speak out in refutation of them and testify against them with polytheism. So, due to the severity of the matter for them, they wish that the earth were levelled over them. It is read: tusawwa, with the ta' dropped from tatasawwa, as one says: sawwaytuhu, fatasawwa, like lawwaytuhu, fatalawa. And tusawwa with the ta' assimilated into the sin, as in His words: yasma'un. Its past form is asawa, like azka.

The dhharra (ذرّة, the smallest ant): the tiny ant. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "mithqal namla" (the weight of an ant). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he put his hand into the dust, lifted it, then blew on it and said: each one of these is a dharra. It was also said: every particle of the dust motes in a window-opening is a dharra. And in this is evidence that if anything, even the least and smallest, were subtracted from the reward, or added to the punishment, it would be injustice; and that He does not do so because it is impossible within wisdom, not because it is impossible within power. ﴿And if it is a good deed﴾, and if the weight of a dharra is a good deed. He made the pronoun feminine [[Mahmud said: "He made the pronoun feminine, though it refers to the mithqal ... etc." Ahmad said: He had already made a similar statement regarding His words: (And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it). I have explained there that returning the pronoun to the pit is permissible, indeed preferable. Likewise its return here to the dharra. This does not preclude that the genitive noun is not the subject of the predicate, because the return of a pronoun does not necessitate predicating it in the first statement.

It is permissible to say: kanat dabbatuka (your beast was), and all of that is easier than the noun in the genitive construction taking the feminine gender from the noun it is annexed to. Abu 'Ali explicitly stated in al-Ta'liqat that this is anomalous.]] because it is annexed to a feminine noun. It is also read with the nominative, as kana being complete (kāna al-tāmma). ﴿He doubles it﴾: He multiplies its reward, because it deserves reward from Him at every time of the future, which has no end. It is reported from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi that he said to Abu Hurayra: "It has reached me that you say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah the Exalted gives His believing servant, for one good deed, a thousand thousand good deeds.'" Abu Hurayra said: "No, rather I heard him say: 'Allah gives him two thousand thousand good deeds.'" [[Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bazzar, al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Shayba through the narration of 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jad'an from Abu 'Uthman. Its wording: "It has reached me that Abu Hurayra narrates from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Allah multiplies the good deed for His believing servant a thousand thousand times." So I went and met Abu Hurayra and said: "It has reached me from you that you say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Allah gives for one good deed a thousand thousand good deeds." Abu Hurayra said: "Rather, I heard him say: Allah gives him two thousand thousand good deeds." Then he recited (Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of a dharra) up to His words (a great reward). Who knows whether the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "a great reward," was raised by Ibn Abi Shayba? Al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it being narrated from Abu Hurayra except with this chain." Thus he said. It was also narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Zuhd through the route of Ziyad al-Jassas from Abu 'Uthman in similar terms. 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Aban, from Abu al-'Aliya, who said: "I came to Abu Hurayra and he mentioned it," as a statement (mawquf) of Abu Hurayra. And Aban is abandoned (matruk).]] Then he recited this verse. What is meant is abundance, not a fixed limit. ﴿And gives from Himself a great reward﴾: He gives its possessor from His own presence, by way of bounty, a great gift. He called it "reward" (ajr) because it follows the reward and does not exist except by its existence. It is read: yudha'ifha, with tashdid and takhfif, from aḍ'afa and ḍa'afa. And Ibn Hurmuz read: nudā'ifhā with the letter nun.

﴿So how will these disbelievers, Jews and others, fare, when We bring from every nation a witness﴾, who will testify against them for what they did, and he is their prophet, like His words: (And I was a witness over them while I was among them). (And We bring you as a witness over these deniers.) It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited Surat al-Nisa to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he reached His words: (And We bring you as a witness over these), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wept and said: "Enough." [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) through the narration of 'Ubayda al-Salmani from him, and in its end he said: "Enough for you now." Then he turned to him and his eyes were shedding tears.]]

﴿They wish the earth were levelled over them﴾: that they would be buried so that the earth would be levelled over them as the dead are. It was also said: they wish they had not been raised, and that they were, along with the earth, equal. It was also said: the beasts turn into dust, so they wish for their state. ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah a statement﴾: they will not be able to conceal it, because their limbs will testify against them. It was also said the waw is for the state, meaning: they wish to be buried under the earth while they do not conceal from Allah any statement. They will not lie in their saying: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists," because when they say that and deny their polytheism, Allah sets a seal upon their mouths at that moment, and their hands and feet speak out in refutation of them and testify against them with polytheism. So, due to the severity of the matter for them, they wish that the earth were levelled over them. It is read: tusawwa, with the ta' dropped from tatasawwa, as one says: sawwaytuhu, fatasawwa, like lawwaytuhu, fatalawa. And tusawwa with the ta' assimilated into the sin, as in His words: yasma'un. Its past form is asawa, like azka.

It is related that Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf prepared food and drink and invited a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at a time when wine was still permitted. They ate and drank, and when they became intoxicated and the time for the Maghrib prayer came, they put one of them forward to lead them in prayer. He recited: "Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor are you worshippers of what I worship," and the verse was revealed. After that they would not drink during the times of the prayers. They would drink after the 'Isha' prayer, and they would not wake in the morning without the intoxication having left them and without knowing what they were saying. Then its prohibition was revealed [[Related by the authors of the three Sunan collections, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, al-Hakim and al-Tabari, in similar form but without the words "they would not drink etc." All of them by way of Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from Ali. The narrations from Ata differ on the name of the host and the name of the one who led the prayer. In the narration of Abu Ja'far al-Razi from him, in al-Tirmidhi, it says: "Abd al-Rahman prepared for us," and likewise al-Hakim, by way of Khalid al-Tahhan from him. In Abu Dawud it says: "A man invited him, and Abd al-Rahman." In al-Hakim, by way of al-Thawri from Ata: "A man of the Ansar invited us." In al-Tirmidhi, from Ali: "They put me forward." In Abu Dawud: "They put Ali forward." In al-Nasa'i, also by way of Abu Ja'far: "They put Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf forward." al-Bazzar left it unnamed, and so did al-Hakim. In al-Tabari from al-Thawri. Al-Tabari also has it from Hammad ibn Salama, and al-Hakim from Khalid. (Note) The words "they would not drink etc." I have not found.]]. The meaning of ﴿do not approach the prayer﴾ is: do not go near it, do not stand up for it, and avoid it. It is like His saying: ﴿and do not approach adultery﴾ and ﴿do not approach the indecencies﴾. It has also been said that its meaning is:

do not approach its places, which are the mosques, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Keep your mosques clear of your children and your insane [[Related by Ibn Adi from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, in which is Abd Allah ibn Mahrur, spelled with unpointed letters, and Qarn Muhammad, and he is weak. There are also narrations on this from Thawban, Mu'adh, Abu al-Darda, Abu Umama and Wathila. The hadith of Thawban in Ibn Majah reads: "Keep your mosques clear of your children, your buying and selling, your disputes, and the raising of your voices... etc." The hadith of Mu'adh was transmitted by Abd al-Razzaq by way of Makhul from him, and it is disconnected (munqati'). The hadith of the others was transmitted by al-Tabarani, al-Uqayli and Ibn Adi by way of Makhul from them, and in it is al-Ala' ibn Kathir, who is weak.]]." It has also been said that it means the drowsy intoxication and the overpowering of sleep, as in the poem:

"...and their hearts were covered (ranu) by the intoxication of their drowsiness, every rust (rayn)."

[[Ranu: their hearts were covered by the intoxication, as iron is covered by rust. Al-sunat: plural of sina, from wasn, like 'idda from wa'd; it is the drooping of the eye and the heedlessness of the heart at the onset of sleep. Al-rayun: plural of rayn, which is upon the heart as rust is upon iron. I saw in al-Asas, from al-Tirmah, something that may be the origin of this, namely his saying:

"And a caravan to which I sent the doomed (radaya), lean camels like the worn-out eyelids,
Fearing that sleep would overcome them, with the intoxication of its drowsiness, every rust."

Radaya: plural of radiya, like qada'ya plural of qadiya, meaning one who has been struck by destruction. Talai': plural of talīḥa or talīḥ, meaning emaciated. Akhlaq: plural of khalq, like sabab, meaning something worn out. He attributed the drowsiness (sina) to the pronoun of sleep (nawm), because it is its beginning, so it was ascribed to it.]]

It is also read as sukara (with a fatha on the sin), and sukra (in the form of a plural, like halka and jawGa), because intoxication is a condition that affects the intellect; or as a singular with the meaning "and you are a group of intoxicated people," as you say "a woman sukra." Or sukra with a damma on the sin, like hublā, to make it a description of the group. Jinah ibn Hubaysh related: kasla and kuslā, with fatha and damma.

﴿nor one in a state of janabah﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿and you are intoxicated﴾, because the position of the clause with the waw is accusative as a circumstantial state, as if it were said: do not approach the prayer while intoxicated, nor in janabah (ritual impurity from sexual intercourse or seminal emission). The word janub is the same for the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine, because it is a noun that functions like the verbal noun ijnab. ﴿except as travellers passing through﴾ is an exception from the general states of those addressed, and its position is accusative as a circumstantial state. If you ask: how is this state combined with the state before it? I answer: it is as if it were said: do not approach the prayer in a state of janabah, unless you have with you another state in which you are excused, and that is the state of travel. "Passing through the way" is an expression for this. It is also permissible that it is not a circumstantial state but a qualifier of ﴿janaban﴾, meaning: do not approach the prayer in janabah, unless you are passing through, that is, in janabah while residing and not excused. If you ask: how is their prayer valid in janabah for the excuse of travel? I answer: by janub is meant those who have not performed ghusl, as if it were said: do not approach the prayer without having washed, until you wash, unless you are travellers.

Whoever interprets "the prayer" as "the mosque" means: do not approach the mosque in janabah except as those passing through it, when the path to the water runs through it, or when the water is in it, or when you have a wet dream in it. It has been said that some men of the Ansar had their doors opening onto the mosque, so they would become junub and would find no way except through the mosque, so it was permitted to them. It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not permit anyone to sit in the mosque or pass through it while junub, except Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), because his house was in the mosque [[The original of this hadith is in al-Tirmidhi with different wording. He related it by way of Salim ibn Abi Hafsa, from Atiyya, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ali: "O Ali, it is not lawful for anyone to be junub in this mosque except me and you." Al-Tirmidhi said: good, strange; we know it only from this route. Muhammad ibn Isma'il (al-Bukhari) heard it from me. Al-Bazzar related it by way of al-Hasan ibn Ziyad, from Kharija ibn Sa'd, from his father Sa'd, the same. He said: we do not know it from Sa'd except by this isnad. Then he related it from the hadith of Abu Sa'id as in al-Tirmidhi. He said: Salim was a Shi'i, but he was not abandoned, and he was not followed in this. Its meaning is that the Prophet (ﷺ) had his dwelling in the mosque. On this there is also a narration from Umm Salama, related by al-Tabari with the wording: "It is not fitting for anyone to be junub in this mosque except me and Ali." Abu Ya'la related from the hadith of Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) closed the doors of the mosque except the door of Ali, so he would enter the mosque junub, and it was his path, having no other way.]].

If you ask: four are included in the condition: the sick, the travellers, those in hadath (minor ritual impurity), and those in janabah, for whom the consequence, which is the command to perform tayammum (dry ablution with earth), applies when water is not available. I answer: the apparent meaning is that it applies to all of them, and that the sick, if they lack water because of the weakness of their movement and their inability to reach it, may perform tayammum; likewise the traveller, if he lacks it, because of its distance. And those in hadath and those in janabah likewise, if they do not find it for some reason.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-sa'id is the surface of the earth [[Mahmud said: "al-sa'id is the surface of the earth, whether earth or otherwise..." Ahmad said: this applies if the pronoun refers to al-sa'id. There is another aspect, that the pronoun refers to the hadath implied by ﴿and if you are sick﴾ to the end of the verse, for what is understood from it is: if you are in hadath in one of these conditions, travel, sickness, coming from the privy, or touching women, and you do not find water with which to purify yourselves from the hadath, then perform tayammum from it. It is said: I performed tayammum from janabah. The position of "min" on this reading is commonly used, and on this parsing it is either for causation or for the beginning of the goal, and both are valid in it, and Allah knows best.]], whether it is earth or other than earth. And if it is a rock with no dust on it, if the one performing tayammum strikes his hand on it and wipes, that would be his purification, and this is the position of Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him). If you ask: what then of His saying in Surat al-Ma'ida: ﴿and wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾, meaning some of it, which cannot be applied to a rock with no dust on it? I answer: they said that "min" is for the beginning of the goal. If you say: their saying that it is for the beginning of the goal is a forced interpretation, and no one of the Arabs understands from the saying of one who says "I wiped his head with oil, with water, with dust" except the meaning of partiality, I answer: it is as you say, and submission to the truth is more deserving than disputation.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ is a metaphor for leniency and facilitation, because one whose habit is to pardon the sinners and forgive them prefers to be easy and not burdensome. If you ask: how did he gather in one row the sick and the travellers, and the one in hadath and the one in janabah, and the sickness and travel being two causes of permission, while hadath is a cause for the obligation of wudu' (ablution) and janabah a cause for the obligation of ghusl? I answer: He, glorified is He, wished to grant permission to those who are obliged to purify themselves but lack water, to perform tayammum with earth. He singled out first among them the sick and the travellers, because they are the foremost in deserving the explanation of the permission for them, by the frequency of sickness and travel and their predominance over the other causes that require permission. Then He generalized to everyone obliged to purify himself who is deprived of water, whether because of fear of an enemy or a beast, or lack of a means of drawing water, or distress in a place without water, and other such things that do not occur as frequently as sickness and travel. It was read: min ghait. It is said that it is a lightening of ghaith, like hayn in hayn; and al-ghait is in the sense of al-ghai'.

Have you not seen (from the seeing of the heart), and it takes "ila" (to); the meaning is: has your knowledge not reached them? Or it means: have you not looked at them? Those who were given a share of the Book: a portion of knowledge of the Torah, and they are the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews. They buy error: they exchange it for guidance, which is remaining upon Judaism, after the clear signs had become evident to them regarding the truth of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that he is the Arab Prophet who was given good news of in the Torah and the Gospel. And they wish that you, O believers, would go astray from the path of truth as they went astray, and enter into their company. Their own misguidance is not enough for them; rather, they love that others should be led astray along with them. It was also read as "an yaḍillū" with the verb in the yā' form, with the ḍād vowelled with fatḥa and with kasra. And Allah is most knowing of your enemies (Allah knows better than you about your enemies); He has informed you of the enmity of these people and made you aware of their conditions and what they intend against you, so beware of them, do not seek their counsel in your affairs, and do not consult them. And sufficient is Allah as a Protector (walī), and sufficient is Allah as a Helper (naṣīr): so put your trust in His guardianship and His support rather than in them. Or, do not concern yourselves with them, for Allah will give you victory over them and suffice you against their plotting.

Have you not seen (from the seeing of the heart), and it takes "ila" (to); the meaning is: has your knowledge not reached them? Or it means: have you not looked at them? Those who were given a share of the Book: a portion of knowledge of the Torah, and they are the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews. They buy error: they exchange it for guidance, which is remaining upon Judaism, after the clear signs had become evident to them regarding the truth of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that he is the Arab Prophet who was given good news of in the Torah and the Gospel. And they wish that you, O believers, would go astray from the path of truth as they went astray, and enter into their company. Their own misguidance is not enough for them; rather, they love that others should be led astray along with them. It was also read as "an yaḍillū" with the verb in the yā' form, with the ḍād vowelled with fatḥa and with kasra. And Allah is most knowing of your enemies (Allah knows better than you about your enemies); He has informed you of the enmity of these people and made you aware of their conditions and what they intend against you, so beware of them, do not seek their counsel in your affairs, and do not consult them. And sufficient is Allah as a Protector (walī), and sufficient is Allah as a Helper (naṣīr): so put your trust in His guardianship and His support rather than in them. Or, do not concern yourselves with them, for Allah will give you victory over them and suffice you against their plotting.

From those who are Jews (min alladhina hadu) is an explanation of "those who were given a portion of the Scripture," because they are Jews and Christians. As for His words (Allah knows best), (and sufficient is Allah), (and sufficient is Allah): these are sentences inserted between the explanation and what is explained, by way of parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ), or as an explanation of "your enemies." What lies between them is either a parenthetical interjection or it is connected to "a helper" (naṣīran), meaning: He will help you against those who are Jews, like His saying ﴿and We helped him against the people who denied Our signs﴾.

It is also permissible that this be a new independent sentence, with "they distort" (yuḥarrifūna) as a qualifier of an omitted subject, the sense being: "from those who are Jews are a people who distort." Like the saying of the poet:

*And the age is nothing but two turns, so of them*
*I die in one, and in the other I seek life, striving,*
*And both have been written for me on a page,*
*So life is not dearer to me, nor is death more restful for me.*

This is by Tamīm ibn ʿAqīl, who says: the age is only two turns and two times. In one of them I die, and in the other I seek life while I strive, that is, I exert myself, tire, and hasten in seeking it. By "the page" is meant the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). Then he says: life is not more beloved to me, because of the toil in it, and death is not more restful for me, because the soul hates it.

That is, of them, in one turn I die.

They distort the words (al-kalim) from their places (ʿan mawāḍiʿihi): they incline them away from those places and remove them, for when they change a word and put another in its place, they have diverted it from the places where Allah placed it and removed it from them. This is like their distortion of "tall, ruddy-brown" (asmar rabʿa) from its place in the Torah by putting "tall, of medium build" (ādam ṭiwāl) in its place, and like their distortion of "stoning" (al-rajm) by putting "the prescribed punishment" (al-ḥadd) in its place.

If you say: why is it said here ʿan mawāḍiʿihi, and in al-Mā'ida min baʿdi mawāḍiʿihi? I say: as for ʿan mawāḍiʿihi, it is according to what we have explained, namely its removal from the places in which the wisdom of Allah had placed it, by what their desires required, substituting something else in its place. As for min baʿdi mawāḍiʿihi, the meaning is: it had places which it deserved to occupy, and when they distorted it, they left it like a stranger who has no place after its places and dwelling-places. The two meanings are close.

It is also read: yuḥarrifūna al-kalām. And al-kalim, with a kasra on the kāf and sukūn on the lām, is the plural of kalima, a lightened form of kalima.

Their saying ghayra musmaʿin is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the addressee. [Al-Zamakhshari said: "ghayra musmaʿin is a ḥāl from the addressee..." Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: his intent by this is that, since he explained ghayra musmaʿin as a supplication, which is an utterance of request, and he made it a ḥāl, and a ḥāl is a predicate, he wanted to show the aspects of the correctness of expressing an utterance in the form of a statement, by way of the fact that these people thought their supplication was granted, informing of the occurrence of what was supplicated. Its parallel is the command given in the form of a statement, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence.]

That is: "hear while you are one not made to hear." It is a saying with two faces: it may carry a reproach, meaning "hear from us, one against whom a curse is made—may you not hear," because if their curse were answered against him, he would not hear, and so he would be deaf, one not made to hear. They said this relying on the fact that their saying "may you not hear" is an accepted supplication. Or it means: "hear, without being answered to what you call to," meaning "ghayra musmaʿin jawāban," that is, one who is not answered in agreement with you, so it is as if you heard nothing. Or: "hear, as one who does not make hear a word you would be pleased with, so your hearing of it is a substitute." It is also permissible on this view that ghayra musmaʿin be the object of "hear": "hear a word that does not make you hear," because your ear does not retain it, out of disdain for it. It may also carry praise: "hear, not made to hear anything disliked," from your saying "aswama fulān fulānan" when he insulted him.

Likewise their saying rāʿinā may mean "let us speak to you," that is, "watch over us and wait for us." It may also be like a word in Hebrew or Syriac which they used to revile one another with, namely "rāʿīnā." So they, in mockery of the religion and derision of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would address him with an ambiguous speech, intending by it insult and humiliation, while showing reverence and honor, ﴿twisting their tongues﴾, that is, they twist the truth into falsehood with their tongues, placing rāʿinā in the place of unẓurnā, and ghayra musmaʿin in the place of "may you not hear what is disliked." Or they twist with their tongues what they conceal of abuse into what they display of reverence, out of hypocrisy.

If you say: how did they come with this ambiguous speech after they had openly said "we heard and we disobeyed"? I say: all the disbelievers used to confront him with disbelief and disobedience, but they did not confront him with cursing and bad supplication. It is also permissible that they said it among themselves. It is also permissible that they did not utter it, but since they did not believe, they were treated as if they had uttered it. Ubayy read: wa-unẓurnā, from al-inẓār, which means delay.

If you say: to what does the pronoun in His saying ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ refer? I say: to "that they said," because the meaning is: had their saying "we heard and we obeyed" been established, that saying would have been better for them, more upright, more just, and more correct.

﴿But Allah cursed them for their disbelief﴾, that is, He forsook them because of their disbelief and removed them far from His kindness, ﴿so they believe not except a little﴾, that is, a weak, feeble faith not worth regard, which is their belief in the One who created them, together with their disbelief in other than Him. Or by "little" He meant none at all, like the saying of the poet:

*Little complaining about the affliction that befalls him,*
*much desire, scattered are his journeys and paths.*
*He lingers in a waterless desert, and by evening in another,*
*a lone camel, mounting the backs of perils bare.*

This is by Ta'abbaṭa Sharran, praising Shams ibn Mālik, one of the chiefs of the Arabs. It was also said that it was said by Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī praising Ta'abbaṭa Sharran. The meaning: he has no complaining, so as to show praise; that is, he does not complain on account of an affliction that befalls him, while he is one whom affliction reaches. He has much desire of the soul. Shatt, like shatāt, is originally a verbal noun, and both are used in the sense of "scattered, dispersed." It is also narrated as nashr al-nawā, which has the same meaning. And it is narrated as shattā al-nawā, the plural of shatīt, meaning scattered and divergent: that is, his destinations and paths are many and diverse. Al-nawā is a collective noun for nawāt, meaning the intention of the traveler; it is also used for distance, and so it is masculine, and it is used for the traveler's intention and so it is feminine. al-Mawmāh is a desert with no water. al-Juḥaysh is the solitary, the lone one. And al-iʿrawrāʾ is riding a horse with its back bare. He used "yumsī" (he reaches evening) rather than "yabīt" (he spends the night), to indicate that he continues travelling and does not stop at night. By his saying "yaʿrawrī" is an indication that he plunges into hardships without protection from them. He likened the perils to something one may mount, in a metaphor (makniyya), and attributed to them "backs" by imagination (takhyīl). In it is also an indication that he is not concerned with them, but rushes toward them without preparation, like a horseman rushing to his horse without patience until he saddles it. And in it is an indication that he prevails and triumphs, since he expressed it with what denotes elevation over them.

That is: one who has no complaining; or, except a few of them who have believed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 47:

"Before We obliterate faces", that is, We erase the outlines of their forms: the eyes, eyebrows, nose and mouth; "and turn them back upon their backs", that is, We make them in the shape of their backs, which are the napes, obliterated like them. The "fa" (fa') here indicates causation. If you take it to indicate sequence, since they were threatened with two punishments, one following the other, the meaning is: We obliterate faces and then turn them back, so the faces go backwards and the napes come forward.

Another interpretation is that "obliteration" (tams) means alteration and change, as when the wealth of the Copts was obliterated and turned into stones. "Faces" then means their leaders and notables, meaning: before We change the conditions of their notables, depriving them of their standing and prestige, and clothing them in humiliation and retreat. Or "turning them back" means returning them to where they came from. That place is Adhruʿat in Syria, and the reference is to the exile of the Banu al-Nadir.

If you ask: to whom does the pronoun refer in "or We curse them" (aw nalʿanahum)? I say: it refers to the faces, if "faces" means the notables, or to the people who possess the faces. The meaning is: before We obliterate the faces of a people, or it refers back to "those who were given the Book" by way of iltifat (shift of pronoun), "or We curse them, or We punish them by transformation (maskh), as We transformed the people of the Sabbath."

If you ask: where is the fulfilment of the threat? I say:

It is conditional upon faith [a note in the text reads: "his words 'it is conditional upon faith' perhaps mean 'conditional upon non-faith'. (ʿ)"]. Some of them did believe. It is also said: it is still awaited, and there must be an obliteration and a transformation for the Jews before the Day of Resurrection. Moreover, Allah, may He be exalted, threatened them with one of two things: obliteration of some faces, or cursing them. The obliteration is the alteration of the conditions of their leaders, or their exile to Syria, and one of the two has occurred. Even if it was not the other, the curse has been fulfilled, for they are cursed in every tongue. The apparent meaning is the common meaning of curse, not transformation, as you see in His saying, exalted is He: "Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and with whom He was angry, and whom He made into apes and swine" (5:60). "And the command of Allah is always accomplished" (33:38). So one of the two must occur if they do not believe.

**Question:** It is established that God, mighty and majestic, forgives shirk for one who repents of it, and that He does not forgive lesser major sins (al-kaba'ir) except through repentance.[[The view that God does not forgive major sins short of shirk except through repentance belongs to the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). The Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni community) hold that such sins are forgiven through repentance, through intercession, and through God's sheer bounty.]] So what is the meaning of God's words ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾?[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: It is established that God, mighty and majestic, forgives shirk for one who repents of it... etc." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The creed of the Ahl al-Sunna is that shirk is absolutely not forgiven, while what is less than it of the major sins is forgiven for whomever God wills to forgive, this being when there is no repentance. With repentance, both are forgiven. The verse was revealed concerning one who did not repent, and no repentance is mentioned in it, as you can see. Therefore God absolutely negated the forgiveness of shirk, and affirmed the forgiveness of what is less than it, conditioned by His will, as you see. This is the way the verse accords with the creed of the Ahl al-Sunna.

As for the Qadariyya (those who affirm human power over one's acts), they suppose that shirk and what is less than it of the major sins are equal in that each kind is not forgiven without repentance, and that God wills to forgive them both only for those who repent. So when al-Zamakhshari presents this doctrine to this verse, the verse rejects it and refutes it, since forgiveness is negated in it for shirk and affirmed for what is less than it, conditioned by His will. If the intended meaning of both is one who did not repent, then there is no basis for distinguishing between them by making forgiveness in one case conditional on His will, and making it unconditional in the other, since they are alike in the impossibility of forgiveness. And if the intended meaning of both is the penitent, then He has said of shirk that it is not forgiven, while the penitent from shirk is forgiven. At this point al-Zamakhshari began to cut one of them off from the other, making the intended meaning for shirk non-repentance and for the major sins repentance, so that the verse would conform to his creed. Thus he burdens it with two things it cannot bear. The first: he attaches repentance to the will (of God), though it is not mentioned and there is no evidence for it in what was stated. Moreover, if it were intended, it would by their assumption be the rational cause necessitating forgiveness, and by their opinion of reason the will could not be connected to its opposite; so how is it fitting to remain silent about what is the principal and the determining factor, and to mention what has no bearing on this corrupt doctrine? The second: after establishing repentance, he judged and restricted it to one of the two categories and not the other. This is nothing but making the Qur'an subordinate to opinion; we seek refuge in God from that. As for the Qadariyya, with this doctrine the well-known proverb applies to them: "The master gives and the slave withholds," because God clearly declares His generosity in forgiving one who persists in major sins if He wills, while they push back against this clear declaration and deny forgiveness on the basis of the principle of what is best and most beneficial (al-aslah wa al-salah), which is more fitting and deserving of corruption.]]

**Answer:** The meaning is that both the negated and the affirmed verbs are directed to His words ﴿for whom He wills﴾, as if it were said: God does not forgive shirk for whomever He wills, and He forgives what is less than shirk for whomever He wills, with the first referring to one who did not repent and the second to one who repented. A parallel to this is your saying: "The amir does not give a dinar, and gives a qintar, to whomever he wills," meaning: he does not give a dinar to one who does not deserve it, and he gives a qintar to one who deserves it.

﴿Then he has indeed fabricated a sin﴾, that is, he committed it, while he is one who fabricates and invents what is not valid for him to attribute.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 49–50:

﴿Those who purify themselves﴾: the Jews and the Christians. They said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved," and they said: "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians."

It is also said: Some men from among the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with their children and said: "Is there any sin upon these?" He said: "No." They said: "By Allah, we are nothing but like them: what we do by day, He expiates for us by night, and what we do by night, He expiates for us by day." [Al-Tha'labi related it from al-Kalbi, saying: "This verse was revealed concerning men from among the Jews who came with their children," and then he mentioned it. His chain to al-Kalbi is at the beginning of the book.] Then this verse was revealed.

It includes everyone who purifies himself, describing himself with the purity of deeds, the increase of obedience and piety, and nearness to Allah. If you say: Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) not say: "By Allah, I am trustworthy in the heavens and trustworthy on the earth"? [I have not found it.] I say: He said that only when the hypocrites said to him: "Be just in the distribution," as a denial of them, since they described him with the opposite of what his Lord described him with. How vast is the difference between one whom Allah testifies to be pure, and one who testifies to himself, or whom one who does not know testifies for: ﴿Nay, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾. This is an announcement that the purification by Allah is the one that is relied upon, not the purification of anyone else, because He is the One who knows who is fit for purification. The meaning of "purifies whom He wills" is: He purifies the chosen among His servants whom He knows to be pure, and describes them with it. ﴿And they will not be wronged a whit﴾: that is, those who purify themselves will be punished for their self-purification to the full measure of their due recompense. Or: whomever He wills will be rewarded for their purity, and nothing will be diminished from their reward. A similar verse is ﴿So do not purify yourselves; He knows best who is pious﴾. ﴿See how they invent lies against Allah﴾ in their claim that they are pure in the sight of Allah. ﴿And sufficient is this claim of theirs as a manifest sin﴾, above all their other sins.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 51–52:

Al-jibt (an idol-like false deity): the idols and everything worshipped besides Allah. And al-taghut (the transgressor, i.e. the devil): Satan. The reason is that Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, two Jews, went out to Mecca with a group of Jews to form an alliance with the Quraysh against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They said: "You are the People of the Book, and you are closer to Muhammad than we are, so we do not feel safe from your scheming. Prostrate to our gods so that we may be reassured about you." They did so. This is their faith in al-jibt and al-taghut, because they prostrated to the idols and obeyed Iblis in what they did.

Abu Sufyan said: "Are we better guided in the way, or Muhammad?" Ka'b said: "What does Muhammad say?" They said: "He commands the worship of Allah alone and forbids association (shirk)." He said: "And what is your religion?" They said: "We are the custodians of the House, we give drink to the pilgrims, we host the guest, and we free the captive." And they mentioned their deeds. He said: "You are better guided in the way."
