Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 100–101:

*Muraghaman* (a place of refuge, i.e. one who emigrates): *tariqan* (a path) by which he defies (*yuraghimu*) his people, meaning he departs from them in spite of their noses. *Al-raghm* (humiliation and disgrace). Its root is the sticking of the nose to the *righam*, which is dust. It is said: "I *raghamtu* the man" when you part from him while he dislikes your parting, because of the abasement that befalls him thereby. Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

*Like a great mountain, one takes refuge in its flanks,*
*Mighty in its places of defiance and its ways of escape.*

[[Of al-Nabigha al-Ja'di. *Al-tawd* is the great mountain. *Yuladh* means he takes shelter. *Al-raghm* is the sticking of the nose to the *righam*, that is the dust, and it is a metaphor for humiliation and disgrace. In taking the path of emigration there is defiance of the adversary, departing from him in spite of his nose. *Al-muraghim*, in the form of the passive participle, is the road, because it is the place of defiance. The noun of place from a non-triliteral verb is on the pattern of its passive participle, and its plural is like *masajid*. "*Al-madhhab*" is narrated instead as "*al-mahrab*", and the second is more specific. It likens a man to a mountain in seeking refuge in it and taking shelter in its dignity.]] It is also read *murghaman*. And it is read (*thumma yudrikhu-hu al-mawt*) with a *raf'* (nominative ending on the *kaf*) [[Mahmud said: "It is read *yudrikuhu* with the *kaf* vowelled with *damma*, as the predicate of an omitted subject ... etc." Ahmad said: The construction of the *raf'* as an omitted subject involves coordinating a nominal clause with a verbal one, and the preferable course is otherwise where a way exists. As for the second way, treating the connected form as if it were a pause, it contains evident irregularity, and moreover the more eloquent form in pausing is contrary to transferring the vowel; and it has added irregularity by treating the connected form as a pause. How then, when I have a sound reading free from irregularity, elevated in eloquence, namely coordination with what occupies the position of *man* (whoever), where the first verb is in the nominative. It is as if he said: "And whoever goes forth from his house as an emigrant, then death overtakes him", and this is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned at his words (*ayna ma takunu yudrikkum al-mawt*) concerning the one who reads with the *raf'*, and he said *thumma* ("then"). It is a grammatical construction of Sibawayh, and its application here is closer and more correct than there. And God knows best.]] as the predicate of an omitted subject. It is said that the *raf'* of the *kaf* is transferred from the *ha'*, as if he intended to pause upon it, then transferred the vowel of the *ha'* to the *kaf*, like the verse:

*Wonder has come upon me, though time's wonders are many, from a man of the 'Anazah who abused me, and I did not strike him.*

[[His words "and time's wonders are many" is a parenthetical clause. *Al-'Anazi* is a relative name of 'Anazah, a clan of Rabi'ah. It is said *al-'Anazi* means short, a relative name from *al-'anazah*, which is a small spear. The original is the quiescence of the *ya'* of *adribhu* for the jussive, but it was made to rhyme with the *ha'* for the metre. It is also narrated as "*ya 'ajaban*, and time's wonders are many from a man of 'Anazah".]]

And it is read *yudrikuhu* with the *nasb* (accusative), by supposing *an* (that) is implied, like the verse:

*I shall leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim, and I shall join the Hijaz and find rest.*

It is attributed to al-Mughirah ibn Hunayn al-Hanzali. *Alhaqa* is like *akrama* in the most eloquent usage, and like *aftaha* in one dialect. Its accusative is by the supposition of *an*, though it does not follow any of the established known particles in grammar, because the imperfect preceding it carries the sense of self-command, or the scent of wishing, or because it is coordinated upon an omitted causal clause, meaning: "so that I may be safe from them, and join the Hijaz, and find rest from the evil of their company." Were it in the *raf'*, that meaning would be lost and it would be merely a report of joining and resting. But the grammarians have stated that the accusative after an affirmative statement free of a conditional is a necessity of poetry, and this is such a case.

*Fa-qad waqa'a ajruhu 'ala Allah*: then his reward has become binding upon God. The real meaning of *wujub* (obligation) is falling and dropping, as in (*fa-idha wajabat junubuha*) and "the sun set" (*wajabat al-shams*), meaning its disc fell. The meaning: God knows how to reward him, and this is incumbent upon Him [[His words "reward him, and this is incumbent upon Him" is the view of the Mu'tazilah. As for the People of the Sunnah, nothing is incumbent upon Him. (Gh.)]].

It is related in the story of Jundab ibn Damrah that when death overtook him he began to clap his right hand upon his left, then said: "O God, this is for You, and this is for Your Messenger; I pledge to You what Your Messenger pledged to You." He died in a praiseworthy state, and news of him reached the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they said: "Had he died in Medina, his reward would have been more complete." The polytheists, laughing, said: "He did not attain what he sought." Then it was revealed. And they said: every emigration for a religious purpose, whether seeking knowledge, or pilgrimage, or jihad, or fleeing to a land where one increases in obedience or contentment and asceticism in this world, or seeking lawful sustenance, is an emigration to God and His Messenger. And if death overtakes him on the way, his reward falls upon God.

*Al-darb fi al-ard* is travel. The minimum duration of journey in which shortening is permitted, according to Abu Hanifah, is three days and their nights at the pace of camels and walking feet at a moderate speed, without regard to the slowness or haste of the traveller. So if he travels three days and nights in one day, he shortens; if he travels a day's journey over three days, he does not shorten. According to al-Shafi'i, the minimum duration of travel is four *barid*, a two-day journey.

His words *fa-laysa 'alaykum junahun an taqsuru min al-salah* apparently indicate a choice between shortening and completing, and that completing is better. To this choice al-Shafi'i inclined. And it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he completed the prayer while travelling [[Recorded by al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bazzar, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi by various routes from 'Ata' from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to shorten in travel and complete, and break his fast and fast," the wording of al-Daraqutni. He said its chain is sound.]]. And from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her: I performed 'umrah with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from Medina to Mecca, and when I arrived at Mecca I said: "O Messenger of God, may my father and mother be your ransom, you shortened and completed, you fasted and broke your fast." He said: "You have done well, O 'A'ishah, and I was not blamed for it" [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i from the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad from her, and he graded it sound (hasan). He cited it through another route from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad from his father from 'A'ishah. He said the first is connected, and 'Abd al-Rahman met 'A'ishah. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it through both routes.]]. 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, used to complete and shorten [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Salim from his father: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed at Mina, 'Arafah and elsewhere the traveller's prayer of two rak'ahs, and Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman for part of his caliphate, then he completed it to four." Both recorded it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid who said: 'Uthman prayed four at Mina; it was said to Ibn Mas'ud, and he said *istirja'* (inna lillahi...), and the hadith continues.]]. According to Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, shortening in travel is a firm obligation, not a concession, and nothing other than it is permitted. And from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "The prayer of travel is two rak'ahs, complete, not shortened, upon the tongue of your Prophet" [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah from the narration of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla from 'Umar. Al-Bazzar narrated it through this route. It was also narrated by Yazid ibn Ziyad ibn Abi al-Ja'd from Zubayd from 'Abd al-Rahman from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah. This route was recorded by Ibn Majah. Al-Bazzar recorded it through another route from Zayd ibn Wahb from 'Umar, in which is Yasin al-Zayyat, who is weak.]]. And from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her: The prayer was first prescribed as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs; it was confirmed for travel and increased for residence [[Agreed upon.]].

If you say: what then do you make of His words *fa-laysa 'alaykum junah an taqsuru*? I say: it is as if they were accustomed to completing, so they were prone to think that there was a deficiency upon them in shortening; therefore the blame was negated from them, so that their hearts might be at ease with shortening and reassured by it. It is also read *tuqsiru* from *aqsara*. And there came in the hadith *iqsar al-khutbah*, meaning shortening the sermon [[Recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Hakim, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar from the narration of Abu Rashid from 'Ammar ibn Yasir: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded us to shorten the sermon." Abu Dawud said: we know of no narration by Abu Rashid from 'Ammar other than this hadith. In Ibn Hibban, from the hadith of Jabir in the story of the prayer of fear, he said: "And God revealed *iqsar al-salah*." In Abu Ya'la from Ya'la ibn Umayyah: I said to 'Umar: "What is the shortening of the prayer..." the hadith.]]. And al-Zuhri read *tuqassiru* with doubling. Shortening is established by explicit text of the Book only in the state of fear, and that is His words (*in khiftum an yaftinakum alladhina kafaru*). As for the state of security, it is by the Sunnah. In the reading of 'Abd Allah: *min al-salah an yaftinakum*, without (*in khiftum*), in which case *an yaftinakum* is an object of purpose, meaning: lest those who disbelieve tempt you. The meaning of *fitnah* is fighting and confronting with what is disliked.

Its accusative is by the supposition of *an*, though it does not follow any of the established known particles in grammar, because the imperfect preceding it carries the sense of self-command, or the scent of wishing, or because it is coordinated upon an omitted causal clause, meaning: "so that I may be safe from them, and join the Hijaz, and find rest from the evil of their company." Were it in the *raf'*, that meaning would be lost and it would be merely a report of joining and resting. But the grammarians have stated that the accusative after an affirmative statement free of a conditional is a necessity of poetry, and this is such a case.

*Fa-qad waqa'a ajruhu 'ala Allah*: then his reward has become binding upon God. The real meaning of *wujub* (obligation) is falling and dropping, as in (*fa-idha wajabat junubuha*) and "the sun set" (*wajabat al-shams*), meaning its disc fell. The meaning: God knows how to reward him, and this is incumbent upon Him [[His words "reward him, and this is incumbent upon Him" is the view of the Mu'tazilah. As for the People of the Sunnah, nothing is incumbent upon Him. (Gh.)]].

It is related in the story of Jundab ibn Damrah that when death overtook him he began to clap his right hand upon his left, then said: "O God, this is for You, and this is for Your Messenger; I pledge to You what Your Messenger pledged to You." He died in a praiseworthy state, and news of him reached the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they said: "Had he died in Medina, his reward would have been more complete." The polytheists, laughing, said: "He did not attain what he sought." Then it was revealed. And they said: every emigration for a religious purpose, whether seeking knowledge, or pilgrimage, or jihad, or fleeing to a land where one increases in obedience or contentment and asceticism in this world, or seeking lawful sustenance, is an emigration to God and His Messenger. And if death overtakes him on the way, his reward falls upon God.

*Al-darb fi al-ard* is travel. The minimum duration of journey in which shortening is permitted, according to Abu Hanifah, is three days and their nights at the pace of camels and walking feet at a moderate speed, without regard to the slowness or haste of the traveller. So if he travels three days and nights in one day, he shortens; if he travels a day's journey over three days, he does not shorten. According to al-Shafi'i, the minimum duration of travel is four *barid*, a two-day journey.

His words *fa-laysa 'alaykum junahun an taqsuru min al-salah* apparently indicate a choice between shortening and completing, and that completing is better. To this choice al-Shafi'i inclined. And it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he completed the prayer while travelling [[Recorded by al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bazzar, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi by various routes from 'Ata' from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to shorten in travel and complete, and break his fast and fast," the wording of al-Daraqutni. He said its chain is sound.]]. And from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her: I performed 'umrah with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from Medina to Mecca, and when I arrived at Mecca I said: "O Messenger of God, may my father and mother be your ransom, you shortened and completed, you fasted and broke your fast." He said: "You have done well, O 'A'ishah, and I was not blamed for it" [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i from the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad from her, and he graded it sound (hasan). He cited it through another route from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad from his father from 'A'ishah. He said the first is connected, and 'Abd al-Rahman met 'A'ishah. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it through both routes.]]. 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, used to complete and shorten [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Salim from his father: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed at Mina, 'Arafah and elsewhere the traveller's prayer of two rak'ahs, and Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman for part of his caliphate, then he completed it to four." Both recorded it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid who said: 'Uthman prayed four at Mina; it was said to Ibn Mas'ud, and he said *istirja'* (inna lillahi...), and the hadith continues.]]. According to Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, shortening in travel is a firm obligation, not a concession, and nothing other than it is permitted. And from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "The prayer of travel is two rak'ahs, complete, not shortened, upon the tongue of your Prophet" [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah from the narration of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla from 'Umar. Al-Bazzar narrated it through this route. It was also narrated by Yazid ibn Ziyad ibn Abi al-Ja'd from Zubayd from 'Abd al-Rahman from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah. This route was recorded by Ibn Majah. Al-Bazzar recorded it through another route from Zayd ibn Wahb from 'Umar, in which is Yasin al-Zayyat, who is weak.]]. And from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her: The prayer was first prescribed as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs; it was confirmed for travel and increased for residence [[Agreed upon.]].

If you say: what then do you make of His words *fa-laysa 'alaykum junah an taqsuru*? I say: it is as if they were accustomed to completing, so they were prone to think that there was a deficiency upon them in shortening; therefore the blame was negated from them, so that their hearts might be at ease with shortening and reassured by it. It is also read *tuqsiru* from *aqsara*. And there came in the hadith *iqsar al-khutbah*, meaning shortening the sermon [[Recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Hakim, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar from the narration of Abu Rashid from 'Ammar ibn Yasir: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded us to shorten the sermon." Abu Dawud said: we know of no narration by Abu Rashid from 'Ammar other than this hadith. In Ibn Hibban, from the hadith of Jabir in the story of the prayer of fear, he said: "And God revealed *iqsar al-salah*." In Abu Ya'la from Ya'la ibn Umayyah: I said to 'Umar: "What is the shortening of the prayer..." the hadith.]]. And al-Zuhri read *tuqassiru* with doubling. Shortening is established by explicit text of the Book only in the state of fear, and that is His words (*in khiftum an yaftinakum alladhina kafaru*). As for the state of security, it is by the Sunnah. In the reading of 'Abd Allah: *min al-salah an yaftinakum*, without (*in khiftum*), in which case *an yaftinakum* is an object of purpose, meaning: lest those who disbelieve tempt you. The meaning of *fitnah* is fighting and confronting with what is disliked.

And when you are among them and lead them in prayer (al-salat, ﴿and when you are among them and establish the prayer for them﴾): whoever does not regard the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf) as valid after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) relies on its outward wording, since it makes his presence among them a condition. Whoever regards it as valid after him says: the imams are deputies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in every age, carrying on what he used to do. So the address to him includes every imam who is present with the congregation in a time of fear, and it is incumbent on him to lead them in prayer as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led the congregations he attended. The pronoun in "fihim" (among them) refers to those who are in fear. ﴿Let a party of them stand with you﴾: divide them into two groups, so that one of them stands with you, and lead them in prayer. ﴿And let them take their weapons﴾: the pronoun may refer to the worshippers [[Mahmud said: it is said that the one commanded to take up weapons is the worshippers... etc.]] Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: the apparent meaning is that the one addressed to take up weapons is the worshippers, since those who have not prayed were appointed only as guards, so it is apparent that they need not be commanded to this or reminded of it, and they only delayed the prayer for that reason. As for those who are praying, they are liable to lay down their weapons, because they are not accustomed to carrying them during prayer, so they were alerted that they should not lay down their weapons even while praying, because of the necessity of fear and the fear of being caught off guard. Also, the structure of the verse supports this, because it says ﴿let a party of them stand with you﴾ and then follows it with ﴿and let them take their weapons﴾, so the apparent meaning is that the pronoun returns to them; and if it is taken to refer to non-worshippers, that requires a strained justification for its return to them, since the context points to them even though they are not mentioned. Or the pronoun refers to others. If it refers to the worshippers, then they take from the weapons whatever does not hinder them from the prayer, such as the sword and dagger and the like. If it refers to others, there is no dispute about it. ﴿And when they have prostrated, let them be behind you﴾, meaning the non-worshippers [[The commentary continues. He said: "and what is meant by his words 'let them be behind you' is those who are not praying." Ahmad said: the apparent meaning of prostration here is prayer. It is frequently expressed by prostration, and what is meant is: when the group has prayed, that is, has completed its prayer, let them be behind you.]] ﴿behind you﴾: guarding you.

This is evidence for the well-known position of the school of Malik (madhhab, school of law) that the first group completes its prayer while the imam waits for the other group. His words ﴿and let another group come who have not yet prayed, and let them pray with you﴾ mean: when the first group has completed its prayer and stands behind you, then let the other group, which has not yet prayed, come and pray with you. This is also clear evidence for one of the two opinions within the school of Malik, that the imam waits for the second group until they complete their prayer and gives the salam with them, because the apparent meaning of the unqualified "with you" requires this; for if they were to make up their prayer after his salam, they would not have been praying with him in the full sense. And Allah knows best. This verse thus fits most of the well-known positions of his school regarding the details of the prayer of fear. And Allah is the Granter of success in what is right.

﴿behind you﴾: guarding you. The manner of the prayer of fear according to Abu Hanifa: the imam leads one group in prayer for one rak'ah, if the prayer is two rak'ahs, while the other group faces the enemy. Then this group stands facing the enemy, and the other group comes, and he prays with them one rak'ah and completes his prayer. Then he stands facing the enemy, and the first group comes and performs the rak'ah without recitation and completes its prayer, then stands guard. Then the other group comes and performs the rak'ah with recitation and completes its prayer. The prostration is taken literally according to Abu Hanifa, whereas according to Malik it means prayer, because the imam leads one group in one rak'ah and remains standing until they complete their prayer and give the salam and depart; then he leads the second group in one rak'ah and remains seated until they complete their prayer, and he gives the salam with them.

This is supported by ﴿and let another group come who have not prayed, and let them pray with you﴾. It is also read as "wa-amti'atikum" (your belongings). If you ask: how did he combine the weapons with caution in taking? I say: caution, which is vigilance and watchfulness, is made into an instrument used by the warrior; for this reason it is combined with the weapons in taking, and both are treated as things taken. A similar example is the words of God Most High: ﴿and those who had homes and faith prepared﴾, where faith is made a dwelling place for them and a settled home because of their firmness in it, so it is combined with the home in "prepared" (tabawwu').

﴿and they would charge at you﴾, meaning they would attack you in a single assault. He granted them dispensation to lay down their weapons if carrying them became burdensome because of rain soaking them or illness weakening them, and at the same time he commanded them to take caution, so that they would not be negligent and the enemy would not fall upon them. If you ask: how does the command to take caution correspond to His words ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾? I say: the command to be cautious against the enemy may give the impression that his victory and power are to be expected; so He removed that impression from them by informing them that Allah humiliates their enemy, disgraces him, and gives them victory over him, in order to strengthen their hearts, and so that they know the command to be cautious is not for that reason, but is an act of worship ordained by Allah, as He said: ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands into destruction﴾.

﴿And when you have finished the prayer﴾: when you have prayed in a state of fear and fighting, ﴿remember Allah﴾, so pray it standing, fighting with swords and striking, ﴿and sitting﴾, crouching on your knees, shooting arrows, ﴿and on your sides﴾, wounded by injuries. ﴿And when you are secure﴾, when the war lays down its burdens and you are safe, ﴿establish the prayer﴾: make up what you prayed in those states, which are states of anxiety and agitation. ﴿Indeed, prayer has been enjoined upon the believers at specified times﴾, limited to set times; it is not permitted to delay it beyond its times in any circumstance, whether in fear or in safety.

This is clear according to the position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, who holds that prayer is obligatory on the fighter during combat, walking, and agitation in battle when its time arrives; and when he is secure, he must make it up. As for Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, he is excused from abandoning it until he is secure. It is also said: its meaning is: when you have finished the prayer of fear, continue the remembrance of Allah, glorifying Him, exalting Him, praising Him, and calling upon Him for victory and support, in all your states, standing, sitting, and lying down, for what you are in of fear and war deserves remembrance of Allah, supplication to Him, and seeking refuge in Him. ﴿And when you are secure﴾: when you are settled, ﴿establish the prayer﴾: complete it.

Do not slacken or weaken in pursuing the people (al-qawm), that is, in seeking out the unbelievers through fighting and confronting them with it. Then he holds them to the proof by saying: ﴿If you are suffering pain﴾. That is, what you endure of pain from wounds and killing is not specific to you; rather it is a shared matter between you and them, which befalls them as it befalls you. Then they endure it and show courage, so what is wrong with you that you do not endure as they endure, when you are more deserving of patience than they are, because you hope from God for what they do not hope for: the making manifest of your religion over all other religions, and the great reward in the Hereafter.

It is recited by al-A'raj as ﴿an takunu ta'lamun﴾ with the hamza vowelled with a fatha, meaning: "And do not slacken, because you are suffering." And his saying ﴿fa-innahum ya'lamuna kama ta'lamun﴾ is a causal clause (ta'lil). It is also recited as ﴿fa-innahum yaylamuna kama tayylamun﴾.

It is narrated that this was at the Lesser Badr (Badr al-Sughra), when they had wounds, so they relied on one another (tawakkalu, i.e. they left the matter to one another). ﴿And God is ever Knowing, Wise﴾: He does not burden you with anything, nor does He command you or forbid you except for what He knows to be beneficial to you.

It is narrated that Ṭu'ma ibn Ubayriq, one of the Banu Ẓafar, stole a coat of mail from a neighbour of his named Qatada ibn al-Nu'man, which was in a bag of flour. The flour kept spilling out through a tear in the bag. He hid the coat of mail with Zayd ibn al-Simin, a man from the Jews. When the coat of mail was searched for, it was not found with Ṭu'ma, and he swore that he had not taken it and had no knowledge of it. So they left him and followed the trail of flour until it led to the Jew's house, and they seized it there. The Jew said, "Ṭu'ma gave it to me," and some Jews testified for him. The Banu Ẓafar then said, "Come with us to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." They asked him to argue on behalf of their companion, and they said, "If you do not do so, he will be destroyed and disgraced, and the Jew will be cleared." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was inclined to do so and to punish the Jew. It was also said that he was inclined to cut off the Jew's hand. [This was reported by al-Tha'labi from the narration of Abu Ṣāliḥ from al-Kalbi from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Wāḥidī transmitted it from the exegetes in his work on the occasions of revelation (asbāb al-nuzūl). Al-Ṭabarī narrated it through Saʿīd from Qatāda, who said: "It has been mentioned to us that this verse was revealed concerning Ṭu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who was one of the Anṣār from the Banu Ẓafar. He stole a coat of mail belonging to his paternal uncle, which had been deposited with him, and then he planted it on a Jew who used to visit them, called Zayd ibn al-Simin," and he mentioned the story. It was also transmitted by al-Tirmidhī and al-Ḥākim in a lengthy form through Muḥammad ibn Salama from Ibn Isḥāq from ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar from his father from his grandfather Qatāda ibn al-Nuʿmān. Al-Tirmidhī said: "It is gharīb (unusual), and we do not know of anyone who traced it back to Ibn Isḥāq except Muḥammad ibn Salama. Yūnus and others narrated it from Ibn Isḥāq from ʿĀṣim as a mursal (a report lacking a companion in its chain)."] Then the verse was revealed.

It is also narrated that Ṭu'ma fled to Makka, apostatized, and broke into a wall in Makka in order to steal from its people, and the wall fell on him and killed him.

﴿By what Allah has shown you﴾: by what Allah has made you know and has revealed to you.

It is narrated from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "None of you should say, 'I have judged by what Allah has shown me,' for Allah did not grant that except to His Prophet (ﷺ). Rather, let him exert his opinion (ijtihad) with effort." [The phrase "let him exert his opinion" appears in al-Khāzin's wording as "let him strive" (yajhad). (ʿ)] Because the opinion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was correct, since Allah was showing it to him, whereas for us it is conjecture and forced effort.

﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾: do not be a disputant on behalf of those who are treacherous, that is, the innocent. He means: do not argue against the Jews on behalf of the Banu Ẓafar.

﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾: for what you were inclined to do, namely the punishment of the Jew.

﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾: do not be a disputant on behalf of those who are treacherous, that is, the innocent. He means: do not argue against the Jews on behalf of the Banu Ẓafar.

﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾: for what you were inclined to do, namely the punishment of the Jew.

﴿They betray themselves﴾

They betray them (anfus) through disobedience. Like His saying: ﴿Allah knows that you were betraying yourselves﴾. The disobedience of the disobedient is made a betrayal by them of themselves, just as it is made an injustice to themselves, because the harm returns to them.

If you ask: why was it said ﴿for the traitors﴾ (lil-khaʾinin) and ﴿they betray themselves﴾, when the thief was Tuʿmah alone?

I answer: for two reasons. First, the clan of Zafar bore witness to his innocence and supported him, so they were partners with him in the sin. Second, the plural is used to include Tuʿmah and everyone who betrays in the manner of his betrayal. So one should never argue on behalf of a traitor or dispute for him.

If you ask: why was it said ﴿a constant traitor, sinful﴾ (khawwanan athiman) in intensive form?

I answer: Allah knew of Tuʿmah his excess in betrayal and his committing of sins, and one whose final end is such does not have his state doubted. It is said: if you catch a man in one bad deed, know that it has siblings (akhawat). It is narrated from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he ordered the hand of a thief to be cut off, and his mother came weeping and said: "This is the first theft he has committed, so pardon him." He said: "You have lied. Indeed Allah does not take His servant to account for the first time." [[I have not found it.]]

(فَإِنَّما يَكْسِبُهُ عَلى نَفْسِهِ) ﴿Then it is only against himself that he earns it﴾. That is, its harm does not pass beyond him to others; so let him keep upon himself the evil he has earned: a sin (khaṭī'a), a minor one, or (ism), a grave one, ﴿and then casts it upon an innocent person﴾, as Ṭu'ma cast it upon Zayd. ﴿Then he has borne a calumny and a manifest sin﴾. For by earning the sin he is a sinner (āthim), and by casting the blame upon the innocent he is a slanderer (bāhit); so he combines both matters.

And Mu'ādh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, read it as "wa-man yakassib" (وَمَن يَكِسِّبْ), with a kasra on the kāf and a shaddah on the sīn, its original form being yaktasib (يَكْتَسِب).

(فَإِنَّما يَكْسِبُهُ عَلى نَفْسِهِ) ﴿Then it is only against himself that he earns it﴾. And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy,

That is, His protection (ʿisma), His subtle kindnesses, and what He revealed to you of the knowledge of their secret.

a group of them would have resolved to lead you astray

From the clan of Ẓafar. To turn you away from judging with the truth and from pursuing the path of justice, although they knew that the offender was one of their own companions. It is related that some of them were aware of the true details of the affair.

But they lead astray only themselves

Because its burden falls upon them.

And they can harm you in nothing

Because you only acted upon the apparent state of affairs, and it did not occur to you that the reality was otherwise.

And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom and taught you that which you did not know

Of hidden matters and the secrets of hearts, or of matters of religion and the sacred law. It is permissible that the "group" (ṭāʾifa) be understood as the clan of Ẓafar, and that the pronoun in "minhum" (of them) refers to the people. It has also been said: the verse refers to the hypocrites.

La khayra fi kathirin min najwahum ("There is no good in much of their secret talk"), illa man amara bi-sadaqah ("except one who enjoins charity"). The phrase illa man amara is in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for kathir, just as you would say: "There is no good in their gatherings except the gathering of Zayd." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as an exception of disconnection (al-inqita'), meaning: "But one who enjoins charity, in his secret talk there is good."

It has been said: al-ma'ruf is lending (al-qard). It has been said: it is relieving the distressed (ighathat al-malhuf). It has been said: it is general to every good deed.

It is permissible that by sadaqah is meant the obligatory (al-wajib), and by al-ma'ruf what one gives in charity by way of voluntary supererogation (al-tatawwu').

From the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related: "All of the speech of the son of Adam is against him and not for him, except enjoining good, forbidding evil, or the remembrance of Allah." [Related by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani, from the hadith of Umm Habibah. Its central narrator is Muhammad ibn Yazid ibn Habish, in the narration of Sufyan al-Thawri; and in the narration of al-Hakim there is an addition from the speech of al-Thawri, that he cited this verse and others as evidence.]

Sufyan heard a man say: "How severe is this hadith!" So he said: "Did you not hear Allah say: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾? That is exactly this. Or have you not heard Him say: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss﴾? That is exactly this."

The stipulation for earning the great reward is that the doer of good intends by it the worship of Allah and drawing near to Him, and that he seeks by it His Face, sincerely, because actions are by intentions.

If you ask: how does He say ﴿except one who enjoins﴾ and then say ﴿And whoever does that﴾? I say: He mentioned the enjoining of good in order to indicate its doer, because when the one who enjoins it enters the company of the good-doers, the one who acts is more deeply included among them. Then He said ﴿And whoever does that﴾, mentioning the doer and linking to him the promise of a great reward. It is also permissible that what is meant is: "And whoever enjoins that," so He expressed the enjoining by the verb "does," as that verb is used for all other actions. It was also read as yu'tihi, with the ya' (in the third person).

﴿وَيَتَّبِعْ غَيْرَ سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: this is the path they are on, the upright and true (ḥanīfī) religion. It is evidence that consensus (ijmāʿ) is a binding proof that may not be opposed, just as opposing the Book and the Sunna is not permitted. God, exalted and majestic, joined following a path other than that of the believers with opposing the Messenger in the conditional clause, and made its recompense a severe threat. So following them is obligatory, like loyalty to the Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him.

﴿نُوَلِّهِ مَا تَوَلَّى﴾: We will make him master (wālī) of what he has chosen of error, by forsaking him and leaving him to what he has chosen. ﴿وَنُصْلِهِ جَهَنَّمَ﴾. It is read ﴿وَنُصْلِهِ﴾ with an open nūn, from ṣallāhu (to roast). It was also said: this was revealed about Ṭuʿma and his apostasy and his departure to Mecca.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَغْفِرُ أَنْ يُشْرَكَ بِهِ﴾ is a repetition for emphasis. It was also said: it was repeated for the story of Ṭuʿma. It is narrated that he died as a polytheist. It was also said:

A man of the Arabs came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and said: "I am an old man immersed in sins, but I have not associated anything with God since I came to know Him and believed in Him, nor have I taken any protector besides Him, nor have I committed sins out of audacity toward God or defiance of Him. I did not imagine for the blink of an eye that I could escape God by flight. I am regretful, repentant, and seeking forgiveness. What do you think of my state with God?" [It is disconnected.] So it was revealed. This hadith supports the view of those who interpret ﴿لِمَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ as referring to the one who repents of his sin. [Note: "This supports the view of ..." is the view of the Muʿtazila. (ʿ)]

﴿إِلَّا إِنَاثًا﴾: these are al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt. It is reported from al-Ḥasan: no living tribe of the Arabs existed without an idol they worshipped, which they called "the female of the clan of so-and-so." It was also said: they used to say of their idols, "They are the daughters of God." It was also said: the intended meaning is the angels, because of their saying, "The angels are the daughters of God." It is read ﴿أُنْثًا﴾, plural of anīth or annāth. And ﴿وُثُنًا﴾ and ﴿أَثُنًا﴾, with and without emphasis, plural of wathan (idol), like your saying asad, usud and asad. **﴿The promise of God is true﴾**: there are two verbal nouns (maṣdar, a verbal noun) here. The first, *wa'd* (promise), emphasizes itself (*mu'akkid li-nafsihi*), and the second, *ḥaqqan* (truly), emphasizes something other than itself (*mu'akkid li-ghayrihi*).

**﴿And who is more truthful in speech than God?﴾**: this is a third emphasis, an eloquent one.

If it is asked, "What is the benefit of these emphases?" I answer: they counter the false promises of Satan and his vain wishes to his companions with the true promise of God to His friends. This is to encourage the servants to prefer what earns them the fulfilment of God's promise over what they will swallow, in its consequence, as the bitter agony of Satan's broken promises.

In the pronoun of **laysa** (it is not), the referent is the promise of God. That is, the reward promised by God is not attained ﴿by your wishful thinking nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾. The address is to the Muslims, because only someone who believes in God's promise wishes for it. The People of the Book are mentioned alongside them because they share with them in belief in God's promise.

It is narrated from Masruq and al-Suddi that the verse concerns the Muslims. It is narrated from al-Hasan: "Faith is not by wishful thinking, but is what settles in the heart and is affirmed by action. Some people were diverted by hopes of forgiveness until they left this world with no good deeds, and they said, 'We think well of God,' and they lied. If they had thought well of God, they would have done good deeds for Him."

It was also said: the Muslims and the People of the Book boasted, so the People of the Book said, "Our prophet came before your prophet, and our book came before your book." The Muslims said, "We have more right than you. Our prophet is the Seal of the Prophets, and our book overrules the books that came before it." So the verse was revealed.

It is possible that the address is to the polytheists, because of their saying: ﴿If it is as these people claim, we will surely be better off than them and in a better condition﴾, and ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾, and ﴿Indeed, with Him I shall have the best﴾. The People of the Book also used to say, "We are the sons of God and His beloved," and "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." This is supported by the earlier mention of the people of polytheism before it. It is narrated from Mujahid that the address is to the polytheists.

As for His words ﴿whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ and His words ﴿and whoever does righteous deeds﴾, after the mention of the wishful thinking of the People of the Book, they are like His saying ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and is encompassed by his sin﴾, and His saying ﴿but those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ following His saying ﴿and they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."﴾ When God nullifies wishful hopes, and establishes that the whole matter is bound to deeds, and that whoever makes his deeds righteous is the successful one, and whoever does evil in his deeds is the ruined one, the matter becomes clear and evident, and it becomes necessary to cut off wishful hopes, put an end to greed, and turn to righteous action. But this is advice that ears do not heed and minds do not receive.

If you ask: what is the difference between the first **min** (from) and the second? I say: the first is partitive (for a part). The meaning is: ﴿and whoever does some of the righteous deeds﴾, because no one can fully perform all righteous deeds, since circumstances differ. A person only does what is incumbent on him and within his capacity. How many a person is not obligated to perform the pilgrimage, nor jihad, nor zakat, and is excused from prayer in some circumstances. The second **min** is explanatory, clarifying the ambiguity in ﴿whoever does﴾.

If you ask: why are the righteous singled out as those who ﴿will not be wronged﴾ while others are equal to them in that? Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "If you ask, why are the righteous singled out as not being wronged while others are equal to them in that? I say: there are two aspects. The first is that the pronoun in ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ refers to both the evildoers and the doers of righteousness together. The second is that its mention in regard to one group indicates its mention regarding the other, because both groups are recompensed for their deeds with no disparity between them. Moreover, the wronging of the evildoer would be to increase his punishment, and it is known that the Most Merciful of the Merciful does not increase the punishment of the criminal, so mentioning it is unnecessary. As for the doer of good, he has a reward and things that follow the reward by God's bounty, which are in the category of reward. So it is permissible for some of the bounty to be reduced, since it is not obligatory, and the negation of wronging indicates that no reduction in bounty occurs."

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "The whole of this lengthy question and answer rests on propagating a corrupt belief: that God, exalted is He, is obligated to reward acts of obedience, and that reward is divided into what is obligatory and not bounty, and into an increase over what is obligatory, which is purely bounty. This belief is the one for which it is true that Satan has stirred up the Qadariyya (those who affirm human free will and reject divine predestination), to the point that they claimed they have a right over God, exalted above that, that He must give them something. Indeed God is free of need for any deed that obligates Him to a right, may He be glorified and exalted. Satan has blown this wish into the ears of the Qadariyya. O God, we have no reliance except on Your bounty, so grant us abundantly of it, O Most Generous."

In the pronoun of **laysa** (it is not), the referent is the promise of God. That is, the reward promised by God is not attained ﴿by your wishful thinking nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾. The address is to the Muslims, because only someone who believes in God's promise wishes for it. The People of the Book are mentioned alongside them because they share with them in belief in God's promise.

It is narrated from Masruq and al-Suddi that the verse concerns the Muslims. It is narrated from al-Hasan: "Faith is not by wishful thinking, but is what settles in the heart and is affirmed by action. Some people were diverted by hopes of forgiveness until they left this world with no good deeds, and they said, 'We think well of God,' and they lied. If they had thought well of God, they would have done good deeds for Him."

It was also said: the Muslims and the People of the Book boasted, so the People of the Book said, "Our prophet came before your prophet, and our book came before your book." The Muslims said, "We have more right than you. Our prophet is the Seal of the Prophets, and our book overrules the books that came before it." So the verse was revealed.

It is possible that the address is to the polytheists, because of their saying: ﴿If it is as these people claim, we will surely be better off than them and in a better condition﴾, and ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾, and ﴿Indeed, with Him I shall have the best﴾. The People of the Book also used to say, "We are the sons of God and His beloved," and "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." This is supported by the earlier mention of the people of polytheism before it. It is narrated from Mujahid that the address is to the polytheists.

As for His words ﴿whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ and His words ﴿and whoever does righteous deeds﴾, after the mention of the wishful thinking of the People of the Book, they are like His saying ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and is encompassed by his sin﴾, and His saying ﴿but those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ following His saying ﴿and they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."﴾ When God nullifies wishful hopes, and establishes that the whole matter is bound to deeds, and that whoever makes his deeds righteous is the successful one, and whoever does evil in his deeds is the ruined one, the matter becomes clear and evident, and it becomes necessary to cut off wishful hopes, put an end to greed, and turn to righteous action. But this is advice that ears do not heed and minds do not receive.

If you ask: what is the difference between the first **min** (from) and the second? I say: the first is partitive (for a part). The meaning is: ﴿and whoever does some of the righteous deeds﴾, because no one can fully perform all righteous deeds, since circumstances differ. A person only does what is incumbent on him and within his capacity. How many a person is not obligated to perform the pilgrimage, nor jihad, nor zakat, and is excused from prayer in some circumstances. The second **min** is explanatory, clarifying the ambiguity in ﴿whoever does﴾.

If you ask: why are the righteous singled out as those who ﴿will not be wronged﴾ while others are equal to them in that? Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "If you ask, why are the righteous singled out as not being wronged while others are equal to them in that? I say: there are two aspects. The first is that the pronoun in ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ refers to both the evildoers and the doers of righteousness together. The second is that its mention in regard to one group indicates its mention regarding the other, because both groups are recompensed for their deeds with no disparity between them. Moreover, the wronging of the evildoer would be to increase his punishment, and it is known that the Most Merciful of the Merciful does not increase the punishment of the criminal, so mentioning it is unnecessary. As for the doer of good, he has a reward and things that follow the reward by God's bounty, which are in the category of reward. So it is permissible for some of the bounty to be reduced, since it is not obligatory, and the negation of wronging indicates that no reduction in bounty occurs."

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "The whole of this lengthy question and answer rests on propagating a corrupt belief: that God, exalted is He, is obligated to reward acts of obedience, and that reward is divided into what is obligatory and not bounty, and into an increase over what is obligatory, which is purely bounty. This belief is the one for which it is true that Satan has stirred up the Qadariyya (those who affirm human free will and reject divine predestination), to the point that they claimed they have a right over God, exalted above that, that He must give them something. Indeed God is free of need for any deed that obligates Him to a right, may He be glorified and exalted. Satan has blown this wish into the ears of the Qadariyya. O God, we have no reliance except on Your bounty, so grant us abundantly of it, O Most Generous."

﴿Aslama wajhahu lillah﴾ (He submitted his face to Allah): he devoted himself sincerely to Allah and made himself wholly His, knowing no lord or object of worship besides Him. ﴿wa huwa muhsin﴾ (while he was a doer of good): he performed good deeds and abstained from evil deeds. ﴿hanifan﴾ (as a ḥanīf, one who turns away from all false religions) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) either from the one who follows or from Ibrahim, as in His words: ﴿Nay, [follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf; and he was not of the polytheists﴾. He is the one who turned (taḥannafa) away from all religions toward the religion of Islam. ﴿wa-ittakhadha Allahu Ibrahima khalilan﴾ (and Allah took Ibrahim as an intimate friend, khalīl) is a metaphor for choosing him and singling him out for an honour resembling the honour a friend shows to his friend. The khalīl is the khallāl, the one who is intimate with you, meaning he agrees with you in your characteristics (khalāl), or he accompanies you on your path, from al-khall, a track through sand; or he fills your gaps (khalal) just as you fill his; or he enters among your dwellings and screens.

If you ask: what is the position of this clause? I answer: it is a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tirāḍiyya) that has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis), like what comes in poetry, such as their saying:

*"Would that I knew, while events are many, whether I shall one day arise and my affair be gathered [in order]?"*

His words "wal-ḥawādithu jammatun" (while events are many) mean numerous; it is a parenthetical clause. "Aghdūna" is emphasised with the light nūn. "wa-amrī mujmaʿ" means a purpose that is resolved upon and firmly settled. Or the meaning is: my scattered affairs are gathered together again, and this is a circumstantial clause that replaces the predicate of aghdūna or its predicate, and the wāw was added to emphasise the connection. Ajmaʿa is used for what is intelligible (maʿqūl), and jamaʿa is used for what is perceptible (maḥsūs).

Its benefit is to affirm the obligation of following his religion, because whoever has attained such nearness to Allah that He took him as a khalīl is worthy that his religion and path be followed. If you made it coordinated (maʿṭūfa) with the clause before it, it would have no meaning.

It is said: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, sent [a message] to a friend of his in Egypt during a crisis that had struck the people, to buy provisions from him. His friend said: If Ibrahim were seeking provisions for himself, I would have done it, but he wants them for his guests. His servants passed by a soft valley and filled their sacks with its sand out of shame before the people. When they informed Ibrahim, peace be upon him, the news grieved him, and his eyes filled with tears. His wife went to one of the sacks, took out the finest flour, kneaded it and baked bread. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, perceived the smell of the bread and said: From where did you get this? His wife said: From your Egyptian friend. He said: Rather, [it is] from the presence of my khalīl, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So Allah named him khalīl.

Qur'anic quotations are in ﴿ ﴾. Translate:

"To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" (﴿وَلِلَّهِ ما فِي السَّماواتِ وَما فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾) — connected with the mention of those who do righteous deeds and the righteous. Its meaning: that to Him belongs the dominion of the people of the heavens and the earth, so obedience to Him is obligatory upon them. "And Allah is ever, of all things, Encompassing" (﴿وَكانَ اللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ مُحِيطاً﴾) — so He is knowing of their deeds, and will recompense them for their good and their evil. Therefore it is incumbent upon them to choose for themselves what is most beneficial for them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 127:

"What is recited" is in the nominative case (fi mahall al-raf'). That is, Allah is the one who gives you a ruling (yuftikum), and what is recited in the Book (al-mutlaw) has the sense of the orphans, meaning His saying: ﴿If you fear that you will not act justly toward orphan girls﴾. This is like your saying: "Zayd impressed me, and his generosity." It is also permissible that ﴿what is recited to you﴾ (ma yutla 'alaykum) is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿in the Book﴾ (fi al-Kitab) is its predicate, making it a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'tarida). The intended meaning of "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in glorification of what is recited to them, and to indicate that justice and equity toward the rights of orphans are among the great matters, exalted in rank with Allah, which must be observed and safeguarded. One who neglects them is a wrongdoer who treats lightly what Allah has glorified. A similar usage in glorifying the Qur'an is: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise﴾. It is also permissible that it be in the genitive case (majrur) by way of an oath, as if it were said: "Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and I swear by what is recited to you in the Book." The oath too serves the meaning of glorification. It is not sound to make it a conjunct (ma'tuf) of the genitive pronoun in ﴿concerning them﴾ (fihinna), because that is defective both in wording and in meaning.

If you say: With what is ﴿concerning the orphans of women﴾ (fi yatama al-nisa') connected? I say: In the first case it is a relative clause (sila) of ﴿is recited﴾ (yutla), meaning: it is recited to you concerning their matter. It is also permissible that ﴿concerning the orphans of women﴾ be a substitute (badal) for ﴿concerning them﴾ (fihinna). In the other two cases it is only a substitute.

If you say: What is the annexation (idafa) in ﴿orphans of women﴾ (yatama al-nisa')? I say: It is an annexation in the sense of "from" (min), as in your saying: "I have a sack of dates (suhq 'amama)," meaning a sack made of... (i.e., the annexation indicates origin/partitive relation).

It was read as ﴿in ييامى النساء﴾ (fi yayama al-nisa'), with two yas, by changing the hamza of ayama into ya.

﴿You do not give them what has been prescribed for them﴾ (la tu'tunahunna ma kutiba lahunna). It was also read: ﴿what Allah has prescribed for them﴾ (ma kataba Allah lahunna), i.e., what He has ordained for them of inheritance.

A man among them would take an orphan girl into his own care along with her property (wa malaha) [[His saying "and her property, etc." — the wording of al-Nasafi: perhaps its original was "wa malaha ila malihi" (and her property to his property). (ʿ)]]. If she was beautiful, he would marry her and consume the property; if she was plain, he would prevent her from marrying until she died, so that he could inherit from her. ﴿And you desire to marry them﴾ (wa targhabuna an tankihuhunna) may mean, because of their beauty, that you desire to marry them, or, because of their plainness, that you desire to refrain from marrying them.

It is related that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, whenever the guardian of an orphan girl came to him, would look. If she was beautiful and wealthy, he would say: "Let someone else marry her, and seek for her one better than you." If she was plain and had no property, he would say: "Marry her, for you have the greater right to her." [[Al-Tabari narrated it through the route of Ibrahim that Umar ibn al-Khattab—and he mentioned it as a mursal report.]]

﴿And the oppressed (al-mustad'afin)﴾ is in the genitive case, conjoined to ﴿orphans of women﴾. In the Jahiliyya, they used to bequeath only to men capable of managing affairs, not to children or women. It is also permissible that this be an address to the guardians (awsiya'), like His saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. ﴿And that you stand firm (an taqumu)﴾ is in the genitive case, like ﴿the oppressed,﴾ meaning: He gives you a ruling concerning orphan women, and concerning the oppressed, and concerning that you stand firm. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative case, meaning: and He commands you that you stand firm. This is an address to the leaders (a'imma), that they look after them, secure their rights for them, and not leave anyone who would oppress them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 128:

She feared (khafat) from her husband (ba'lihā) — she anticipated it from him, because signs and indications of it had appeared to her. Nushuz (rebellion/ill-treatment) is that he should turn away from her by withholding himself from her, and his maintenance, and the affection and mercy that exist between a man and a woman, and that he should harm her by abuse or beating. I'rad (aversion) is that he should turn away from her by reducing conversation with her and companionship, and that is for some reason: an advanced age, ugliness, some defect in her form or character, boredom, or the eye's aspiring to another woman, or other things. There is no harm in the two of them making peace between themselves (an yuslihā baynahumā).

It was also read yuṣāliḥā and yuṣlihā, meaning yataṣāliḥā and yaṣṭaliḥā. And the form aṣlaḥa is like aṣbara in iṣṭabara, with yuṣlihā being in the sense of the verbal noun of each of the three verbs. The meaning of ṣulḥ (reconciliation):

That they make peace on the basis that she gives up, willingly, her turn of division or part of it, as Sawda bint Zam'a did when she disliked that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) should part from her, and she recognised the place of 'Ā'isha in his heart, so she gave her day to her. [[Narrated by al-Ḥākim from a ḥadīth of 'Ā'isha, and it is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs through the narration of 'Urwa from 'Ā'isha, who said: "I have not seen a woman I would love more to be in the state of Sawda bint Zam'a, a woman who had a sharpness (ḥidda)..." — the ḥadīth.]] Likewise it is related that a man wished to divorce his wife because of his aversion to her, and she had a child by him, so she said: "Do not divorce me, and leave me to look after my child, and divide (your nights) for me every two months." He said: "If this would be acceptable, it is more beloved to me," and he kept her. Or she gives him part of the dower, or all of it, or the maintenance. If she does not do so, then he has no option except to keep her with kindness or release her (yusarriḥuhā).

"And reconciliation is better" than separation, or than rebellion, aversion and bad companionship. Or it is better than contention in everything. Or reconciliation is better than all good things, just as contention is worse than all evils. This sentence is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ), and likewise His saying: "And souls are made to be present with stinginess" (wa-uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥ). The meaning of "souls are made present with stinginess" is that stinginess is placed present before them, never absent from them and never separated from them; that is, they are naturally disposed to it. The point is that a woman scarcely allows her turn of division to be given up, nor anything other than her turn, such as separation, maintenance and dower [[His words "and other than her turn" perhaps should read "other than her turn", like separation, maintenance and dower. The phrasing of al-Nasafi is: "she scarcely allows her turn... and the man..." — so verify. (ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd / editor's note.)]], and the man scarcely allows his soul to give her her turn, or to keep her when he turns away from her and loves another. "And if you do good" by remaining with your wives even though you dislike them and love others, and "are patient" over that, out of regard for the right of companionship, "and guard against" rebellion and aversion and whatever leads to harm and contention, then "indeed Allah is ever, of what you do" of good and piety, "Acquainted" (khabīran), and He will reward you for it.

'Imrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān, the Khārijite, was among the darkest of the children of Adam, and his wife was among the most beautiful of them. One day she looked at his face and then continued praising Allah. He said: "What is the matter with you?" She said: "I praised Allah that you and I are among the people of Paradise." He said: "How?" She said: "Because you were given the likes of me and you were thankful, and I was given the likes of you and I was patient, and Allah has promised Paradise to His thankful and patient servants." [[I have not found it.]]

And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you are eager to do so. (Impossible that you could be able to do justice between women and treat them equally, so that there is no inclination whatsoever, neither excess nor deficiency, in what is due to them.) Thus, the complete and ultimate justice has been lifted from you, and you are only obligated to do what you are able to do, on condition that you exert your utmost effort and capacity in it, because imposing what cannot be done falls within the definition of injustice: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾. It is also said that the meaning is: that you be equitable in love.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would divide [his time] among his wives equitably and say: "This is my division in what I possess, so do not blame me for what You possess and I do not," [Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, from the narration of Abu Qilabah, from Abdullah ibn Yazid, from Aisha. In it, "what You possess" refers to the heart.] meaning love, because Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) was more beloved to him.

It is also said: equitability among them is a difficult matter, extremely difficult to the point that it gives the impression that it is not attainable, because it is obligatory to treat them equally in division, maintenance, care, attention, affection, kind conversation, cheerful company, companionship, and other things beyond which enumeration can hardly reach. So it is as if it lies outside the limit of what is attainable. This is when they are all beloved; how much more so when the heart inclines toward some of them. ﴿So do not incline completely [to one] and leave [another] as if suspended.﴾ That is, do not wrong the one who is disliked completely, withholding her share without her consent. The meaning is: avoiding complete inclination is within the limit of ease and capacity, so do not neglect it if you fall short in complete justice. There is in this a kind of rebuke. ﴿And leave her as if suspended﴾: this is the one who is neither married nor divorced. A poet said:

هَلْ هِىَ إلّا حَظَّةٌ أَوْ تَطْلِيقْ ... أوْ صَلَفٌ أَوْ بَيْنَ ذَاكَ تَعْلِيقْ

[By Bint al-Hamaris. The interrogative is one of denial, i.e., the state of a wife with her husband is nothing but a small portion of the husband's favor toward her, or divorce from him, or neglect (ṣalaf), i.e., the husband's lack of favor toward her—one says "ṣalafat ṣalafan" in the pattern of "ta'iba"—and "ṣālifāt" are women whom the husband does not favor; or suspension between those mentioned states. Completing a shortened meter by adding a sakin at its end, as here, is rare.]

In the recitation of Ubayy: "so you leave her like one who is imprisoned." In a hadith: "Whoever has two wives and inclines toward one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one of his sides leaning." [Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, from the narration of Bashir ibn Nahik, from Abu Hurairah. Al-Tirmidhi said: it is not known as marfu' except from the hadith of Hammam.]

It is also reported that Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) sent money to the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "Did Umar send the same amount to all the wives of the Messenger of Allah?" They said: "No, he sent to the Qurashi women the same amount and to others something else." So she said: "Raise your head, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to treat us equitably in division, with his wealth and his person." The messenger returned and informed him, so he completed it for all of them. [I have not found it in this form. In the Musnad of Ahmad, from the narration of Basirah ibn Sumayn: I heard Umar ibn al-Khattab say, while he was addressing the people on the day of al-Jabiyah: "Allah made me a treasurer of this wealth and its divider," then he said: "Rather, Allah divides it, and I am the first of the people of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He assigned to his wives ten thousand, except Juwayriyah, Safiyyah and Maymunah. Aisha said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to treat us equitably." So Umar treated them equitably—the hadith. It is recorded in the Sunan of Abu Amr ibn Hafs, in the Musnad of the Meccans.]

Mu'adh had two wives. When he was with one of them, he would not perform wudu' in the house of the other. Both of them died in the plague, and he buried them in one grave. [Narrated by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, in the biography of Mu'adh, from the narration of al-Laith from Yahya ibn Sa'id that Mu'adh ibn Jabal—and he mentioned it—and added: "He cast lots between them as to which of them would go first." This is a mursal report.]

﴿And if you set right [what has passed of your inclination] and guard yourselves [in what is to come], then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

And it is read: "wa-in yatafarraqa" (and if they separate), meaning: and if each of them parts from his companion, Allah will enrich each of them by granting him a spouse better than his spouse and a life more pleasant than his life. Al-sa'ah (abundance) is richness. Al-muqtadir (the capable): and al-Wasi' is the Rich, the Capable.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 131–133:

"From before you" is connected either to "We enjoined" or to "were given." "And you" is conjoined to "those who were given the Book." "The Book" (al-Kitab) is a generic noun that encompasses the heavenly scriptures. "That fear Allah" means "that you fear Allah," and the "that" here is explanatory (al-mufassira), because the act of enjoining carries the sense of saying. The clause "And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs..." is conjoined to "fear Allah," because the meaning is: We commanded them and commanded you to be mindful of Allah, and We said to them and to you: if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs... The meaning is: to Allah belongs all creation; He is their Creator, their Owner, and the Bestower upon them of all kinds of blessings. Therefore His right is that He be obeyed among His creatures and not disobeyed, that they fear His punishment and hope for His reward.

"And We have enjoined those who were given the Book from the earlier nations, and We have enjoined you, to fear Allah," meaning that this is an ancient injunction which Allah has always enjoined upon His servants; you are not singled out for it, for by taking heed (taqwa) they attain felicity in His presence and by it they obtain salvation in the end. And We said to them and to you:

"And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, from among the angels and the two weighty creations (humans and jinn), who affirm His oneness, worship Him, and fear Him. And Allah is, besides this, Self-Sufficient (Ghani) above His creation and above their worship, all of them, deserving to be praised for the abundance of His blessings, even if none of them praises Him." The repetition of His words "To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" is an affirmation of what necessitates His taqwa, so that they fear Him, obey Him, and do not disobey Him, because fear and taqwa are the root of all good.

"If He wills, He can take you away (yudhhibkum)," meaning He can annihilate and destroy you just as He brought you into existence and created you, "and bring others (ya'ti bi-akharin)," meaning He can create other humans in your place, or other creatures besides humans. "And Allah is Able (qadir) to do that," meaning, to annihilate and to create, with a powerful, complete ability; nothing He wills is beyond Him. This is a warning and a threat against them and a demonstration of His power. It has also been said that this is an address to those among the Arabs who opposed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). That is: if He wills, He can destroy you and bring other people who will be loyal to him.

It is narrated that when these verses were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck Salman's back with his hand and said: "They are the people of this one." [[Narrated by al-Tabari from the narration of Suhayl from his father from Abu Hurayrah with this wording, and he said: "meaning the non-Arab Persians (ajam al-Furs)."]] He intends the sons of Persia (Fars).
