"And Allah is Able (qadir) to do that," meaning, to annihilate and to create, with a powerful, complete ability; nothing He wills is beyond Him. This is a warning and a threat against them and a demonstration of His power. It has also been said that this is an address to those among the Arabs who opposed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). That is: if He wills, He can destroy you and bring other people who will be loyal to him.

It is narrated that when these verses were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck Salman's back with his hand and said: "They are the people of this one." [[Narrated by al-Tabari from the narration of Suhayl from his father from Abu Hurayrah with this wording, and he said: "meaning the non-Arab Persians (ajam al-Furs)."]] He intends the sons of Persia (Fars).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 131–133:

"From before you" is connected either to "We enjoined" or to "were given." "And you" is conjoined to "those who were given the Book." "The Book" (al-Kitab) is a generic noun that encompasses the heavenly scriptures. "That fear Allah" means "that you fear Allah," and the "that" here is explanatory (al-mufassira), because the act of enjoining carries the sense of saying. The clause "And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs..." is conjoined to "fear Allah," because the meaning is: We commanded them and commanded you to be mindful of Allah, and We said to them and to you: if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs... The meaning is: to Allah belongs all creation; He is their Creator, their Owner, and the Bestower upon them of all kinds of blessings. Therefore His right is that He be obeyed among His creatures and not disobeyed, that they fear His punishment and hope for His reward.

"And We have enjoined those who were given the Book from the earlier nations, and We have enjoined you, to fear Allah," meaning that this is an ancient injunction which Allah has always enjoined upon His servants; you are not singled out for it, for by taking heed (taqwa) they attain felicity in His presence and by it they obtain salvation in the end. And We said to them and to you:

"And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, from among the angels and the two weighty creations (humans and jinn), who affirm His oneness, worship Him, and fear Him. And Allah is, besides this, Self-Sufficient (Ghani) above His creation and above their worship, all of them, deserving to be praised for the abundance of His blessings, even if none of them praises Him." The repetition of His words "To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" is an affirmation of what necessitates His taqwa, so that they fear Him, obey Him, and do not disobey Him, because fear and taqwa are the root of all good.

"If He wills, He can take you away (yudhhibkum)," meaning He can annihilate and destroy you just as He brought you into existence and created you, "and bring others (ya'ti bi-akharin)," meaning He can create other humans in your place, or other creatures besides humans. "And Allah is Able (qadir) to do that," meaning, to annihilate and to create, with a powerful, complete ability; nothing He wills is beyond Him. This is a warning and a threat against them and a demonstration of His power. It has also been said that this is an address to those among the Arabs who opposed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). That is: if He wills, He can destroy you and bring other people who will be loyal to him.

It is narrated that when these verses were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck Salman's back with his hand and said: "They are the people of this one." [[Narrated by al-Tabari from the narration of Suhayl from his father from Abu Hurayrah with this wording, and he said: "meaning the non-Arab Persians (ajam al-Furs)."]] He intends the sons of Persia (Fars).

Whoever desires the reward of this world (like the fighter who in his fighting desires the spoils of war): then with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. So why does he seek one of them to the exclusion of the other? And what he seeks is the baser of the two, because whoever fights for Allah sincerely, the spoils of war will not miss him, and he has from the reward of the Hereafter that beside which the spoils are nothing. The meaning is: with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter for him, if he desires it, so that the recompense is tied to the condition.

Qawwamina bil-qisti (standing firmly for justice), striving in establishing justice, lest you act unjustly. Shuhadaa lillah (witnesses for Allah): you establish your testimonies for the sake of Allah, as you were commanded to establish them, walaw ala anfusikum (even against yourselves), even if the testimony is against yourselves or your parents or your relatives.

If you say: testimony against parents and close relatives would be to say, "I testify that so-and-so has such-and-such a claim against my parent," or against my relatives. So what is the meaning of testimony against oneself? I say: it is acknowledgment against oneself, because it has the sense of testifying against oneself by imposing the right upon oneself.

It is also permissible that the meaning be: "even if the testimony is against yourselves, or against your parents and relatives," and this is when one testifies against someone whose harm is feared from a tyrannical ruler or other such person. In iy yakun (if he be), if the one testified against is in iy yakun ghaniyyan (wealthy), do not withhold testimony against him out of regard for his wealth, seeking his favor; aw faqiran (or poor), do not withhold it out of compassion for him. Fallahu awla bihima (Allah is more worthy of both of them): with regard to the wealthy and the poor, that is, by considering them and intending their benefit. Had testifying against them not been a benefit to them, He would not have prescribed it, for He is more caring for His servants than any caretaker.

If you say: why was the pronoun in "awla bihima" made dual, when it should have been singular, since his saying "in yakun ghaniyyan aw faqiran" means "in yakun ahad hadhayn" (if one of these two be)?

I say: the pronoun refers to what is indicated by his saying "in yakun ghaniyyan aw faqiran," not to the explicitly mentioned noun. Therefore it is dual, not singular, referring to the category of wealth and the category of poverty, as if it were said: "Allah is more worthy of the two categories, wealth and poverty," that is, of the wealthy and the poor. In the reading of Ubayy: "Fallahu awla bihim" (Allah is more worthy of them), and this supports that. ʿAbdullah recited: "in yakun ghaniyyun aw faqirun," reading yakun as the complete verb "kana" (to exist). An tadilu (that you act justly) may mean justice or deviation: as if it were said, "Do not follow desire, out of aversion to being just among people," or "out of intention to deviate from the truth." Wa in talluu aw tuʿridu (and if you distort or turn away): if you distort your tongues from testifying to the truth or from judging with justice, or you turn away from testifying with what you possess and withhold it. It is also recited: "wa in talu" or "aw tuʿridu," meaning: if you take charge of establishing testimony, or if you turn away from establishing it. Inna Allaha kana bima taʿmalmuna khabiran (Indeed Allah is ever Aware of what you do), and will recompense you for it.

O you who have believed: an address to the Muslims. The meaning of "have believed" (āmanū) is: remain steadfast in faith, persist in it, and increase in it.

"And the Book which He sent down before": what is meant by it is the category of the books sent down upon the prophets before him. The evidence for this is His saying "and His books" (wa-kutubih). It was also read as "wa-kitābihi" (and His Book), intending the category; and it was read as "nazzala" (He sent down, intensive form).

"And sent down" is read with the active verb (anzala). It has also been said: the address is to the People of the Book, because they believed in some of the books and messengers and disbelieved in others. It is related that it was addressed to ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, Asad and Usayd, the two sons of Kaʿb, Thaʿlabah ibn Qays, Salam ibn Ukht ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, Salamah the nephew of ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, and Yamin ibn Yamin. They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we believe in you and your Book, and in Moses, the Torah, and ʿUzayr, and we disbelieve in whatever else there is of books and messengers." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Rather, believe in Allah and His Messenger Muhammad, and His Book, the Qur'an, and in every book that came before it." They said: "We will not do that." So the verse was revealed, and they all believed. [[Related by al-Thaʿlabi from the narration of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Wahidi also mentions it in al-Asbab from al-Kalbi without a chain.]] 

It has also been said: it is addressed to the hypocrites, as if it were said: "O you who have believed" in hypocrisy, "believe" in sincerity.

If you say: how is it said to the People of the Book, "and the Book which He sent down before," when they believed in the Torah and the Gospel? I say: they believed in those two only, and they did not believe in everything that had been sent down of books. So they were commanded to believe in the whole category. Moreover, their belief in some of the books is not valid as belief in it, because the path to believing in a book is the miracle, and the miracle is not specific to some books rather than others. So if their belief in what they believed had been on account of the miracle, they would have believed in all of it. Since they believed in part of it, it is known that they did not regard the miracle, and so their belief was not belief. This is what He, Mighty and Majestic, meant in His saying: "And they say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in some,' and they intend to adopt a way between that. Those are the disbelievers in truth" (4:150–151).

If you say: why is it said "He sent down upon His Messenger" (nazzala ʿalā rasūlihi) and "He sent down before" (anzala min qablu)? I say: because the Qur'an was sent down in portions, gradually, over twenty years, unlike the books before it.

As for His saying "And whoever disbelieves in Allah..." the verse means: whoever disbelieves in any of that, "has certainly strayed," because disbelief in part of it is disbelief in all of it. Do you not see how He placed first the command to believe in all of it together?

لَمْ يَكُنِ اللَّهُ لِيَغْفِرَ لَهُمْ وَلا لِيَهْدِيَهُمْ سَبِيلًا

﻿﴿Allah would not forgive them nor guide them to a way.﴾

نفى للغفران والهداية

[[قال محمود: «نفى للغفران والهداية ... الخ»

Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "It is a negation of forgiveness and guidance..."

قال أحمد: وليس في هذه الآية ما يخالف ظاهر القاعدة المستقرة على أن التوبة مقبولة على الإطلاق، لأن آخر ما ذكر من حال هؤلاء ازدياد الكفر، ولو كان المذكور في آخر أحوالهم التوبة والايمان لاحتيج إلى الجمع بين الآية والقاعدة إذاً، وإنما يقع هذا الفصل الذي أورده الزمخشري موقعه في آية آل عمران، وهو قوله تعالى: (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بَعْدَ إِيمانِهِمْ ثُمَّ ازْدادُوا كُفْراً لَنْ تُقْبَلَ تَوْبَتُهُمْ وَأُولئِكَ هُمُ الضَّالُّونَ) وقد ظهر الآن في الجمع بين هذه الآية والقاعدة وجه آخر سوى ما تقدم في آل عمران، وهو أن يكون المراد: لن يصدر منهم توبة فلن يكون قبول، من باب على لا حب لا يهتدى بمناره وعلى هذا يكون خبراً لا حكما، والمخبر عنهم من سبق في علم اللَّه أنه لا يتوب من المرتدين، واللَّه أعلم. وفي قول الزمخشري «إن الناكث للتوبة العائد إليها يغلب من حاله أنه يموت بشر حال» نظر، فقد ورد في الحديث «المؤمن مفتن تواب» قال الهروي:

معناه يقارف الذنب لفتنته، ثم يعقبه بالتوبة.]]

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: There is nothing in this verse that contradicts the apparent sense of the established principle that repentance is accepted without qualification, because the last thing mentioned about these people is the increase in disbelief. Had the last of their conditions mentioned been repentance and faith, it would then have been necessary to reconcile the verse with the principle. The section that al-Zamakhshari cites belongs in its proper place in the verse of Al 'Imran, which is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief—their repentance will never be accepted, and those are the astray.﴾ Now there has appeared, for reconciling this verse with the principle, another aspect apart from what was mentioned regarding Al 'Imran, namely that the meaning is: no repentance will proceed from them, so there will be no acceptance—in the manner of "a beloved whose beacon is not followed" (على لا حب لا يهتدى بمناره). On this reading it is a report (khabar), not a ruling (hukm), and those reported about are those whom Allah knew beforehand would not repent of apostasy. And Allah knows best. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "the one who breaks his repentance and returns to it, it is most likely that his condition will be that he dies in the worst state," there is room for objection, for it has been transmitted in a hadith: "The believer is one who is tested and repeatedly repents" (المؤمن مفتن تواب). Al-Harawi said:

Its meaning: he commits sin because of his temptation, then follows it with repentance.

وهي اللطف على سبيل المبالغة التي يعطيها اللام، والمراد بنفيهما نفى ما يقتضيهما وهو الإيمان الخالص الثابت. والمعنى:

It is "forgiveness" and "guidance" in the emphatic manner that the lām (the emphatic particle of negation, lām al-jaḥd) conveys. The intended negation of both is the negation of what calls for them, namely sincere and steadfast faith. The meaning is:

إنّ الذين تكرر منهم الارتداد وعهد منهم ازدياد الكفر والإصرار عليه، يستبعد منهم أن يحدثوا ما يستحقون به المغفرة ويستوجبون اللطف، من إيمان صحيح ثابت يرضاه اللَّه، لأن قلوب أولئك الذين هذا ديدنهم قلوب قد ضربت بالكفر ومرنت على الردّة، وكان الإيمان أهون شيء عندهم وأدونه، حيث يبدو لهم فيه كرّة بعد أخرى وليس المعنى أنهم لو أخلصوا الإيمان بعد تكرار الردّة ونصحت توبتهم لم يقبل منهم ولم يغفر لهم، لأنّ ذلك مقبول حيث هو بذل للطاقة واستفراغ للوسع، ولكنه استبعاد له واستغراب، وأنه أمر لا يكاد يكون، وهكذا ترى الفاسق الذي يتوب ثم يرجع ثم يتوب ثم يرجع، لا يكاد يرجى منه الثبات. والغالب أنه يموت على شرِّ حال وأسمج صورة. وقيل: هم اليهود، آمنوا بالتوراة وبموسى ثم كفروا بالإنجيل وبعيسى. ثم ازدادوا كفراً بكفرهم بمحمد صلى اللَّه عليه وسلم.

Those who repeatedly apostatise, and from whom an increase in disbelief and persistence in it is known, are regarded as unlikely to produce the kind of sound and steadfast faith that Allah approves, the sort that would merit forgiveness and call for grace. This is because the hearts of such people, whose habit this is, have been hardened by disbelief and accustomed to apostasy, and faith is the least and lowest thing to them, since it appears to them again and again. The meaning is not that if they were to sincerely return to faith after repeated apostasy, and their repentance were sincere, it would not be accepted from them or they would not be forgiven. That is accepted, since it is an exertion of effort and an expenditure of capacity. Rather, it is an expression of improbability and surprise, that it is a matter that scarcely comes about. Likewise you see the sinner who repents, then returns, then repents, then returns, from whom steadfastness is scarcely to be hoped for. Most likely he dies in the worst state and the most ugly form. It was said: they are the Jews, who believed in the Torah and in Moses, then disbelieved in the Gospel and in Jesus, then increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Announce to the hypocrites (bashshir) is used in place of "inform," in mockery of them. "Alladhina" is in the accusative case as a form of censure, or in the nominative, meaning "those who are intended," or "they are the ones who."

They used to side with the disbelievers (yumaylunna al-kafara) and befriend them, and some of them would say to one another: "Muhammad's affair will not succeed, so ally yourselves with the Jews." [Footnote in the original: the phrase "yumaylun al-kafara" is perhaps "yumalin al-kafara." (ʿAyn)]

﴿Then surely all honour belongs to God﴾: he means that honour and victory over the Jews and others belong to His friends, for whom He has decreed honour and victory. And He said: ﴿Honour belongs to God, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾.

﴿Then surely all honour belongs to God﴾: he means that honour and victory over the Jews and others belong to His friends, for whom He has decreed honour and victory. And He said: ﴿Honour belongs to God, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾.

Concerning the words "that when you hear" (أَنْ إِذا سَمِعْتُمْ): the أن here is the lightened form (المخففة) of the heavy أنّ. The meaning is: when you hear, that is, when it has been sent down to you that the matter is such-and-such, where "the matter" (الشأن) is what the sentence conveys with its condition and its response. The أن together with what follows it is in the place of the nominative after نزل, or in the place of the accusative after نزّل, according to the reading of whoever reads it that way.

As for "what has been sent down to you in the Book" (وَالْمُنَزَّلُ عَلَيْكُمْ فِي الْكِتابِ), it is what was sent down to them in Makkah, namely the words of Allah: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk about Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a conversation other than it﴾. This is because the polytheists used to engage in talk about the Qur'an in their gatherings and mock it, so the Muslims were forbidden to sit with them as long as they were engaged in it. The rabbis (أحبار) of the Jews in Madinah used to do the like of what the polytheists did, so they were forbidden to sit with them, just as they had been forbidden to sit with the polytheists in Makkah. Those who sat with the rabbis who engaged in talk about the Qur'an were the hypocrites, so it was said to them: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers﴾, meaning those who sit and those with whom they sit.

If you say: To whom does the pronoun in His words ﴿so do not sit with them﴾ refer? I say: It refers to what is indicated by ﴿disbelieved in and mocked﴾, as if it were said: "Do not sit with those who disbelieve in them and mock them."

If you say: Why would they not be like them by sitting with them at the time of their vain talk? I say: Because when they do not object to them, they are content, and whoever is content with disbelief is a disbeliever.

If you say: Then why were the Muslims in Makkah, when they used to sit with the polytheists engaged in vain talk, not hypocrites? I say: Because they did not object due to their inability, whereas these did not object although they were able, so their abandoning objection indicated their contentment.

﴿Who wait in suspense about you﴾ (الَّذِينَ يَتَرَبَّصُونَ) is either a substitute for ﴿those who take﴾, or an attribute of the hypocrites, or an accusative in dispraise of them. (﴿about you﴾, i.e., they await for you what befalls you of victory or failure [[Regarding his words "or failure": in al-Sihah: akhfaqa al-rajul if he went on a raid and did not gain booty. (Gh.)]]). ﴿Were we not with you?﴾ (أَلَمْ نَكُنْ مَعَكُمْ), supporting you, so give us a share of the spoils. ﴿Did we not gain control over you?﴾ (أَلَمْ نَسْتَحْوِذْ عَلَيْكُمْ), i.e., did we not overcome you and gain the ability to kill you and take you captive, yet we spared you? ﴿And protect you from the believers﴾ (وَنَمْنَعْكُمْ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ), by discouraging them from you, and by suggesting to them what weakened their hearts, so they became sick of fighting you, and we were lax in supporting them against you. So bring us a portion of what you have obtained.

The reading "and We protect you" (وَنَمْنَعْكُمْ) with the accusative is also transmitted, with أن implied; al-Hutay'ah said:

﴿Did I not be your neighbour, and between me and you there were affection and fraternity?﴾

[[The poet addresses al-Zibriqan, who are the Banu Awf ibn Ka'b. He had been their neighbour, then moved to the Banu Rafi'. So he reminds al-Zibriqan of the right of neighbourhood and that they should not sever ties with him. The interrogative is for affirmation: that is, acknowledge the right of neighbourhood, so that affection and fraternity remain in place, meaning agreement in hardship and ease, and in adversity and affliction.]]

﴿Who wait in suspense about you﴾ (الَّذِينَ يَتَرَبَّصُونَ) is either a substitute for ﴿those who take﴾, or an attribute of the hypocrites, or an accusative in dispraise of them. (﴿about you﴾, i.e., they await for you what befalls you of victory or failure [[Regarding his words "or failure": in al-Sihah: akhfaqa al-rajul if he went on a raid and did not gain booty. (Gh.)]]). ﴿Were we not with you?﴾ (أَلَمْ نَكُنْ مَعَكُمْ), supporting you, so give us a share of the spoils. ﴿Did we not gain control over you?﴾ (أَلَمْ نَسْتَحْوِذْ عَلَيْكُمْ), i.e., did we not overcome you and gain the ability to kill you and take you captive, yet we spared you? ﴿And protect you from the believers﴾ (وَنَمْنَعْكُمْ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ), by discouraging them from you, and by suggesting to them what weakened their hearts, so they became sick of fighting you, and we were lax in supporting them against you. So bring us a portion of what you have obtained.

The reading "and We protect you" (وَنَمْنَعْكُمْ) with the accusative is also transmitted, with أن implied; al-Hutay'ah said:

﴿Did I not be your neighbour, and between me and you there were affection and fraternity?﴾

[[The poet addresses al-Zibriqan, who are the Banu Awf ibn Ka'b. He had been their neighbour, then moved to the Banu Rafi'. So he reminds al-Zibriqan of the right of neighbourhood and that they should not sever ties with him. The interrogative is for affirmation: that is, acknowledge the right of neighbourhood, so that affection and fraternity remain in place, meaning agreement in hardship and ease, and in adversity and affliction.]]

If you say: Why did they call the victory of the Muslims a "conquest" (فَتْح), and the victory of the disbelievers a "portion" (نَصِيب)? I say: To magnify the status of the Muslims and to belittle the share of the disbelievers, because the victory of the Muslims is a great matter [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "He named the victory of the Muslims a conquest, to magnify the status of the Muslims..." Ahmad said: This is one of the finest secrets of the Qur'an's subtleties, for what used to befall the Muslims in it was the uprooting of the disbelievers' strength and their seizure of their lands, homes, wealth, and lands they had not trodden. As for what befell the disbelievers, it was like mere dominance and power, whose status does not reach being called a conquest. So the distinction between them also corresponds to reality. And Allah knows best.]]: ﴿The gates of heaven are opened for them until He sends down [revelation] upon His allies.﴾ As for the victory of the disbelievers, it is nothing but a base portion and a morsel of this world that they obtain [[Regarding his words "a morsel of this world": in al-Sihah: lamaza yalmazu, with damma, lamazan, when one follows with the tongue the remnants of food in the mouth. And al-lumzah, with damma, is like a spot of whiteness. (Gh.)]].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 142–143:

﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾

They do what the deceiver does, by showing faith while concealing disbelief.

﴿وَهُوَ خادِعُهُمْ﴾

He does to them what the one who prevails in deception does. He left them with their blood and property protected in this world, and prepared for them the lowest depth of the Fire in the Hereafter. In the immediate world He did not spare them from disgrace, from being overtaken by calamity, from vengeance, and from constant terror. Al-khadi' (the deceiver) is the active participle of khada'tuhu, "I deceived him," when I overcame him and was more cunning than him.

It is said: on the sirat (the bridge over Hell), they will be given a light just as the believers are given light. They will proceed by their light, then their light will be extinguished and the light of the believers will remain. Then they will call out: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾.

﴿كُسالى﴾

It is read with a damma and with a fatha on the kaf, plural of kasлан, like sakara in sakran. That is, they stand up sluggishly and reluctantly, as you see someone who does something unwillingly and not with a willing heart and desire.

﴿يُراؤُنَ النَّاسَ﴾

They intend by their prayer showing off (riya') and seeking reputation.

[Mahmud said: "They pray only for show as long as someone is watching them. When they are alone with themselves, they do not pray, or they do not mention God with tahlil (saying "there is no god but God") and tasbih (saying "Glory be to God") except a little, rarely. Thus you will see that many of those who display Islam, if you were in their company through days and nights, you would not hear from them a single tahlil or tahmid, but the talk of this world occupies their times and they never cease from it. It is not permissible that the 'little' be meant as 'none.'" End of his words.] I say: He prevented the meaning of "little" being "none" only because it is a report, and so it must be true. They used to remember God at certain times, so the remembrance of God cannot be completely denied of them. And if we proceed on the basis that the 'remembrance' means the prayer, which is the apparent meaning, then what is meant is also the proper prayer by which a person remembers God's right over him and so refrains from indecency and wrongdoing. In this sense prayer is entirely denied of the hypocrites. So it is permissible, when the 'little' is taken as 'none' with this interpretation, and God knows best.

﴿وَلا يَذْكُرُونَ اللَّهَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا﴾

They do not pray except a little, because they never pray away from people's eyes, except what they perform openly. What they perform openly is also little, because they found no alternative to affecting what is not in their hearts, so they did not affect it. Or: they do not mention God with tasbih and tahlil except a little, rarely. Thus you will see that many of those who display Islam, if you were in their company through days and nights, you would not hear from them a single tahlil, tasbih or tahmid, but the talk of this world occupies their times and they never cease from it. It is also permissible that the 'little' be meant as 'none.'

If you say: What is the meaning of muraa'ah (showing off), when it is a mufa'alah (form III verb) from ra'y (seeing)?

I say: It has two aspects. One: the one showing off shows them his deed, and they see it and approve of it. Two: it is from the mufa'alah in the sense of the taf'il (form II), so one says: raa'a al-nas, meaning "he showed them," like your saying: na'amahu and na'ama-hu, and fanaqahu and fanaqahu [the editor's note: his words "and fanaqahu and fanaqahu": in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari) they both mean the same, i.e. na'amahu. (ʿAyn)], and ʿaysh mufanaq (a luxurious life). Abu Zayd reported: "The woman saw the man," when she held him so that she could see his face. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abi Ishaq: ﴿yurā'ūnahum﴾ with a doubled hamza, like yar'ūnahum, meaning they make them see their deeds, and they show them the same way.

﴿مُذَبْذَبِينَ﴾

It is either a circumstantial state (hal), like his saying: ﴿and they do not mention God﴾, from the waw in yurā'ūn, meaning they show off to them while not remembering, wavering; or it is in the accusative on the basis of dispraise. The meaning of mudhabdhabīn: Satan and desire have made them waver between faith and disbelief, so they are hesitant between them, bewildered. The root meaning of al-mudhabdhab is one who is pushed away from both sides, that is, he is repelled and driven off and does not settle on one side, as it is said: "So-and-so is thrown about by the two millstones." (The editor's note: his words "thrown about by the two millstones": in al-Sihah, the ruha (millstone) is well known and its alif is changed from ya'. One says: hama ruhayan. Also in it: the snake rahat (coiled), when it curved. And al-ruha: a piece of land that rises above what is around it. Ruha al-qawm: their chief. Al-arha': the molars. Al-arha': the tribes that stand independent and need no others. Its apparent meaning is that the ruha here is a valley; let it be examined. (ʿAyn))

However, the dhabdhabah (wavering) contains a repetition that the dhabb (driving off) does not. As if the meaning is: whenever he inclines to one side, he is driven away from it.

Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿mudhabdhabīn﴾ with a kasra on the dhal, meaning they make their hearts, their religion or their opinion waver; or it means yatadhabdhabūn (they waver), as in: ṣalṣala and tasalṣala with the same meaning. In the codex of ʿAbd Allah it is mutadhabdhabīn. From Abu Jaʿfar: mudabdibīn, with the unpointed dal, and the meaning seems to be: they are taken by it at one time along one path and at another time along another path, so they do not proceed on a single path. The dabba is the path, and from it comes the "dabbat Quraysh" (the way of Quraysh).

﴿وَذلِكَ﴾ refers to disbelief and faith. ﴿لا إِلى هؤُلاءِ﴾ means they are not attributed to these, so they would be believers, ﴿وَلا إِلى هؤُلاءِ﴾ and not attributed to those, so they would be named polytheists.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verse 144:

"O you who believe, do not take the disbelievers as allies (awliya') rather than the believers. Do you want to give Allah a clear proof against yourselves?" (Qur'an 4:144)

Do not imitate the hypocrites in taking as allies (awliya') the Jews and others among the enemies of Islam. "A clear authority (sultanan mubinan)" means a manifest proof; it means that allying oneself with the disbelievers is a clear evidence of hypocrisy (nifaq).

It is narrated from Sa'sa'a ibn Suhan that he said to a nephew of his: "Be sincere (khalis) with the believer, and be courteous (khaliq) with the disbeliever and the wicked, for the wicked will be pleased with you through good conduct, and it is your duty to be sincere with the believer."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 145–146:

the lowest level of the Fire (al-Dark al-Asfal): the stratum at the bottom of Hell. The Fire has seven levels (darakat), so called because they follow one another in succession, one above the other. It is also read with the ra' sukun (Dark), but the correct reading is with a vowel (tahrik), following their saying: adraka Jahannam. If you ask: why is the hypocrite's punishment more severe than the disbeliever's? I answer: because he is like him in disbelief, and he adds to his disbelief mockery of Islam and its people, and duplicity (mudajat) toward them [[His words "and duplicity toward them": in al-Sihah, al-mudajat means al-mudara (outward courtesy/accommodation). (Gh.)]]. ﴿And made amends﴾: they corrected what they had corrupted of their secrets and their states during the time of hypocrisy. ﴿And held fast to Allah﴾: they trusted in Him as sincere believers trust. ﴿And made their religion sincere for Allah﴾: they seek by their obedience nothing but His countenance. ﴿Then those will be with the believers﴾: they are the companions and associates of the believers in both abodes. ﴿And Allah will give the believers a great reward﴾: so they will share in it and partake of it with them. If you ask: who is the hypocrite?

I answer: in the Sharia, he is one who displays faith and conceals disbelief. As for calling one who commits what constitutes sinfulness a "hypocrite," this is for emphasis, like his saying: "Whoever abandons prayer deliberately has disbelieved" [[Mentioned earlier in Al 'Imran and al-Baqarah.]]. And among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Three qualities whoever has them is a hypocrite, even if he fasts, prays, and claims to be a Muslim: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays" [[Narrated by Muslim from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah with the wording "The sign of the hypocrite is three," to the end; in another narration, "Among the signs of the hypocrite are three."]]. It was said to Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him: who is the hypocrite? He said: the one who describes Islam but does not act by it. It was said to Ibn 'Umar: we enter upon the ruler and speak words, then when we leave we speak the opposite. He said: we used to count that as hypocrisy. And from al-Hasan: a time came upon hypocrisy when it was struck (maqru' fihi) [[His words "when it was struck" perhaps mean struck with a stick. In al-Sihah, al-qari'ah is a severe calamity of time, a disaster; one says: the calamities of time struck them, i.e., befell them. And he struck his head with a stick, like qaraha. (Gh.)]], so one morning he had turned his turban, put on a sword, and been given a sword; he means al-Hajjaj.

(Gh.)]], so one morning he had turned his turban, put on a sword, and been given a sword; he means al-Hajjaj.

What would Allah gain by punishing you, if you are grateful and believe? Does He seek to cool His anger by it, or to avenge Himself, or to bring about some benefit, or to ward off some harm, as kings do with their punishments? He is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), to whom none of that can apply. Rather, it is a matter that wisdom requires: that the wrongdoer be punished. So if you give thanks for His blessing and believe in Him, you have removed from yourselves the deserving of punishment. ﴿And Allah is ever Grateful (Shakir), Responsive (Mathib), repaying you your rewards in full﴾, ﴿All-Knowing (Alim) of the reality of your gratitude and your faith.﴾

If you ask: why did he place gratitude before faith? I say: because the rational person looks at the great blessing upon him in his creation and in being made the recipient of benefits, so he gives thanks in a general way. Then, when his reflection leads him to know the Bestower, he believes in Him, and then he gives thanks in a detailed way. Thus gratitude precedes faith, and it is, as it were, the root of the obligation (taklif) and its axis.

*Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 4, verses 148–149:*

﴿Except one who has been wronged﴾ [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Its implied meaning is: Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except the public utterance of one who has been wronged, which is that he calls down curses upon the wrongdoer and mentions what is in him… etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "The reason for the difference is that the wrongdoer is not included in the excepted-from (al-mustathna minhu), just as Allah, exalted is He, is too holy to be in the heavens or in the earth, so his inclusion in the excepted-from is impossible. Likewise, the excepted is not included in the excepted-from in your saying: 'Zayd did not come to me except 'Amr.' Al-Zamakhshari's discussion in this section does not make clear to me anything that would justify its metaphorical interpretation, because of the obscurity of his expression. And Allah knows best what he intends."]]

He excepted from the public utterance that Allah does not love the public utterance of the one who has been wronged. This means that he calls down curses upon the wrongdoer and mentions the evil that is in him. It has also been said that it means one who begins with insult and then answers the insulter. ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾. It has also been said: a man was a guest of a people who did not feed him, so he woke in the morning complaining, and he was rebuked for the complaint, and so this was revealed.

It was also read as ﴿illa man ẓulima﴾ with the verb in the active voice (al-binā' lil-fā'il), as a discontinuous exception (lil-inqiṭā'). That is: "But the wrongdoer is engaged in what Allah does not love, so he publicly utters evil." It is also permissible for ﴿man ẓulima﴾ to be in the nominative case (marfū'), as if it were said: "Allah does not love the public utterance of evil, except the wrongdoer," in the dialect of one who says: "Zayd did not come to me except 'Amr," meaning "No one came to me except 'Amr." From this is His saying: ﴿None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾.

Then he urged pardon, and that no one should publicly utter evil about anyone, even if it is by way of retaliation. This comes after he had permitted the public utterance of it and made it beloved, as an urging toward what is more beloved to Him, more excellent in His sight, and more inclusive of generosity, humility, and servitude. He mentioned the disclosure of good and its concealment as an indication (tashbīban [[His saying "tashbīhan" is probably a distortion, and its original is "tanbīhan," so verify it. (ʿ)]]) toward pardon. Then he joined it to them, as a counting of its worth and an alert to its rank, and that it has a place in the category of good, as an intermediate (wasīṭan [[His saying "wasṭan" means "mutawassiṭan" (intermediate). (ʿ)]]).

The evidence that pardon is the intended purpose of mentioning the disclosure of good and its concealment is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent﴾, meaning He pardons the wrongdoers while having the power to retaliate, so you should follow the example (sunna) of Allah.

It was also read as ﴿illa man ẓulima﴾ with the verb in the active voice (al-binā' lil-fā'il), as a discontinuous exception (lil-inqiṭā'). That is: "But the wrongdoer is engaged in what Allah does not love, so he publicly utters evil." It is also permissible for ﴿man ẓulima﴾ to be in the nominative case (marfū'), as if it were said: "Allah does not love the public utterance of evil, except the wrongdoer," in the dialect of one who says: "Zayd did not come to me except 'Amr," meaning "No one came to me except 'Amr." From this is His saying: ﴿None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾.

Then he urged pardon, and that no one should publicly utter evil about anyone, even if it is by way of retaliation. This comes after he had permitted the public utterance of it and made it beloved, as an urging toward what is more beloved to Him, more excellent in His sight, and more inclusive of generosity, humility, and servitude. He mentioned the disclosure of good and its concealment as an indication (tashbīban [[His saying "tashbīhan" is probably a distortion, and its original is "tanbīhan," so verify it. (ʿ)]]) toward pardon. Then he joined it to them, as a counting of its worth and an alert to its rank, and that it has a place in the category of good, as an intermediate (wasīṭan [[His saying "wasṭan" means "mutawassiṭan" (intermediate). (ʿ)]]).

The evidence that pardon is the intended purpose of mentioning the disclosure of good and its concealment is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent﴾, meaning He pardons the wrongdoers while having the power to retaliate, so you should follow the example (sunna) of Allah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 150–151:

Those who believe in Allah and disbelieve in His messengers, or who believe in Allah and some of His messengers and disbelieve in others, are disbelievers in Allah and His messengers altogether, for the reason we mentioned [[His saying "for the reason we mentioned," i.e., in the explanation of the Exalted's saying: (O you who believe, believe in Allah and His Messenger...), etc. (ʿ)]] from the cause. The meaning of their taking a path between that (ittikhādhuhum bayna dhālika sabīlan) is that they take a religion midway between faith and disbelief, like His saying: (And do not recite your prayer aloud or silently, but seek between those a way) — that is, a middle course in recitation, which is between loudness and silence. But they have erred, for there is no intermediate position between disbelief and faith [[His saying "for there is no intermediate position between disbelief and faith" is the view of the Ahl al-Sunnah. As for the Mu'tazilah, the one who commits a major sin and dies without repentance is neither a believer nor a disbeliever, but in an intermediate position between the two positions. So reflect. (ʿ)]]. That is why He said: (They are the disbelievers truly), that is, they are the complete disbelievers. "Truly" (ḥaqqan) is an emphasis on the content of the sentence, like your saying: "He is truly a servant of Allah," meaning: that is true, truly, namely that they are complete in disbelief. Or it is a qualifier of the verbal noun of "the disbelievers," meaning: they are those who disbelieved with a true disbelief, firmly established and certain, without doubt.

**Question:** How is it permissible for *bayna* (between) to govern *aḥad* (anyone), when *bayna* requires two or more?

**Answer:** *Aḥad* is a general term that applies to a single male or female, and to the dual and plural forms of both. You say *mā ra'aytu aḥadan* ("I did not see anyone"), intending generality. Do you not see that you say *illā banī fulān* ("except the sons of so-and-so") and *illā banāt fulān* ("except the daughters of so-and-so")? So the meaning of *lam yufarriqū bayna aḥadin minhum* is: they did not make a distinction between two of them or between a group of them. From the same usage is the verse ﴿You are not like anyone among the women﴾ (﴿لَسْتُنَّ كَأَحَدٍ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ﴾). As for ﴿He will give them their rewards soon﴾ (﴿سَوْفَ يُؤْتِيهِمْ أُجُورَهُمْ﴾), its meaning is that giving them is certain to occur without doubt, even if it is delayed. The purpose of the expression is to confirm and establish the promise, not to indicate that it is postponed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 153–159 (part 1 of 2):

It is narrated that Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Finhas ibn 'Azura and others said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you are a truthful prophet, then bring us a Book from the heaven all at once, as Musa (Moses) brought it." [[I have not found it worded thus. al-Tabari narrated it through Asbat from al-Suddi, who said: "The Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If you are truthful that you are the Messenger of Allah, then bring us a Book from the heaven as Musa brought it.' So it was revealed."]] So it was revealed. It is also said: (they asked for) a book to so-and-so and a book to so-and-so, (declaring) that you are the Messenger of Allah. And it is said: (they asked for) a book that we could witness as it descends. They only proposed this as a form of obstinacy. al-Hasan said: "Even if they had asked in order to clarify the truth, He would have given it to them, and what He had given them was sufficient." "So they asked Musa..." is the answer to an implied condition. [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "'So they asked Musa': the answer to an implied condition... etc." Ahmad said: This is one of the places where heedlessness has overtaken him, and his following of his desires has led him to the abyss of error. For he built upon the premise that the wrongdoing attributed to them was only because they asked to see Allah, and that this is impossible by reason, in this world and the Hereafter, according to the claim of the Qadariyyah (those who affirm human free will and reject divine predestination), because they hold that if it were said to be permissible, it would entail belief in anthropomorphism. Therefore he named the People of the Sunnah, who hold that it is permissible and that it will occur in the Hereafter, in fulfilment of the true promise, "anthropomorphists" (mushabbihah). He was heedless of the fact that the Jews proposed to Musa (peace be upon him) a specific thing upon which they made their faith conditional, and did not consider the miracle as such, as it must be considered, and they said: "We will never believe you until we see Allah plainly." This proposal and obstinacy is enough to make them wrongdoers. Do you not see that those who said: "We will never believe you until you bring down to us a Book from heaven," or "until you cause a spring to gush from the earth," or "until you have a house of gold," how are they among the most wrongdoing of wrongdoers? And even if they only asked for things that were permissible, yet they prescribed for Allah concerning the signs, whereas their duty was to ground their faith in whatever miracle Allah chose. This indicates clearly that their wrongdoing was caused by their proposal, not by the proposed thing being impossible by reason. How strange is the analogy of this question, if the thing asked for were permissible, to the question of Ibrahim about the reviving of the dead, according to al-Zamakhshari's claim, out of heedlessness of what was contained in Ibrahim's question of pure faith, when He (Exalted is He) said to him: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes." And of what was contained in the question of these accursed ones of pure disbelief and persistence in it, in their saying: "We will never believe you." They began their speech with denial and negation. As for al-Zamakhshari's invocation against the People of the Sunnah with ruin and thunderbolts, Allah knows which of the two groups is more deserving of them. His heedlessness suffices him, which calls out to him of following desire, which blinds and deafens. We ask Allah for protection from misguidance and error.]] Its meaning: if you consider what they asked of you to be great, then they asked Musa something greater than that. The question was attributed to them, although it was found among their fathers in the days of Musa, namely the seventy chiefs, because they were upon their path, content with their request, and matching them in obstinacy. "Openly" (jahratan) means visibly, i.e. "Show us Allah that we may see Him openly." "For their wrongdoing" means because of their request to see (Allah). If they had asked for something permissible, they would not have been called wrongdoers, nor would the thunderbolt have seized them. Just as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) asked to be shown the reviving of the dead, and He did not call him a wrongdoer nor strike him with a thunderbolt. So ruin upon the anthropomorphists and may thunderbolts be hurled at them. [[His saying "so ruin upon the anthropomorphists and may thunderbolts be hurled at them" means the People of the Sunnah, since they permitted the seeing of Allah, as is verified in its proper place. And may Allah forgive the believer who wrongs the believers. (ʿ)]] "We gave Musa a clear authority" means an apparent domination and power over them when He commanded them to kill themselves so that they would be forgiven, and they obeyed him, sitting with their courtyards while the swords fell upon them. How clear is that authority! "For their covenant" means because of their covenant, so that they would fear and not break it. "And We said to them, while the mount was overshadowing them: Enter the gate prostrating, and do not transgress on the Sabbath." The covenant had been taken from them on this, and their saying "We hear and we obey," and their pledge to fulfil it, and then they broke it afterwards. It is recited also as "do not transgress" (la ta'tadu) and "do not transgress" (la ta‘addu), with the assimilation of the taʾ into the dal. "So for their breaking" means "because of their breaking." "Ma" is extra, for emphasis. If you ask: With what is the bāʾ connected, and what is the meaning of the emphasis? [[Mahmud said: "If you ask: with what is the bāʾ in His saying 'So for their breaking their covenant' connected? I say: either it is connected to an omitted element, as if it were said: 'So, for their breaking their covenant, We did to them what We did.' Or it is connected to His saying 'We made unlawful for them,' with 'So for wrongdoing from those who were Jews' being an apposition to 'So for their breaking'... end of his words." I say: there is a secret in mentioning that apposition: the speech had grown long after "So for their breaking," so that it was far from its governing element, which is "We made unlawful," so He reinforced it with "So for wrongdoing from those who were Jews," until it comes adjacent to its governing element. The composition came with it in a manner of brevity in summarising what had been detailed earlier, because all that preceded of breaking the covenant, killing, their saying "Our hearts are wrapped," their disbelief, and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander, and their claim to have killed the Messiah, son of Maryam, is contained in the summary mentioned at the end in a comprehensive way, along with the recording that all their deeds that proceeded from them were wrongdoing. Similar examples of this exposition have preceded. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] I say: either it is connected to an omitted element, as if it were said: "So for their breaking their covenant, We did to them what We did." Or it is connected to His saying "We made unlawful for them," on the basis that His saying "So for wrongdoing from those who were Jews" is an apposition to His saying "So for their breaking their covenant." As for the emphasis, its meaning is to affirm that the punishment, or the prohibition of the good things, was only because of the breaking of the covenant and what was joined to it of disbelief, killing of the prophets, and other things. If you ask: why do you not claim that the omitted element to which the bāʾ is connected is what is indicated by His saying "Rather, Allah has sealed it," so the meaning would be: "So for their breaking their covenant, Allah sealed upon their hearts. Rather, Allah sealed it because of their disbelief." I say: this estimate is not valid, because His saying "Rather, Allah sealed it because of their disbelief" is a rejection and denial of their saying "Our hearts are wrapped," so it was connected to it. That is because they meant by their saying "Our hearts are wrapped" that Allah created our hearts wrapped, i.e. in coverings that nothing of the remembrance and admonition can reach, as Allah related about the polytheists when they said: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them." And like the doctrine of the Mujbirah (determinists), may Allah disgrace them. So it was said to them: "Rather, Allah abandoned them and withheld from them the kindnesses because of their disbelief, so they became like the sealed." [[His saying "like the doctrine of the Mujbirah, may Allah disgrace them" means by them the People of the Sunnah, and far be it from them to intend by their doctrine what the disbelievers intended by what they said. Its verification is in the science of tawhid. And may Allah forgive whoever among the believers exceeds the limit of the Law, and may He not disgrace them on the Day of Judgement. (ʿ)]] not that they were created wrapped, unable to receive remembrance nor empowered to accept it. If you ask: upon what is His saying "and because of their disbelief" conjoined? I say: the proper view is that it is conjoined to "So for their breaking." And His saying "Rather, Allah sealed it because of their disbelief" is a speech following "And they said: Our hearts are wrapped," in the manner of digression, and it is permissible to conjoin it to what immediately follows it, namely "because of their disbelief." If you ask: What is the meaning of bringing in disbelief conjoined to what is mentioned in it, whether it is conjoined to what precedes the particle of transition, or to what follows it, which is "and their disbelief in the signs of Allah," and "because of their disbelief"? I say: disbelief occurred from them repeatedly, because they disbelieved in Musa, then in ʿIsa, then in Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon them. So some of their disbelief was conjoined to some other disbelief, or the whole of the conjoined was conjoined to the whole of what it is conjoined to, as if it were said: "So He gathered them between breaking the covenant, and disbelief in the signs of Allah, and killing the prophets, and their saying 'Our hearts are wrapped,' and their gathering between their disbelief and their slander of Maryam [[His saying "and their slander of Maryam" means their casting upon her what was not in her, namely fornication, i.e. the accusation of adultery. (ʿ)]] and their boasting of killing ʿIsa, We punished them." Or: "Rather, Allah sealed it because of their disbelief, and their gathering between their disbelief and such and such." And "the tremendous slander" is the accusation of fornication. If you ask: they were disbelievers in ʿIsa (peace be upon him), his enemies, intent on killing him, calling him "son of the sorceress" and "son of the adulteress." How then did they say: "Indeed we killed the Messiah, ʿIsa son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah"? I say: they said it in mockery, like the saying of Pharaoh: "Indeed your messenger who was sent to you is surely mad." It is also permissible that Allah placed a good mention in place of their ugly mention, in narrating about them, to elevate ʿIsa above what they used to mention him by, and to glorify what they intended by a similar expression, like His saying: "They will surely say: The Mighty, the Knowing created them. He who made the earth for you a cradle..." It is narrated that a group of Jews reviled him and reviled his mother, so he invoked against them: "O Allah, You are my Lord, and by Your word You created me. O Allah, curse whoever reviled me and reviled my mother." So Allah transformed whoever reviled the two of them into apes and swine. The Jews then unanimously agreed to kill him, so Allah informed him that He would raise him to heaven and purify him from companionship with the Jews. He said to his companions: "Which of you is content that my likeness be cast upon him, so that he is killed and crucified and enters Paradise?" A man among them said: "I." So his likeness was cast upon him, and he was killed and crucified. It is also said: he was a man who was a hypocrite toward ʿIsa, and when they wanted to kill him he said: "I will show you where he is," and he entered ʿIsa's house, and ʿIsa was raised, and his likeness was cast upon the hypocrite, so they entered upon him and killed him, thinking that he was ʿIsa. Then they differed. Some of them said: "He is a god, it is not possible to kill him." Some said: "He was killed and crucified." Some said: "If this is ʿIsa, where is our companion? And if this is our companion, where is ʿIsa?" Some said: "He was raised to heaven." Some said: "The face is the face of ʿIsa, and the body is the body of our companion." If you ask: to what is "it was made to appear" (shubbiha) attributed? If you make it attributed to the Messiah, then the Messiah is the one compared (mushabbah bihi), not the one made to appear; and if you attribute it to the one killed, the one killed has not been mentioned. I say: it is attributed to the prepositional phrase, which is "to them," like your saying: "It was made to appear to him," as if it were said: "But the resemblance occurred for them." It is also permissible that it be attributed to the pronoun of the one killed, because His saying "We killed" indicates it, as if it were said: "But it was made to appear to them, the one they killed." "Except the following of conjecture" is an exceptive that is disconnected, because the following of conjecture is not of the kind of knowledge; meaning: "But they follow conjecture." If you ask: they have been described with doubt, and doubt is that neither of two possibilities is preferred; then they were described with conjecture, and conjecture is that one of them is preferred. How then can they be doubting and conjecturing? I say: it is meant that they were in doubt, having no knowledge at all, but if some sign appeared to them, they conjectured; that is the meaning. "And they did not kill him for certain" means they did not kill him with certainty, or they did not kill him being certain, as they claimed in their saying "Indeed we killed the Messiah." Or "for certain" may be taken as an emphasis for His saying "And they did not kill him," like your saying: "They did not kill him truly," i.e. the truth of the negation of his killing is true. It was also said: it is from their saying "I killed the thing with knowledge" and "I slaughtered it with knowledge," when one exerts his knowledge fully in it. In this there is mockery, because when He negated knowledge from them with a total negation, by the particle of comprehensiveness, then it was said: "They did not know it with the knowledge of certainty and comprehension," and this is nothing but mockery of them. "Surely every one of the People of the Book will believe in him before his death" is an oath-clause that is an attribute of an omitted noun, its estimate being: "And there is not one of the People of the Book except that he will surely believe in him." Similar is: "And there is none of us but has a known station" and "And there is none of you but will come to it." The meaning: there is none of the Jews and Christians but will surely believe before his death in ʿIsa, and that he is the servant of Allah and His messenger; that is, when he witnesses it before his soul departs, at the time when his faith will not benefit him, since the time of obligation has ended. [[Mahmud said: "That is, when he witnesses it before his soul departs..." Ahmad said: Like the saying of Pharaoh when he witnessed the destruction: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe."]] And from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: al-Hajjaj said to me: "A verse, did you not recite it..." [[The text continues here: Mahmud said: "And from Shahr ibn Hawshab who said: al-Hajjaj said to me: 'A verse, have you not recited it...' " Ahmad said:]]

This interpretation is made less likely by His words: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾. Its apparent meaning is a threat. But what is meant by His words concerning this Community, ﴿and that the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾, is God knows best.]] Nothing of it has troubled my mind [[I have not found it. I say: it is in the tafsir (exegesis) of al-Kalbi, who narrated it from Shahr. I have seen it in an old copy of al-Mubtada' wa Qisas al-Anbiya' (The Beginning and the Stories of the Prophets) by Wathima, with its chain of narration through this route.]] meaning this verse. He said: "I am brought a captive from the Jews and the Christians, and I strike off his neck, and I do not hear that from him." I said: "When a Jew is present at death, the angels strike his back and his face and say: 'O enemy of God, Moses came to you as a prophet and you denied him.' He says: 'I believe that he is a servant, a prophet.' And to the Christian they say: 'Jesus came to you as a prophet and you claimed that he was God or the son of God.' He believes that he is a servant of God and His messenger, when his faith no longer benefits him." He said: "He had been reclining, then sat up straight, looked at me and said: 'From whom?' I said: 'Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Hanafiyya told me.' He began tapping the ground with his staff and then said: 'You have taken it from a clear spring, or from its source.'" Al-Kalbi said: "I said to him: 'What did you intend by saying, Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Hanafiyya told me?' He said: 'I intended to vex him,' meaning by adding the name 'Ali,' because he is well known as Ibn al-Hanafiyya."

And from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained it in this way. Ikrimah said to him: "If a man comes to him and strikes off his neck?" He said: "His soul does not leave until he moves his lips with it." He said: "And if he falls from the top of a house, or burns, or a predator eats him?" He said: "He speaks it into the air, and his spirit does not leave until he believes."]] . The evidence for this is the reading of Ubayy: ﴿except that they will surely believe in him before their death﴾, with the nun vowelled with a damma, in the sense: "And there is none of them but they will believe in him before their death," because "aḥad" (anyone) is suitable for the plural. If you say: what is the benefit of informing them that they will believe in 'Isa before their death? I say: its benefit is a warning, so that they know they will inevitably believe in him soon, at the moment of seeing, and that this will not benefit them. It is an incitement and an admonition to hasten belief in him at the time when it can benefit, and so that the proof is established against them. Likewise His words ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾: he will bear witness against the Jews that they denied him, and against the Christians that they called him the son of God.

It has been said: the two pronouns refer to 'Isa: meaning, "And there is none of them but they will believe in 'Isa before 'Isa's death," and they are the People of the Book who will be alive at the time of his descent. It is related that he will descend from heaven at the end of time, and no one of the People of the Book will remain without believing in him, until the religion becomes one, which is the religion of Islam, and God will destroy the Masih al-Dajjal (the false messiah) in his time. Security will prevail, so that lions graze with camels, panthers with cattle, wolves with sheep, and children play with snakes. He will remain on earth for forty years, then he will die, and the Muslims will pray over him and bury him [[Ibn Hibban and Abu Dawud related it through the narration of Hammam from Qatada from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Adam from Abu Hurayrah, in a hadith whose beginning is: "The prophets, peace be upon them, are brothers, sons of different mothers (ʿallāt) with one religion. I am the closest of people to 'Isa ibn Maryam, because there was no prophet between me and him, and he is descending. When you see him, recognise him: he is a man of medium build, inclining to red and white, with straight hair, as if his head were dripping though no water touches it. Between two garments (muḥaṣṣarayn), he will break the cross, kill the pig, abolish the jizya, and wealth will overflow, and he will fight people for Islam until God makes all the religions one in his time except Islam," to the end. As for his words at the beginning here, "No one of the people of the earth will remain but he will believe in him," al-Tabari related it as a saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both.]]. It is also possible that what is meant is that none of all the People of the Book will remain but that they will believe in him, because God will revive them in their graves at that time, and inform them of his descent and what was revealed for him, and they will believe in him when their belief no longer benefits them.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿him﴾ refers to God, the Exalted. It has been said: it refers to Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace.

O Allah, curse whoever reviled me and reviled my mother." So Allah transformed whoever reviled the two of them into apes and swine. The Jews then unanimously agreed to kill him, so Allah informed him that He would raise him to heaven and purify him from companionship with the Jews. He said to his companions: "Which of you is content that my likeness be cast upon him, so that he is killed and crucified and enters Paradise?" A man among them said: "I." It is also said: he was a man who was a hypocrite toward ʿIsa, and when they wanted to kill him he said: "I will show you where he is," and he entered ʿIsa's house, and ʿIsa was raised, and his likeness was cast upon the hypocrite, so they entered upon him and killed him, thinking that he was ʿIsa. O Allah, curse whoever reviled me and reviled my mother." So Allah transformed whoever reviled the two of them into apes and swine. The Jews then unanimously agreed to kill him, so Allah informed him that He would raise him to heaven and purify him from companionship with the Jews. He said to his companions: "Which of you is content that my likeness be cast upon him, so that he is killed and crucified and enters Paradise?" A man among them said: "I." It is also said: he was a man who was a hypocrite toward ʿIsa, and when they wanted to kill him he said: "I will show you where he is," and he entered ʿIsa's house, and ʿIsa was raised, and his likeness was cast upon the hypocrite, so they entered upon him and killed him, thinking that he was ʿIsa. [[I have not found it worded thus. al-Tabari narrated it through Asbat from al-Suddi, who said: "The Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'If you are truthful that you are the Messenger of Allah, then bring us a Book from the heaven as Musa brought it.' So it was revealed."]] So it was revealed. It is also said: (they asked for) a book to so-and-so and a book to so-and-so, (declaring) that you are the Messenger of Allah. And it is said: (they asked for) a book that we could witness as it descends. They only proposed this as a form of obstinacy. al-Hasan said: "Even if they had asked in order to clarify the truth, He would have given it to them, and what He had given them was sufficient." "So they asked Musa..." is the answer to an implied condition. [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "'So they asked Musa': the answer to an implied condition... etc." Ahmad said: This is one of the places where heedlessness has overtaken him, and his following of his desires has led him to the abyss of error. Therefore he named the People of the Sunnah, who hold that it is permissible and that it will occur in the Hereafter, in fulfilment of the true promise, "anthropomorphists" (mushabbihah). He was heedless of the fact that the Jews proposed to Musa (peace be upon him) a specific thing upon which they made their faith conditional, and did not consider the miracle as such, as it must be considered, and they said: "We will never believe you until we see Allah plainly." This proposal and obstinacy is enough to make them wrongdoers. Do you not see that those who said: "We will never believe you until you bring down to us a Book from heaven," or "until you cause a spring to gush from the earth," or "until you have a house of gold," how are they among the most wrongdoing of wrongdoers? And even if they only asked for things that were permissible, yet they prescribed for Allah concerning the signs, whereas their duty was to ground their faith in whatever miracle Allah chose. They began their speech with denial and negation. As for al-Zamakhshari's invocation against the People of the Sunnah with ruin and thunderbolts, Allah knows which of the two groups is more deserving of them. ﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews﴾, meaning: "for what wrongdoing of theirs?" The meaning is that We did not forbid them the good things except because of a great wrongdoing they committed, namely the great disbelief and major sins that have been enumerated for them.

The good things that were forbidden to them are what He mentioned in His words, ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾. Also forbidden to them were milk products. Whenever they committed a sin, minor or major, some of the good foods and other things were forbidden to them.

﴿And for their turning many away from the way of Allah﴾, meaning many people, or a great deterrence, ﴿and their taking usury, though they were forbidden it, and their consuming people's wealth by falsehood﴾, through the bribes they used to take from their lowly ones for altering the Book.

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾ means those among them who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. "Those firm in knowledge" means those who are established in it, who are proficient, and who have clear insight. ﴿And the believers﴾ means the believers among them, or the believers from among the Emigrants and the Helpers.

"Those firm in knowledge" (al-rasikhun) is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and ﴿believe﴾ (yu'minun) is its predicate (khabar). ﴿And those who establish prayer﴾ (al-muqimin) is in the accusative (nasb) as a praise (madh), to clarify the excellence of prayer. This is a broad topic, and Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian) divided it into examples and evidences.

One should not give heed to what they claimed about it being a grammatical error (lahn) in the orthography of the Mushaf. Perhaps someone who did not examine the Book (Sibawayh's Kitab) and did not know the practices of the Arabs, and their variety in the accusative of specification (nasb 'ala al-ikhtisas), has given heed to it. It was hidden from him that the foremost early ones, who are described in the Torah and the Gospel, were more ambitious in zeal for Islam and in defending it against attacks than to leave a breach in the Book of Allah for those who come after them to repair, or a tear for those who follow them to mend.

It has also been said: it is coordinated with ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾, meaning they believe in the Book and in those who establish prayer, who are the prophets. In the codex of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it reads "wal-muqimun" with a waw, and this is the reading of Malik ibn Dinar, al-Jahdari, and Isa al-Thaqafi.

This is a broad topic, and Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian) divided it into examples and evidences.

Perhaps someone who did not examine the Book (Sibawayh's Kitab) and did not know the practices of the Arabs, and their variety in the accusative of specification (nasb 'ala al-ikhtisas), has given heed to it. It was hidden from him that the foremost early ones, who are described in the Torah and the Gospel, were more ambitious in zeal for Islam and in defending it against attacks than to leave a breach in the Book of Allah for those who come after them to repair, or a tear for those who follow them to mend.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 163–166:

﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ﴾ is a reply to the People of the Book, concerning their demand that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bring down to them a book from heaven, and an argument against them: his revelation is of the same kind as the revelation given to the prophets who came before him. It is also read as ﴿زَبُورًا﴾ with a damma on the zay, the plural of zabr, which means a book. ﴿وَرُسُلًا﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb meaning the same as "We revealed to you," namely "We sent" or "We appointed as prophets," and the like. Alternatively it is governed by what is explained by "We have related to you." In the reading of Ubayy: "and messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you." It is reported from Ibrahim and Yahya ibn Wathhab that they both read ﴿وَكَلَّمَ اللَّهُ﴾ with the accusative. Among the strange interpretations (bid' al-tafsir, the odd exegetical opinions) is that it derives from the root kalm, meaning "wounds." [Mahmud said: "Among the strange interpretations is that kallama is from kalm..." Ahmad said: This interpretation is reported only from some of the Mu'tazilah, because they deny the eternal speech which is an attribute of the Essence. They affirm only letters and sounds established in bodies, not in the Essence of Allah, the Exalted. So their denial of the speech of the self is refuted by the fact that they thereby nullify the special distinction of Musa (peace be upon him) in being spoken to, since they affirm it only in the sense of hearing letters and sounds established in some bodies, and that is shared by Musa and by every hearer of these letters, including the polytheist about whom Allah said ﴿حَتَّى يَسْمَعَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ﴾ (until he hears the speech of Allah). The Mu'tazili is therefore forced to nullify the Mosaic distinction by taking the speaking to mean "wounding." Al-Zamakhshari spoke truly and fairly: it is among the interpretations from which understanding recoils and which reveal nothing but illusion. And Allah is the One who grants success.] Its meaning is: Allah wounded Musa with the claws of trials and the talons of afflictions.

﴿رُسُلًا مُبَشِّرِينَ وَمُنْذِرِينَ﴾: the most likely view is that it is in the accusative as a praise. It may also be in the accusative by repetition.

If you say: how can people have a proof against Allah before the Messengers? [Ahmad said: The Mu'tazilah's principle of rational goodness and badness drags them and emboldens them to establish the rulings of Allah, the Exalted, by reason alone even if He has sent no messenger. So they make things obligatory, forbidden, and permitted by their intellects according to their own claims. Among what they make obligatory before the revelation of the Law is reflection on the proofs of knowledge of God, and they do not wait for the obligating Law to arrive. Hence they are compelled, after much confusion and prolixity, to hold that whoever neglects reflection on the proofs before the Law arrives has abandoned an obligation for which he deserves punishment, and the proof against him stands regarding the obligation even if there is no Law. When this verse is recited to them, ﴿رُسُلًا مُبَشِّرِينَ وَمُنْذِرِينَ لِئَلَّا يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ عَلَى اللَّهِ حُجَّةٌ بَعْدَ الرُّسُلِ﴾ (messengers bearing good news and warning, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers), and they are told: this verse calls to you, O party of the Qadariyya, that the proof was established over creation by the legal rulings leading to reward through the sending of messengers, not by reason alone, what do you say about it? Their ears are struck dumb, and they alter the face of this text and change it from what it was meant for. They say: the meaning is that the messengers complete Allah's proof and alert people to what was obligatory before their sending through reason, as al-Zamakhshari answered. Close to this artifice they say, when the verse ﴿وَمَا كُنَّا مُعَذِّبِينَ حَتَّى نَبْعَثَ رَسُولًا﴾ (We do not punish until We send a messenger) is put to them. Al-Zamakhshari's statement that the proofs of tawhid and knowledge are set up before the sending of messengers, and that by this the proof is established, is sometimes used to mislead weaker readers of this section of his words, so that we suppose it runs according to sound principles, since knowledge is agreed upon and tawhid by consensus. Yet its path is reason, not transmitted report, which confuses them into thinking that reflection on the proofs of tawhid is the act of the responsible person and not a legal ruling. The ruling is the obligation to reflect, knowledge is received from pure reason, and the obligation is received from pure transmitted report, and by it the proof is established and reward is ordered. And Allah, glorified is He, is the Guardian of success and help.] and they are refuted by the proofs which Allah has set up, reflection upon which leads to knowledge, and the Messengers themselves did not reach knowledge except by reflection on those proofs, nor was it known that they were the messengers of Allah except by reflection upon them? I say: the Messengers are those who awaken from heedlessness and urge reflection, as you see the scholars of the People of Justice and Tawhid [He said "as you see the scholars of the People of Justice" meaning as the Mu'tazilah hold. They made reason the judge and made it sufficient for knowing the rulings, such as the obligation of justice and the prohibition of injustice. The Ahl al-Sunnah said: there is no ruling before the Law. The matter is well known in the science of legal theory (usul al-fiqh), so the question is built on the Mu'tazili position. (A)] together with conveying what they carried: the explanation of the matters of religion, the statement of the conditions of obligation, and the teaching of the laws. So their sending removes the excuse and completes the binding of the proof, so that they will not say: "If only You had sent us a messenger, so that he would rouse us from the sleep of heedlessness and alert us to what required awakening."

Al-Sulami read ﴿لَكِنِ اللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ﴾ with the doubled nun, ﴿لَكِنَّ﴾. If you say: the exception (istidrak, correction) must have something it corrects; what is it in ﴿لَكِنِ اللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ﴾? I say: when the People of the Book asked for a book to be sent down from heaven, and made difficulties about it, and the Prophet argued against them by saying ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ﴾, He said: ﴿لَكِنِ اللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ﴾, meaning: they do not bear witness, but Allah bears witness. It is also said: when ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ﴾ was revealed, they said: "We do not testify to this for you," and then ﴿لَكِنِ اللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ﴾ was revealed. The meaning of Allah's witnessing to what was sent down to him is His affirming its soundness by manifesting miracles, just as claims are established by proofs. The witnessing of the angels is their testimony that it is true and right. If you say: what do they answer if they say: "By what means is it known that the angels bear witness to this?" I say: they are answered that it is known through Allah's witness, for when He made known, by manifesting miracles, that He bears witness to its soundness, it is known that the angels bear witness to the soundness of what He has witnessed to, since their testimony follows His testimony. If you say: what is the meaning of His words ﴿أَنْزَلَهُ بِعِلْمِهِ﴾ (He has sent it down with His knowledge), and what is its place relative to the sentence before it? I say: its meaning is that He sent it down accompanied by His special knowledge, which no one else knows, namely its composition in an arrangement and style which every eloquent and skilled speaker is unable to match. Its place relative to what precedes is the place of an explanatory sentence, because it explains the witnessing, and that His witnessing to its soundness is that He sent it down in an arrangement that is miraculous and beyond power. It is also said: He sent it down while knowing that you are fit to receive it and that you will convey it. It is also said: He sent it down out of what He knows of the interests of His servants, containing them. 

It is possible also that He sent it down while knowing it, watching over it, and guarding it from the devils by a watch of angels, and the angels bear witness to this, as He said at the end of Surah al-Jinn. Do you not see His words ﴿وَأَحَاطَ بِمَا لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ (and He has encompassed what is with them)? Encompassing here means knowledge. ﴿وَكَفَى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيدًا﴾ (and Allah suffices as a witness), even if no one else bears witness, because affirming the miracle is truly testimony. ﴿قُلْ أَيُّ شَيْءٍ أَكْبَرُ شَهَادَةً قُلِ اللَّهُ﴾ (Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: Allah).
