(A)] together with conveying what they carried: the explanation of the matters of religion, the statement of the conditions of obligation, and the teaching of the laws. So their sending removes the excuse and completes the binding of the proof, so that they will not say: "If only You had sent us a messenger, so that he would rouse us from the sleep of heedlessness and alert us to what required awakening."

Al-Sulami read ﴿لَكِنِ اللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ﴾ with the doubled nun, ﴿لَكِنَّ﴾. If you say: the exception (istidrak, correction) must have something it corrects; what is it in ﴿لَكِنِ اللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ﴾? I say: when the People of the Book asked for a book to be sent down from heaven, and made difficulties about it, and the Prophet argued against them by saying ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ﴾, He said: ﴿لَكِنِ اللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ﴾, meaning: they do not bear witness, but Allah bears witness. It is also said: when ﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ﴾ was revealed, they said: "We do not testify to this for you," and then ﴿لَكِنِ اللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ﴾ was revealed. The meaning of Allah's witnessing to what was sent down to him is His affirming its soundness by manifesting miracles, just as claims are established by proofs. The witnessing of the angels is their testimony that it is true and right. If you say: what do they answer if they say: "By what means is it known that the angels bear witness to this?" I say: they are answered that it is known through Allah's witness, for when He made known, by manifesting miracles, that He bears witness to its soundness, it is known that the angels bear witness to the soundness of what He has witnessed to, since their testimony follows His testimony. If you say: what is the meaning of His words ﴿أَنْزَلَهُ بِعِلْمِهِ﴾ (He has sent it down with His knowledge), and what is its place relative to the sentence before it? I say: its meaning is that He sent it down accompanied by His special knowledge, which no one else knows, namely its composition in an arrangement and style which every eloquent and skilled speaker is unable to match. Its place relative to what precedes is the place of an explanatory sentence, because it explains the witnessing, and that His witnessing to its soundness is that He sent it down in an arrangement that is miraculous and beyond power. It is also said: He sent it down while knowing that you are fit to receive it and that you will convey it. It is also said: He sent it down out of what He knows of the interests of His servants, containing them. 

It is possible also that He sent it down while knowing it, watching over it, and guarding it from the devils by a watch of angels, and the angels bear witness to this, as He said at the end of Surah al-Jinn. Do you not see His words ﴿وَأَحَاطَ بِمَا لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ (and He has encompassed what is with them)? Encompassing here means knowledge. ﴿وَكَفَى بِاللَّهِ شَهِيدًا﴾ (and Allah suffices as a witness), even if no one else bears witness, because affirming the miracle is truly testimony. ﴿قُلْ أَيُّ شَيْءٍ أَكْبَرُ شَهَادَةً قُلِ اللَّهُ﴾ (Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: Allah).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 163–166:

﴿إِنَّا أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ﴾ is a reply to the People of the Book, concerning their demand that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bring down to them a book from heaven, and an argument against them: his revelation is of the same kind as the revelation given to the prophets who came before him. It is also read as ﴿زَبُورًا﴾ with a damma on the zay, the plural of zabr, which means a book. ﴿وَرُسُلًا﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb meaning the same as "We revealed to you," namely "We sent" or "We appointed as prophets," and the like. Alternatively it is governed by what is explained by "We have related to you." In the reading of Ubayy: "and messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you." It is reported from Ibrahim and Yahya ibn Wathhab that they both read ﴿وَكَلَّمَ اللَّهُ﴾ with the accusative. Among the strange interpretations (bid' al-tafsir, the odd exegetical opinions) is that it derives from the root kalm, meaning "wounds." [Mahmud said: "Among the strange interpretations is that kallama is from kalm..." Ahmad said: This interpretation is reported only from some of the Mu'tazilah, because they deny the eternal speech which is an attribute of the Essence. They affirm only letters and sounds established in bodies, not in the Essence of Allah, the Exalted. So their denial of the speech of the self is refuted by the fact that they thereby nullify the special distinction of Musa (peace be upon him) in being spoken to, since they affirm it only in the sense of hearing letters and sounds established in some bodies, and that is shared by Musa and by every hearer of these letters, including the polytheist about whom Allah said ﴿حَتَّى يَسْمَعَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ﴾ (until he hears the speech of Allah). The Mu'tazili is therefore forced to nullify the Mosaic distinction by taking the speaking to mean "wounding." Al-Zamakhshari spoke truly and fairly: it is among the interpretations from which understanding recoils and which reveal nothing but illusion. And Allah is the One who grants success.] Its meaning is: Allah wounded Musa with the claws of trials and the talons of afflictions.

﴿رُسُلًا مُبَشِّرِينَ وَمُنْذِرِينَ﴾: the most likely view is that it is in the accusative as a praise. It may also be in the accusative by repetition.

If you say: how can people have a proof against Allah before the Messengers? [Ahmad said: The Mu'tazilah's principle of rational goodness and badness drags them and emboldens them to establish the rulings of Allah, the Exalted, by reason alone even if He has sent no messenger. So they make things obligatory, forbidden, and permitted by their intellects according to their own claims. Among what they make obligatory before the revelation of the Law is reflection on the proofs of knowledge of God, and they do not wait for the obligating Law to arrive. Hence they are compelled, after much confusion and prolixity, to hold that whoever neglects reflection on the proofs before the Law arrives has abandoned an obligation for which he deserves punishment, and the proof against him stands regarding the obligation even if there is no Law. When this verse is recited to them, ﴿رُسُلًا مُبَشِّرِينَ وَمُنْذِرِينَ لِئَلَّا يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ عَلَى اللَّهِ حُجَّةٌ بَعْدَ الرُّسُلِ﴾ (messengers bearing good news and warning, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers), and they are told: this verse calls to you, O party of the Qadariyya, that the proof was established over creation by the legal rulings leading to reward through the sending of messengers, not by reason alone, what do you say about it? Their ears are struck dumb, and they alter the face of this text and change it from what it was meant for. They say: the meaning is that the messengers complete Allah's proof and alert people to what was obligatory before their sending through reason, as al-Zamakhshari answered. Close to this artifice they say, when the verse ﴿وَمَا كُنَّا مُعَذِّبِينَ حَتَّى نَبْعَثَ رَسُولًا﴾ (We do not punish until We send a messenger) is put to them. Yet its path is reason, not transmitted report, which confuses them into thinking that reflection on the proofs of tawhid is the act of the responsible person and not a legal ruling. The ruling is the obligation to reflect, knowledge is received from pure reason, and the obligation is received from pure transmitted report, and by it the proof is established and reward is ordered. And Allah, glorified is He, is the Guardian of success and help.] and they are refuted by the proofs which Allah has set up, reflection upon which leads to knowledge, and the Messengers themselves did not reach knowledge except by reflection on those proofs, nor was it known that they were the messengers of Allah except by reflection upon them? I say: the Messengers are those who awaken from heedlessness and urge reflection, as you see the scholars of the People of Justice and Tawhid [He said "as you see the scholars of the People of Justice" meaning as the Mu'tazilah hold. They made reason the judge and made it sufficient for knowing the rulings, such as the obligation of justice and the prohibition of injustice. The Ahl al-Sunnah said: there is no ruling before the Law. The matter is well known in the science of legal theory (usul al-fiqh), so the question is built on the Mu'tazili position. Say: Allah).

Those who disbelieved and did wrong: they combined disbelief with sins. [[He (Mahmud) said: "That is, they combined disbelief with sins... etc." Ahmad said: He deviates from the apparent sense; perhaps he is inclining toward inserting a strand of the corrupt doctrine concerning the obligation of punishment for sinners, and that they abide forever (in the Fire) like the disbelievers. This has been repeated from him. This verse rebuts that doctrine, for he made both verbs, namely disbelief and wrongdoing, a relative clause (ṣila) of the collective relative pronoun, so both verbs necessarily apply to each one of its members. Do you not see that when you say "The Zaydun (the people named Zayd) stood up," you have attributed standing to each individual of the plural? Likewise, if you conjoin another verb to it, it necessarily applies in the same way. And God is the Granter of success.]] Some of them were disbelievers and some were wrongdoers who committed major sins, since there is no difference between the two groups in that God will not forgive them [[His words "that He will not forgive them except through repentance" — this is the position of the Mu'tazila. As for the Ahl al-Sunna, a major sin may be forgiven through intercession, or through mere grace. (Ea.)]] except through repentance, and He will not guide them to a path, meaning He will not show them kindness so that they would take the path leading to Hell. Or, He will not guide them on the Day of Resurrection to any path except the path of Hell, ﴿forever therein, and that is always easy for God﴾, meaning there is no one to turn Him away from it.

"So believe, (it is) better for you. And (do not say "Three"; desist, it is) better for you." Its accusative is governed by an implied verb. The reason is that when He urged them to believe and to desist from the Trinity, He knew that He was directing them to a matter, so He said: "better for you," meaning: aim for, or adopt, a matter better for you than what you are in of disbelief and Trinitarianism, namely faith and monotheism. "Do not exceed the bounds in your religion": the Jews exceeded the bounds in belittling Jesus, peace be upon him, by making him born of an illegitimate union [[The phrase "born of an illegitimate union" means born of fornication; al-Sihah says: one says "he is of rushdah," the opposite of saying "he is of zinyah." (ʿ)]]; and the Christians exceeded the bounds in elevating him beyond his rank by making him a god. "And do not say of God except the truth": this is declaring Him free of partners and offspring.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad recited "innama al-Masih" with the pattern of al-sikkit (the Masih being read in the form "innama al-Masihu"). It was said that Jesus was called "the Word of God" and "a word from Him" because he came into being by His word and command alone, without an intermediary father or a drop of semen. He was also called "the Spirit of God" and "a spirit from Him" for this reason: he is a living being who came into existence without being a part of a living spirit-bearing thing, unlike a drop separated from a living father. Rather, he was brought into being by invention from God, by His sheer power. The meaning of "He cast it to Mary" is that He conveyed it to her and placed it within her. "Three" is the predicate of an omitted subject. If the report about them is sound, that they say: "He is one substance, three hypostases: the hypostasis of the Father, the hypostasis of the Son, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit," and that by the hypostasis of the Father they mean the essence, by the hypostasis of the Son they mean knowledge, and by the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit they mean life, then the implied sense is "God is three"; otherwise the implied sense is "the gods are three." What the Qur'an indicates is their explicit declaration that God, the Messiah and Mary are three gods, and that the Messiah is the son of God through Mary. Do you not see His saying: "Did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God'?" and "The Christians said: 'The Messiah is the son of God.'" The well-known and widely transmitted position from them is that they say there is divinity and humanity in the Messiah, from the side of the Father and of the Mother. This is indicated by His saying: "The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is only..." He thus affirmed that he was a child of Mary, connected to her as children are connected to their mothers, and that his connection to God the Exalted is in that he is His messenger, and that he exists by His command and originating power as a living body without a father. He denied that he is connected to Him in the manner of sons to fathers. And His saying: "Glory be to Him that He should have a son" is God's report, which is more trustworthy than the report of others.

The meaning of "Glory be to Him that He should have a son" is: He glorifies Himself with an exalting of Himself above having a son. al-Hasan recited "in yakun" with a kasra on the hamza and a raised nun, meaning: "Glorified is He; there is not for Him a son," so that the speech is two sentences. "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth" is an explanation of His transcendence above what is attributed to Him, meaning that everything in them is His creation and possession; how then could part of His possession be a part of Him? Moreover, partness applies only to bodies, and He is exalted above the attributes of bodies and accidents. "And sufficient is God as a Trustee": He entrusts all creatures with their affairs; He is the One who needs nothing from them, and they are the ones who are needy of Him.

(ʿ)]]; and the Christians exceeded the bounds in elevating him beyond his rank by making him a god. "And do not say of God except the truth": this is declaring Him free of partners and offspring.

[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: he will not scorn (to be a servant of Allah) and will not regard himself as too proud for it..." etc.] Ahmad said: The disagreement over whether prophets are superior to angels has been widespread. The majority of the Ash'ariyya (the followers of al-Ash'ari, a school of theology) held that prophets are superior. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr from among us, al-Halimi, and a group of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) held that angels are superior. The Mu'tazila made this verse their main proof for the superiority of the angels, in the way that al-Zamakhshari used it. With Allah's help, we will explain the matter fully from the standpoint of the verse. We say: the Ash'ariyya raised several questions against using it as a proof.

The first: our master Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to Jesus (peace be upon him), so it does not follow from the angels being superior to the Messiah that they are superior to Muhammad (ﷺ). This objection only applies if the one who cites the verse does not claim that each individual prophet is superior to each individual angel, and among our own school there is disagreement on this point.

The second question: his saying ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ is a plural form that encompasses the whole group of angels, so this requires that the group of angels as a whole is superior to the Messiah, but it does not require that each one of them is superior to the Messiah. There is also a point to consider regarding this question: if its basis is that the Messiah is superior to each individual angel, it may be said that it follows that he is superior to all of them, just as the Prophet (ﷺ), since he is superior to each individual prophet, is superior to all of them. No one among those who wrote on this subject has distinguished between superiority in detail and superiority in the whole. Some contemporaries did distinguish between the two kinds of superiority and claimed that superiority in detail does not necessarily entail superiority in the whole, but this view is not reliably attributed to him. If anyone did say it, it is refuted by a subtle argument: the superiority intended is, for the most part, marked by raising the rank of the superior in Paradise, and the hadiths on this are abundant. In that case, either the rank of one of the lesser ones is raised above the one who is agreed to be superior to each of them, or the rank of none of them is raised above him. The first is not possible, because it would entail raising the inferior over the superior, so the second is necessarily determined: the rank of the superior is elevated above the ranks of the whole group. Therefore, his superiority over the whole group follows with certainty from his superiority over each one of them.

The third: he joined the angels to the Messiah with the conjunction "and" (wa), which does not imply order. As for the argument that the second is always of higher rank, based on the example mentioned, it is countered by examples that do not imply this, such as a speaker's saying: "Neither Zayd nor 'Amr criticized me for this matter."

I say: and like your saying: "Do not harm a Muslim nor a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection)." This order is the normal form of speech, and the second is of lower and inferior rank. If you reversed this and said: "Do not harm a dhimmi nor a Muslim," so as to make the higher one come second, you would depart from the norms of speech and the rules of eloquence.

This example is among those raised to refute an established rule, but truth is more deserving than dispute, and there is no contradiction between the two examples.

We will introduce a preliminary explanation that removes the confusion and uncovers the veil. We say: the point in the order in the two examples that are thought to conflict is one and the same, and it requires in some places placing the higher first and in others placing it last. That point is the demand of eloquence, which avoids repetition and is free from descent. So when you adopt this, whenever it leads to your final statement being lower in rank than the first, or the final statement being contained within the first, which has already conveyed it, so that you are without need of the latter, then turn away from that to what is an ascent from the lower to the higher, and a resumption for a benefit not contained in the first. An example is the verse mentioned: if you were to take it that the Messiah is superior to the angels and of higher rank, then mentioning the angels after him would be like something unnecessary, because if the superior, who on this assumption is the Messiah, is a servant of Allah not scorning servanthood, it follows that whoever is lower than him in virtue is even more fitting not to scorn being a servant of Allah, and these are the angels on this assumption. Thus nothing new is added by ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ beyond what was already stated at the beginning of the speech. But if you assume the Messiah is inferior in relation to the angels, then you have ascended from glorifying Allah the Exalted, by saying that the inferior does not scorn being His servant, to saying that the superior does not scorn that either. It does not follow that if the inferior does not scorn, the superior does not scorn. So there is need to mention the angels, since the first does not imply the second. Thus the speech under this assumption has continually new and increasing benefits, and whatever is like this must be the reading imposed on the Mighty Book, because it is the pinnacle of eloquence. By this point, you must say: "Do not harm a Muslim nor a dhimmi," placing the lower after the higher, contrary to the order in the verse. For when you forbid harming the Muslim, it may be said: that is one of his special privileges, out of respect for Islam. So it does not follow from this a prohibition against harming the non-Muslim, from whom this special privilege has been removed. So when you say "nor a dhimmi," you have added a benefit that was not in the first, and you have ascended from forbidding some kinds of harm to forbidding more than that. But if you ordered this example like the order of the verse, saying: "Do not harm a dhimmi," the one prohibited would understand that harming a Muslim is even more included in the prohibition, since he shares with the dhimmi the cause of respect, which is humanity for example, and differs from him by a more noble and greater cause, which is Islam. This prohibition satisfies him, so there is no need for a further prohibition against harming the Muslim. But if you say "nor a Muslim," you have added no benefit and have not taught him anything other than what he already knew. You know now that it is one point which at times requires placing the higher first and at other times placing it after, and only context distinguishes this for you. I have no doubt that the context of the verse requires placing the lower first and the higher after.

From the eloquence arranged on this point is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾, which dispenses with prohibiting beating them or anything beyond it, by implication of the lesser. It does not befit the eloquence of the Mighty Book to intend a prohibition against something higher than mere "uff" and reproach, because that is needless, and the reflective reader of the verses of the Qur'an, with confirmation, needs no other witness than ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾.

Since fairness required conceding that the verse's requirement favors the superiority of the angels, and since the proofs for the superiority of the prophets were ready at hand for those who hold that view, he combined the verse with those proofs by interpreting the superiority in the verse as applying to a matter other than the point of disagreement. That superiority is the angels' strength, the vigor of their force, and the breadth of their capacity and power. He said: This kind of superiority is the one appropriate to the context of the verse, because the intent is to refute the Christians in their belief in the divinity of Jesus (peace be upon him), relying on the fact that he brought the dead to life, healed the blind and the leper, and extraordinary great signs occurred at his hands. So it is fitting to say: this one, at whose hands these extraordinary things occurred, does not scorn worshipping Allah the Exalted, but rather those who are greater in extraordinary acts and clearer in effects are the angels brought near, among whom is Gabriel (peace be upon him), whose strength and Allah's empowerment of him reached the point that he uprooted cities and carried them on a feather of his wing, overturning their upper part to lower. So the superiority of the angels here is on this basis, and there is no disagreement that they are stronger and mightier, and that their extraordinary acts are more numerous. The disagreement lies only in superiority regarding increased reward, honors, and elevation of ranks in the abode of recompense, and the verse contains no proof for that.

Since most of what confused the Christians regarding the divinity of Jesus was that he was created, that is, that he came into existence without a father, Allah the Exalted informed us that this one who came into existence without a father does not scorn worshipping Allah, and neither do the angels, who were created without father or mother. So their mention is delayed because their creation is more remarkable than the creation of Jesus. This is supported by the fact that Allah the Exalted compared Jesus with Adam (peace be upon them both), comparing the strange with the stranger and likening the wonder of His power to what is more wondrous: Jesus was created from a mother, while Adam was created without mother or father. Therefore He said: ﴿He created him from dust, then said to him: "Be," and he was﴾.

The basis of this discussion rests on the point I have indicated. Whenever the mention of a thing later includes a benefit not included in the first, by any means, whether superiority or other benefits, then the arrangement is sound and matches the form of the verse. And Allah knows best.

In sum, the matter is transmitted through revelation (sam'iyya), and certainty concerning it is known through the explicit text, which admits no interpretation, though finding it is difficult. May the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all.

How excellent is al-Zamakhshari's emphasis on his argument from the sending of the angels described as "the ones brought near." From this, the clear exposition of those who explained the matter of angels and prophets becomes evident. He did not generalize the superiority of the angels, nor that of the prophets, but made distinctions and then specified. The aim here is only to mention the possible meanings of the verse, not to investigate the disputes between the schools. And Allah grants success.

[Ahmad's commentary ends here.]

﴿nor the angels brought near﴾, from "nakaftu al-dam'" (I wiped away the tear), meaning: when I removed it from my cheek with my finger.

Nor is there anyone higher than him in rank, greater than him in standing, namely the cherubic angels around the Throne, such as Gabriel, Michael, and Israfil, and those of their rank.

If you ask: from where does His saying ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ indicate that the meaning is "nor whoever is above him"? I say: from the fact that the science of meanings (ilm al-ma'ani) does not require anything else. This is because the speech was directed to refute the doctrine of the Christians and their extremism in raising the Messiah above the station of servanthood. So it was necessary to say to them: Jesus will not rise above servanthood, nor will one who is higher than him in rank, as if it were said: the angels brought near do not scorn servanthood, so how much less the Messiah?

And a clear, manifest proof of this is the specification of "the brought near," because they are the highest of the angels in rank and the most exalted in station.

An example of this is the saying of the poet:

"Nor is one like him among those who rival Hatim in generosity, nor the sea of many waves whose surging waters swell."

[The commentary on this verse, from al-Zamakhshari's glossators, is as follows: "yaltaj" means its depths are agitated, and it is the bulk of its water. "Al-zakhir" means the risen. He says: no one resembling my patron among those who compete with Hatim in generosity, nor among those whom the sea competes with in bounty; that is, equals them in generosity. The sea is conjoined with "Hatim," exaggerating in describing his patron, that his like is not comparable in generosity, so it follows that he himself is also not comparable. Denying comparability of the like is a metaphor for denying it of the patron. There is also exaggeration in ascending from denying the rivalry of the most generous of men to denying rivalry with the most beneficial of things. The action in relation to the sea is figurative or by analogy (mushakala). Or the sea is likened to a person and rivalry is attributed to it by way of implicit metaphor (makniyya). This holds if "yujawid" is active. If it is passive, the meaning is that Hatim is not like one who is compared in generosity, just as the sea is not comparable in benefit, and so he is implicitly likened to the sea.]

There is no doubt that by "the sea of many waves" he intended something above Hatim in generosity. Whoever has taste, let him taste together with this verse His saying: ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians﴾, until he acknowledges the clear distinction.

Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, read ʿUbaydan lillah, in diminutive form.

It is narrated that the delegation of Najran said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Why do you disparage our companion? He said: And who is your companion? They said: Jesus. He said: And what should I say? They said: Say that he is the servant of Allah and His messenger. He said: He is not a disgrace for him to be a servant of Allah. They said: Yes, indeed. Then it was revealed: that is, Jesus does not scorn that, so do not scorn it for him. For if it were a matter of scorn, he would be more entitled to scorn it, since disgrace clings more closely to him. [Al-Wahidi related this in al-Asbab from Ibn al-Kalbi.]

If you ask: on what is the phrase ﴿nor the angels﴾ conjoined? I say: it may be conjoined either to the Messiah, or to the subject of "yakūn" (to be), or to the pronoun concealed in "ʿabdan" (servant), because it carries the sense of a description, indicating the meaning of worship, as when you say: "I passed by a man whose father is a servant." Conjoining to the Messiah is the most apparent, because conjoining to something else leads to some deviation from the purpose, namely that the Messiah does not scorn that he himself or whoever is above him be described as servants, or that he and whoever is above him worship Allah.

If you ask: you have made the angels, who are a group, servants of Allah in this conjunction, so what is its justification? I say: there are two aspects. One is that it means: nor does each one of the angels, or nor do the angels brought near, scorn to be servants of Allah, and this is omitted because "servant of Allah" indicates it, for the sake of brevity. As for when you conjoin them to the pronoun in "ʿabdan," then this question falls away.

[The reading "sa-yahshuruhum" is recited with the shin vowelled with damma and with kasra, and with the nun.]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 4, verses 173–175:

If you say: the detailed explanation does not correspond to what was detailed ([[Mahmud said: "If you say the detailed explanation does not correspond to what was detailed..." etc. Ahmad said: What is meant by "what was detailed" is: the one who did not disdain and the one who disdained, because both have been mentioned previously. Do you not see that the Messiah, the near angels, and those below them among the servants of God did not disdain worship of God, and they have been mentioned? What points to this is the emphasis of the pronoun by his saying ﴿all of them﴾ (jami'an). So it is as if he said: "He will gather to Him the near ones and others, all of them." And the verb connected to the pronoun occurring as the answer (jaza', the apodosis of a conditional) to his saying ﴿And whoever disdains...﴾ does not specify that the pronoun is restricted to those who disdain, because the link that connects the speech has been found, contained within this pronoun which includes them and others. In that case, what was detailed includes both groups, and its detailed explanation corresponds to it, and God knows best.]]), because it includes both groups, while what was detailed concerns one group.

I say: it is like your saying: "The imam gathered the Kharijites (Khawarij, early dissenting sect). Whoever did not rebel against him, he clothed and carried; and whoever rebelled against him, he punished severely." The soundness of this is for two reasons. The first: one of the two groups is omitted from mention because the detailed explanation indicates it, and because mentioning one of them indicates the second, just as one of them was omitted in the detailed explanation in his saying after this, ﴿As for those who believed in God and held fast to Him﴾, and the second [group]. The second reason: kindness to the others (the other group) is something that grieves them, so it falls within the category of punishing them. So it is as if it were said: "And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant, he will be punished with regret when he sees the rewards of the workers, and with what befalls him of God's punishment."

﴿Proof﴾ (al-burhan) and ﴿clear light﴾ (al-nur al-mubin): the Qur'an. Or he meant by "proof" the true religion, or the Messenger of God (ﷺ). And by "clear light": what makes clear and confirms it from the miraculous Book.

﴿Within mercy from Him and bounty﴾: in deserved reward and grace. ﴿And guide them to Him﴾: to His worship, ﴿on a straight path﴾, which is the path of Islam. The meaning: their being granted success and being made firm.

Narrated: it was the last of the rulings revealed. [[His words "it is narrated that it was the last of what was revealed of the rulings," i.e. the verse of Allah, the Exalted: (They ask you for a ruling...) etc. (Ghurar)]] The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on the road to Mecca in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, when Jabir ibn Abd Allah came to him and said: "I have a sister; how much of her inheritance do I take if she dies?" [[Al-Tha'labi reported it through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.]] It is also said: he was ill, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited him, and he said: "I am a kalala (one with neither ascendant nor descendant heir); how should I deal with my property?" [[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim) through the narration of Ibn al-Mundhir from him. The compilers of the Sunan also reported it, but in none of their narrations is there "then it was revealed: (If a man dies...)" except in Muslim, through the narration of Ibn Uyaynah from him, with the wording "then it was revealed: (They ask you...)" — the verse. (Benefit) al-Nasa'i reported through the route of Yazid al-Nahwi from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The last verse revealed upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was (And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah)" — the verse. In al-Bukhari, through the narration of al-Sha'bi from Ibn Abbas: "The last verse revealed was the verse on fornication." al-Tabari reported through the route of Yusuf ibn Mihran from Ibn Abbas from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "The last verse revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ) was (There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves)" — the verse.]] So it was revealed: "If a man dies..." The word "a man" (imru') is in the nominative, governed by a implied verb that the apparent word explains. The position of "who has no child" (laysa lahu walad) is nominative as a qualifier, not accusative as a circumstantial state. That is: "If a man dies who has no child," meaning a man with no child. By "child" is meant a son, and it is a shared term that may apply to a male or a female, because a son excludes the sister, whereas a daughter does not exclude her, except in the view of Ibn Abbas. By "sister" is meant the full sister (of the same father and mother), not the uterine sister, because Allah the Exalted prescribed for her one half and made her brother an agnatic heir, and said: "For the male is the equivalent of the portion of two females." As for the uterine sister, in the verse on inheritance she has a sixth, equalized between her and her brother, "and he inherits her" and her brother inherits her, if the matter is reversed, by her death and his survival after her. "If she has no child," that is, no son, because a son excludes the brother but not the daughter. If you say: a son does not exclude the brother alone, for the father is his counterpart in exclusion, so why did it limit itself to negating the child? I say:

It states the ruling for the absence of a child, and it leaves the ruling for the absence of a parent to the explanation of the Sunnah, which is his (ﷺ) saying: "Give the fixed shares to their people, and what remains goes to the nearest male agnate." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas with the wording "then to the nearest male." It was also reported by al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar. (Benefit) Ibn al-Jawzi said: the wording "agnate" ('asabah) is not known in this hadith.]] The father has priority over the brother, and the two are not the first of two rulings in which one is established by the Book and the other by the Sunnah. It is also permissible that the ruling for the absence of a child indicates the ruling for the absence of a parent, because the child is closer to the deceased than the parent; so if the brother inherits when the nearer heir is absent, it is more fitting that he inherit when the more distant one is absent. Also, kalala covers the absence of both parent and child together, so mention of the absence of one indicates the absence of the other. If you say: to what does the dual and plural pronoun refer in His saying "If there are two," and "if they are brothers"? I say: the original is: "If the one who inherits by siblingship is two," and "if the one who inherits by siblingship is males and females." It is said "if they are two" and "if they are" just as one says "whoever your mother is." Just as the pronoun of "whoever" is feminine because the predicate is feminine, so the dual and plural pronouns of the heir in "they two" and "they" are dual and plural because the predicate is dual and plural. By "brothers" is meant brothers, not sisters, giving precedence to the masculine. "Lest you go astray" is an object of purpose; its meaning is: out of aversion, lest you go astray. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Nisa', it is as if he has given charity to every believing man and woman, inherited a share, was given the reward of one who freed a slave, was cleared of shirk, and was among those whom Allah may pardon." [[Its chains were discussed at the end of Surat Al 'Imran.]]
